item.title: SALES: 8 best hotels in Ischia where la dolce vita comes naturally
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
We’re sorry to disappoint, but the secret’s finally out. For years, the beautiful little volcanic island of Ischia managed to evade the spotlight thanks to its close, glitzy neighbour Capri. With anti-trend hotspots firmly on the travel agenda, that’s changing. What sets this isolated rock apart from the competition? It’s a question of substance and that ghastly overused word, “authenticity.” Capri will always be the pretty one – the view from the Via Krupp and the Faraglioni as seen from La Fontalina are starlet gold – and the island of Procida took recent fame as Europe’s 2022 culture capital. Still, Ischia wins hands down when it comes to a rugged, fuss-free throwback. The best hotels in Ischia – among some of the best hotels in Italy – are juxtaposed with scenes of Italian nonnas hanging out laundry, religious street parades and zooming Vespas. It’s wondrously idyllic. Unlike the other Neapolitan islands, you don’t have to dig deep to find a dose of the real Italy. And now, finally, Ischia is having its moment. Here we share the best hotels in Ischia. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Ischia - For old-school Italian glamour: San Montano Resort & Spa Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page.

item.title: REVIEW: AGM Pad P3 rugged tablet review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The AGM Pad P3 takes a different direction from the majority of rugged tablets. It is slim, compact and priced to tempt. The Helio G99 and the HD+ screen keep its ambitions modest, but they are sensible compromises at this price point. If you want a tough tablet that does not weigh down a bag, this is the one to consider. - +Slim at 14.5mm and designed for one-hand use - -HD+ resolution is soft on an 8.68-inch panel Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Rugged tablets usually follow one rule. Make them big, make them heavy and hope the specification sheet distracts you. The AGM Pad P3 does not play that game. It is an 8.68-inch tablet that measures 232 x 146 x 14.5mm. That is thin for a device that claims IP68 and IP69K protection. It means the tablet can survive brief submersion and high-pressure water jets. AGM says it is built for one-handed use, and it includes an adjustable strap for hands-free carrying. Inside is the MediaTek Helio G99. It is an octa-core chip built on a 6nm process. It is paired with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. A microSD slot can add up to 1TB more if you need extra capacity. The SoC wouldn’t be classed as fast in 2026, but it has proved dependable in a lot of budget hardware, and it’s better than many of its competitors. Android 16 is the real surprise, since many rivals are still shipping with Android 14. And some of those won’t be getting an upgrade to the latest release. If this tablet has a weakness, it might be the screen. It has a 120Hz IPS panel with an 800 x 1340 resolution, and AGM quotes a peak brightness of 600 nits. That smooth refresh rate helps scrolling feel quick, but the limited resolution only supports 720p video playback. Connectivity is practical, but hardly concurrent. You get dual 4G SIM support and eSIM, plus NFC, GPS and WiFi. But there is no 5G, which will matter to some buyers and not to others. The 7,200mAh battery charges at 18W, so this is not a device you can top up in a hurry. On the back is a 50MP main camera, and on the front is an 8MP selfie, not great but not terrible either. The system supports at least Widevine L1, meaning Netflix and other streaming services can play in HD. So this is a compact, tough and affordable tablet. It makes sensible choices where cheaper rivals make clumsy ones with even older technology and lesser specifications. It might not be the best rugged tablet I’ve tested, but it represents good value for money. - Where can you get it? Directly from AGM Mobile To avoid confusion, this hardware has several naming options, including the AGM G3 Compact tablet and the AGM Pad P3, so I’ll use the latter. The AGM Pad P3 is sold through the AGM EU store at a price range of €299 to €329, depending on whether you choose to include a tablet stand. The store lists versions with and without a tablet stand. AGM is also running a promotion that includes a free stylus with purchase, although this wasn’t included with my review model. In the USA, you can get this hardware on Amazon for $235.99, and in the UK it’s £249.99. That is a lot of tablet for the money. It is also significantly cheaper than AGM's own Pad P2 Active, which lists at €369 to €408.90 in the same store. The Pad P2 Active still runs Android 14. The P3 is smaller, has a faster 120Hz screen and runs a newer operating system. Looking at the usual brand suspects for rugged tablets reveals that the Pad P3 may have found a niche, since most alternatives are more expensive, some excessively so. The Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 is closer to $500. However, you get a much better software ecosystem, guaranteed updates, Samsung Knox enterprise security, and an included IP68-rated S Pen stylus. Samsung also have the Galaxy Tab Active 4 Pro, but that 10.1-inch design is north of $650. A more affordable Samsung option is the Galaxy Tab A9 (8.7-inch), a tablet that mirrors the size of the AGM P3. It is incredibly affordable at around $175, features a great UI, and has mass-market accessory support. However, it lacks the smooth 120Hz fluid display, comes with only 64GB of storage, 4GB of RAM and lacks the processing power of the P3's Helio G99 chip. The two competitors that AGM is truly up against are Ulefone and Oukitel, with the Armor Pad Pro from Ulefone and the RT3 Pro from Oukitel. The Armor Pad Pro is only $220, and that price includes 8GB of RAM and better cameras, but the SoC is less powerful. The Oukitel RT3 Pro is the same price, comes with 4GB of RAM and 128GB of ROM, has only a 16MP main camera and runs Android 14. As with the Ulefone, it uses a less powerful SoC, in this case the G81. The bottom line is that as a new product, the AGM Pad P3 is slightly more expensive than the closest competitor options, but the amount of processing power, RAM, and the 50MP primary camera sensor more than justify the extra money. Most rugged tablets are built like paving slabs. The AGM Pad P3 tries to avoid that form factor, being only 14.5mm thick, making it slimmer than many ordinary tablets with a protective case on. My scales say it weighs 535g, although the official numbers are 540g, but that might include the provided strap. That is well under half the weight of the 8849 Tank Pad Ultra, which is a big difference if you carry a tablet all day. The smaller 8.68-inch screen is critical to the design, letting you hold it in one hand like a large phone. That suits tradespeople on a job site, delivery staff and anyone using a tablet on their feet. An included strap supports hands-free carrying, connecting via loops through slots in each corner. AGM offers an optional metal stand, which was included with my review machine. This relatively lightweight stand uses four tiny screws to secure it to the back of the P3. It offers a reasonably wide range of positions, from almost upright to nearly flat. In at least one position, it also supports the tablet in portrait orientation. My only concern with the stand is that the small screws might easily be lost if you decide to remove them outdoors, and without those you won’t be able to reattach it. The button layout is simple and predictable, with no custom buttons or special functions other than the power button and volume rocker. Because the buttons are small, there is no fingerprint reader, but it supports facial recognition from the front-facing camera. The SIM and microSD tray was one of my least desirable aspects of the P3. The rubber plug is thin and difficult to remove, and once it's shifted, you need to then find the tray ejector from the box to get the SIM tray out. It’s all excessively fiddly, and it might have been easier without requiring a tool. The tray accepts either two SIMs or a SIM and microSD, but as this tablet supports an eSIM, that’s hardly a significant limitation. The IP68 and IP69K ratings are the expected baseline, providing serious protection. IP69K adds resistance to high-pressure, high-temperature water jets. The AGM promotional material also cites a MIL-STD 810H drop test, but it doesn't say how far it fell or what surface it landed on. It’s normally impossible for reviewers to test devices to destruction, but the P3 looks like it could take some abuse and keep working. The Helio G99 is an old friend, as I’ve covered it in both tablet and phone reviews previously. It uses two fast Cortex-A76 cores and six efficient A55 cores on a 6nm process. The Mali G57 GPU is modest, but better than what you find in budget phones. The G99 is a platform for apps, maps, documents, and video, not demanding games. AGM has paired it with 6GB of RAM, which is adequate but not exactly indulgent. The 128GB of storage is equally fine, and the microSD slot means you can get more storage space if you need it. Cards up to 1TB are supported, although you can only use one physical phone SIM if you install a microSD. From a hardware perspective, the most compromised feature is the screen. At 800 x 1340 on an 8.68-inch panel, it delivers only about 180 pixels per inch. That is on the low side, making text slightly lumpy and fine detail in photos appears missing until you zoom in. On the plus side, the 120Hz refresh rate makes everything feel smoother than the resolution suggests. AGM claims a peak of 600 nits, and it can be bright, but the glossy display still makes it hard to see in natural outdoor light. If you can find a screen protector with an anti-reflection coating that fits, it might work better outdoors. As I mentioned in the intro, Widevine L1 certification is included, enabling it to stream HD content from most content providers. The only caveat to that is that the screen resolution doesn’t allow for anything higher than 720p, which has been designated ‘HD’ by marketing gurus. I wish this tablet had an HDMI port, where it could display 1080p to a suitable TV, because the tablet is undoubtedly capable of doing that. But given how many tablets have only Widevine L3 encryption, even expensive ones, AGM deserves recognition for using L1. The 7,200mAh battery is modest, but the screen is small, and the SoC is reasonably frugal, so it still lasts a decent amount of time. The snag is that the fastest charging you can get with the included charger is 18W. Some phones can charge at 55W, and some tablets take more power than that. In my performance assessment, I’ll cover how 18W charging affects speed. The last few points about the hardware in the P3 are that it has no 5G, though dual 4G SIM and eSIM support covers most uses. NFC and GPS are on board. Overall, not a spectacular platform, but one that is appropriate to its price and potential uses. The AGM Pad P3 has two cameras: The main camera is a 50MP unit by Omnivision, the OV50B40. For a camera sensor in a tablet, this one is reasonable, as it uses pixel binning to achieve better colour representation. But, in my testing, it didn’t care much for low-light conditions, resulting in grainy results. It is possible to take some good pictures with this sensor, but most are taken outside in strong natural light. As you can see in my indoor shots, this sensor tends to crush contrast and slightly wash out saturation below a certain lighting threshold. Looking at the drivers compiled for the Android distro on this phone, it suggests there might also be a 0.3MP focusing sensor, but AGM doesn’t explicitly mention it or list it in the phone's specifications. What it does mention for selfie taking is an 8MP BYD chip designed by that brand for cars, like parking cameras and self-driving functionality. With many phones now coming with Sony 32MP selfie cameras, this one appears to be intended as a cost-saving measure for the makers. What’s slightly fascinating is that the best video resolution available is the same for both front- and rear-facing cameras, that being 1080p. Although the rear can offer 60fps over 30fps on the front. The 50MP Omnivision OV50B40 specification says it supports video at 8K at 30fps, 4K at 90fps, 1080p at 240fps, and 720p at a whopping 480fps. However, the G99 can only process 2K (2048 x 1080) at 30 fps, but the camera app doesn’t have those as options. So what does it do with all those unused sensor pixels? It has stabilisation, which is useful for shooting on the move. Let us be realistic. Nobody buys a tablet like this for photography, I hope. It is a tool for documenting. Think site inspections, damage records and stock checks. What matters is whether the camera is quick, steady and legible. The primary sensor is good enough for that, and the selfie camera is acceptable for quick face-to-face conversations. The Helio G99 is no speed demon, but it’s better than the G88 that Ulefone used in its original Armor Pad Pro. That puts it in the middle of the budget field. The natural comparison was AGM's own Pad P2 Active, which uses the same chip, but there wasn’t much to gain from comparing such similar machines. The more interesting aspects of these results are to do with battery life, since the G99 is a 6nm chip, and the G88 is 12nm. The reduction in track size for the G99 provides greater power efficiency, and that is reflected in the nearly 20 hours it ran PCMark battery test versus the 15 that the G88 system managed. Admittedly, the Ulefone Armour Pad Pro still had 20% of power left, hinting at another two hours and 15 minutes of runtime. But given that the battery is 6.25% larger on the Pad Pro, it's still an impressive win for the Pad P3. Charging was abysmal on the Ulefone tablet, and while it's better on the AGM, it could still take between 2.5 and three hours to get a full charge using the included charger. I also noticed that if you use a high-end charger, like one of the Ugreen Nexode power packs, it actually charges slower than normal. Phones and tablets that are tuned to a specific charger is a recent development, and one I’m not keen on. Looking at these numbers, I expect everyday use to be fine with the Pad P3. The 120Hz screen helps the interface feel snappier than the silicon deserves, which is why I expect it was used. Android 16 is also a bonus, as it brings better security and, in theory, longer support. But AGM could improve Android update availability, since they’ve historically never made it a selling point. For tradespeople, delivery staff and field workers, the AGM Pad P3 is easy to recommend. It is tough, small and cheap. It also gets the details right that matter in daily use, like Widevine L1 and a modern version of Android. For everyone else, it is a sensible rugged option that doesn't cost much or take up much luggage space. At this price, one shouldn’t expect miracles, obviously. The shortcomings are plain. The screen resolution is low for the size. The Helio G99 is a budget chip, and 18W charging is slow. There is also no 5G, if that’s important to you. None of these caveats is a surprise at this price, but it's best to go into this with your eyes wide open. Compared with the AGM Pad P2 Active, the P3 is cheaper, smaller, newer and has a faster screen, but the same underlying SoC. It lacks the removable case of the older tablet. If you need something more powerful, bigger or with a projector, you should look elsewhere. Which device suits you depends on how much you value portability, because that’s probably the strongest aspect of the AGM Pad P3. Buy it if... At 14.5mm thick and with a small screen, it fits places that larger rugged tablets cannot. For those who need to hike to a remote location, or want to travel light, the AGM Pad P3 will be your lightweight companion. Widevine L1 means HD playback on major streaming services, so you can watch movies in at least 720p, not 480p. It’s only the screen resolution that holds it back from using 1080p sources. Don't buy it if... Don’t buy if... At 800 x 1340, text and images are not crisp, and it’s not ideal for reviewing video or still image captures that are at much higher resolution than the display. An 18W charger will take a while to fill the battery, so this isn’t the tablet you need for work and forget to connect to the charger the night before. Also, you need to use the charger that came in the box to get the fastest possible charge. A 200-lumen DLP projector, 120W charging, heavier at 1.6kg, but with dual 1000-lumen floodlights and auto-keystone correction. The issue is that this tablet is much more expensive, even if it has better all-around specs. Another practical, rugged design with an inbuilt camping light, with a slightly older SoC than that in the AGM Pad P3. However, it has better camera sensors and 8GB of RAM. And it has the uSmart expansion port that enables the attachment of endoscopes or microscopes. For more ruggedized devices, we've reviewed the best rugged phones, the best rugged laptops and the best rugged hard drives

item.title: REVIEW: Corsair Warthog case review: A rugged, military-themed chassis with plenty of airflow
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The Warthog’s rugged military looks are the standout feature of this mid-tower, but its higher price and noise-normalized cooling performance on the video card keep it from soaring above the rest - -Below average noise-normalized cooling for GPU - -Can’t mount rads in front and side simultaneously Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Fractal arguably kicked off the wood accent PC trend with the North line, and the company says its new Summit case is built for “...expressive, high-performance systems combining distinctive Scandinavian design and advanced cooling potential.” The chassis sports FSC-certified wood (timber verified to come from responsibly managed, socially beneficial, and economically viable forests) for details like the front surround and solid wood feet. There’s no doubt it’s a good-looking case, but if you want to show off the wood, you’ll want to stick to the Chalk White or Black versions, as it blends in with the Blackout SKU we tested. Corsair’s latest case, the Warthog, is a military-inspired chassis that resembles a fuel canister (jerry can) you’d see on military vehicles. Based loosely on the Vengeance C70 case from 2012, which looked more like an ammunition container, the new Warthog evolved into a much better-looking, more functional chassis for today’s hardware in either of the two colorways. The Warthog does resemble its predecessor, and Corsair borrowed some features from the C70 while updating the design with “...even more rugged exterior, significantly more expansion options, and an emphasis on excellent airflow throughout the chassis,” and the company largely succeeded. The Warthog updates include the InfiniRail Fan Mounting System for flexible fan mounting, a pegboard motherboard tray for custom cable management, room for today’s massive video cards (plus built-in GPU support), and three mounting locations for 360mm radiators and 13 120mm fans. It even has bump guards on the front I/O for that all-in military aesthetic. The fighter jet-style front IO includes USB ports, one fast USB 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port, plus an on/off button for a unique integrated light on the back of the case that illuminates the rear IO area and down. If you’re into the military look, the Corsair Warthog ($179) and Warthog RS ($199 with fans) absolutely nails it, with plenty of other features that make it a compelling mid-tower chassis. We'll cover more details inside and outside the chassis, showcasing the features and any issues we encounter during the build. We'll also run the case through thermal and noise testing to show how it performs compared to others and whether it could make our best PC cases list. Below are the case's specifications from Corsair. Externally, the Warthog doesn’t look like many other cases. Sure, it has the general shape of a classic mid-tower, but the front and windowed panel break up the monotony we’re used to, with bars resembling a fuel tank breaking up the window pane and front of the chassis. The front and side panels also use Corsair’s steel 3D-Y perforations (also found on the 4000) for increased airflow, and they look different from most other cases. It also has a military-inspired front I/O, sturdy built-in steel handles, and the familiar army olive drab color (it also comes in black). It just screams military industrial design. Looking more closely at the front of the case, we get a better view of the door that covers the front panel fans. We get a close-up of the contrasting black 3D-Y perforations, which not only look better than the typical circular holes, but are said (by Corsair) to allow 12% better airflow. Next to the red handle, Corsair stamps the model WX-01 in white on a thin crossmember in the upper-right corner (it’s WX-02 for the black SKU). Pull the red tab on the left, and it opens via two hinges on the right, revealing the magnetically attached dust filter. At the bottom of the front panel is the fighter-jet-inspired I/O panel, complete with bump guards and a flip-up cover over the reset button. On flight control panels, the guards prevent accidental activation of critical or dangerous switches. A flip-up toggle would be cool here, too. Port-wise, it has everything you could want. On the left is a 3.5mm audio jack for headphones and a microphone. Next to it is the recessed power light that glows red when powered on. Next to it is the USB 3.2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port. Between the bump guards are a square power button, the cool flip-up reset button, and the light button. All buttons feel solid under my fingers and not wobbly or cheap. On the right are two USB 3.2 (5 Gbps) Type-A ports. What’s here is typical fare, but it looks a lot cooler than most front IOs. The tempered-glass side panel doesn’t offer a full view inside. Instead, diagonal, crossmember-like ribs break it into one main viewable area, with two smaller triangles at the ends. On military vehicles, this reinforces the weaker glass while still allowing visibility. On the Warthog, it just adds to the rugged look, and maybe lets you get away with a little less time managing cables — I kid, clean up those cables! The panel is secured to the frame with two tabs at the bottom and four ball-and-socket joints at the top, two on each side. Pull toward you at the top to release, then pull up to remove. Simple, and it felt secure. The other side panel is solid, except for side venting. The venting matches the front and top panels with the 3D-Y pattern, but here it’s olive drab instead of the black we see everywhere else. Inside is another magnetically attached dust filter. The ‘service panel’ (stenciled in the upper-right corner) is secured the same way as the front, using tabs on the bottom and ball-and-socket joints on top. At the top of the case, there’s not much to see—just more 3D-Y perforations for airflow. Many cases let you easily remove the top for easier access to the Infinirail fan/radiator mounts, and the Warthog does too. Loosen the thumbscrews on the back, remove both side panels, and pull the nylon strap. Flipping the case around, we see the power supply sits at the bottom, and Corsair includes two captive screws for tooless mounting. Above it, seven vertical expansion slots offer plenty of room for large graphics cards and other expansion. The Warthog also supports vertical GPUs up to three slots wide, but you need a riser card accessory. Above that is space for up to a 140mm fan (120mm RS fan included for RS model), and to the left is the IO area. Corsair installed a small light above that shines down on the rear of the case, illuminating the rear IO area and back of the case, which is certainly useful when plugging in cables. On the bottom of the case, there isn’t too much going. The Warthog does have a removable dust filter that slides out from the windowed side of the chassis. I prefer this location because, if the filter pulls out from the rear, you'll likely need to move your heavy case to get it out. Inside the case, we see a single-chamber design with visual separation only between the power supply area at the bottom and the rest of the case. You won’t find a fancy air guide to feed the video card, but we do spy the small (but effective) adjustable GPU support strut. Beyond that, there’s nothing special at first glance. The motherboard tray has plenty of cutouts for wiring, but there isn’t much space to route connectors through. Sometimes you need to flex the frame a bit to get larger ones through, like the ATX connector. That’s not ideal, but it isn’t a big deal, even with a motherboard already mounted. The good news is there are no rubber grommets to pull through the holes. While we’re here, we also get a better look at the pegboard feature, which lets you custom-manage cables on the back side. For those planning to build a PC with rear-connect motherboards, the Warthog supports all of them (Asus BTF, Gigabyte Stealth, MSI Project Zero). Looking at the front of the case from the inside, we see the massive pre-installed 200mm RS fans that come with the “RS” version of the chassis. Corsair says the magnetic half-dome-bearing fans spin up to 1,000 RPM and move up to 135 CFM of air at a low 36.5 dBA. They are quiet and move a fair amount of air. The front area supports up to 3x120mm fans or radiators. Looking up at the ceiling from below, you'll see Corsair’s Infinirail system (also on the front, but hidden by the fans), which lets you slide and position fans and radiators where you need them. Although the case fits up to 3x120mm radiators here, they will protrude into the case and can cover the top of your motherboard in many cases. Be sure to mount your motherboard and connect the EPS plugs before you install a top radiator. At the bottom rear, you can see the power supply area, along with space to route cables for any headers along the bottom of the motherboard. The bottom chamber is also vented into the rest of the chassis. It won’t radiate much heat, since the power supply draws filtered, cool air from below. Opening up the other side of the chassis gives a better look at the side fan/rad mounts and the default cable-routing options. There is 50mm between the motherboard tray and the outside panel, which is plenty of room to route cables, even with reckless abandon. The pegboard motherboard tray, part of Corsair’s RapidRoute 2.0 cable management system, gives you plenty of freedom to move the cable-ratcheting strap mounts. From the back, we can see the motherboard tray mounting for your SSD and HDDs. Corsair uses a combo drive plate connected via a thumbscrew. You can install two 2.5-inch drives and one 3.5-inch drive on the combo plate, which should be enough for most users in 2026. Note that to access the back of your motherboard (to mount a cooler, for example), you need to remove this combo plate. Overall, I do like the look of this rugged, military-themed case, particularly in the olive drab colorway. The fighter jet-inspired front IO panel and jerry can-like look stand out among the played-out designs we’re used to, without looking like a failed attempt at abstract art. Inside, there’s plenty of room for components, even multiple radiators. That said, it is polarizing. Either you like the look, or you don’t. There isn’t much in between.

item.title: REVIEW: 8BitDo’s new Xbox Elite-style controller sets a high bar for customization
item.description:
Source: The Verge
It’s hard to make an Xbox controller that stands out these days, especially one that’s expensive, due to a wealth of great semi-affordable options. Still, 8BitDo’s $150 Ultimate 3E is a bold controller that holds its own against other feature-packed options. It’s made for Xbox and PC gamers who want a deeper level of customization and a more refined design than Microsoft’s pricier Xbox Elite Series 2 and 8BitDo’s own $60 Ultimate 2. 8BitDo’s new Xbox Elite-style controller sets a high bar for customization The retro controller maker’s first real swing at a premium controller feels great, but it doesn’t earn its high price tag. If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Basically every feature I’m looking for in a controller is here, plus some, including drift-proof TMR joysticks, extra shoulder buttons, rear paddles, motion control support, modular buttons and joysticks, a 3.5mm audio jack for chat or private listening, and a 1,000Hz polling rate over a low-latency wireless connection (only when connected to a PC). It includes a carrying case and a wireless charging dock that you can stash the USB dongle within. 8BitDo’s first premium controller competes directly with other big names, like Razer, PowerA, SteelSeries, and rising star GameSir. But the Ultimate 3E is also among the most expensive of the bunch, and I’m not sure the company delivers enough additional features to pull it off. The Ultimate 3E’s modular design opens up more customization than a lot of other controllers I’ve tried. It includes two four-button modules (one with membrane buttons and another with clickier microswitch buttons), two directional pads, and three extra joysticks. That level of customization and included accessories should hopefully help it age more gracefully than cheaper alternatives. Its TMR joystick mechanisms shouldn’t wear down, so you’ll only need to be concerned with replacing the joystick tops down the line, and the controller includes several to choose from. However, 8BitDo doesn’t sell replacement accessories for the Ultimate 3E, as it does for many of its other controllers, and it hasn’t responded to The Verge as to whether it ever will. The Ultimate 3E’s modularity also helps somewhat to make up for the high price tag. 8BitDo’s Pro 3 already lets you swap individual magnetically attaching buttons to accommodate different console layouts. The Ultimate 3E doesn’t offer as much freedom of per-button placement as the Pro 3, likely due to being intended for use with Xbox and PC, but the joy of using its microswitch button module makes up for the limitation. They’re sharp and clicky, although they have a bit more travel than I’d like. My other complaints are relatively minor. The clips that hold the face button module in place are very tight, and I found myself having to carefully use a plastic toothpick to pop them out. Similarly, swapping out joysticks requires a surprising amount of force, and I had to work up the courage to yank them off the first time. And, even when set to their higher response point, the triggers feel a bit soft and, like the membrane buttons, have more travel than I prefer, although the extra shoulder button can offset that travel distance in some situations. The soft touch grips and back gather dust and gunk pretty quickly, but you can at least clean the joystick tops by removing them. It’s as weird of a time to be releasing a new high-end Xbox controller as it is shopping for one. Assuming you’re not content with the solid but basic Microsoft model that’s around $50, it seems unwise to commit to spending well over $100 on one given the increased frequency of Xbox Elite Series 3 leaks. What we’ve seen of that, while unofficial, seems interesting: It doesn’t appear to offer the modular customization of the Ultimate 3E, but its screen and knobs might be what some people want in their next controller. As for how the Ultimate 3E stacks up to other great controllers, Microsoft’s Elite Series 2 is a poor value by comparison. It uses potentiometer joysticks that are likely to drift over time, which to me feels disqualifying given the price point. I don’t think anyone using 8BitDo’s Ultimate 2 should feel the urge to upgrade to the Ultimate 3E. There just aren’t enough differences to make it worthwhile. However, there’s also a non-modular 8BitDo Ultimate 3 for $99, which may end up being a sweet spot for more budget-conscious gamers who don’t need to tinker as much. For what it’s worth, I’ll be sitting down with the GameSir G7 Pro to play GTA VI. It’s one of my favorite Xbox controllers, and it has a nearly identical set of features and specs to the 8BitDo. Better yet, it’s only $80 at full price and comes in a variety of colors, with swappable faceplates for sale. Overall, the Ultimate 3E feels similar to use as other Elite-style controllers I’ve tried, and that’s impressive for a company that hasn’t tried to take on pricier competition before. Whether you opt for the cheaper Ultimate 3 with mostly similar specs or the pricier, more customizable Ultimate 3E, 8BitDo’s high-end gamepads make a strong impression, but they’re tough to recommend when there are cheaper alternatives that don’t slack on features.

item.title: REVIEW: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s Stranded mission had me hooked for hours, yet left me wanting more
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
For years, Call of Duty’s campaign mode has used big, scripted set pieces to tell the overarching story amid all the adrenaline-pumping action. The 2023 Modern Warfare 3 tried to shake up the established formula by introducing a handful of short open combat missions, and I genuinely liked the idea, but the game’s overall negative reception seeped into how those missions were received. I feared the next iteration might abandon the idea because of the backlash, but I am glad it didn’t. MW4’s “Stranded” mission uses the same approach, but instead of fragmenting it across the campaign, it puts it all in a single large-scale open-world mission. It’s easily the longest and most unique mission in the game. Stranded throws Call of Duty off the rails It’s easily the longest and most unique mission in the game. It might also be the one that shapes your opinion of the overall campaign. If you love the freedom to do things however you like, similar to an open-world RPG, this will probably be the highlight of the game for you. If you prefer the tighter, more linear missions, it will test your patience and push you well outside your comfort zone. I happen to fall into the first camp. The mission starts with your team on its way to drop into North Korea and destroy an artillery base near Rajin. Before you can reach the drop zone, North Korean anti-aircraft fire and fighter jets bring your transport helicopter down. You crawl out of the wreckage and make your way through the snow, dodging searchlights and patrols, until you reach an abandoned house with a basement. That basement becomes your base camp. One of the North Korean patrol leaders, instead of turning you in, offers to defect and points you to three nearby targets. The first is a jamming station up in the mountains, with scouts all along the climb, so sneaking up is the smart move. Then there’s a SAM site out in the open next to a village full of dug-in enemies, where I found it much easier to pick people off with a suppressed sniper before moving in. Finally, there’s an explosives bunker that’s cramped, dark, and half underwater, with flooded sections you have to swim through on night vision. Stranded rewards patience more than firepower Between them lies a vast area full of outposts, K-9 patrols, supply crates, and hidden bunkers. With a wounded squadmate back at camp, you also need to reach headquarters to plan an evacuation, but how you go about all of it is entirely up to you. Getting spotted has deadly consequences, as I learned more than once. Patrols sound a siren to alert nearby allies, and certain areas get a lot tougher once the alarm goes off. The atmosphere is brutal. It’s cold, snowy, and the wind never stops. Up near the mountains, visibility gets so bad you can barely spot an outpost until you’re right on top of it. That’s handy for sneaking up on enemies, but it sometimes works the other way around as well. One of the most useful tools here is a heartbeat sensor, which I kept equipped at all times. There’s also a looter-shooter side to the mission. You gather supplies out in the field and bring them back to base camp to repair your gear. A ghillie suit reduces how quickly enemies detect you, tactical gloves speed up reloads, and snow boots let you sprint faster. You can upgrade weapon attachments as well. You can even build special equipment like a mortar and a grenade launcher, both of which come in handy when completing your main objectives. I took my time and did as much as I could, enjoying everything this vast mission had to offer. It was a nice change of pace from the rest of the game. Placing it just before the final few action-packed missions was also a smart call. That said, I can see why Stranded doesn’t work for everyone. It slows the campaign right down at a point where the story is building towards its finale, and if you’re invested in what happens next, spending hours looting crates and clearing outposts can seem like a detour. The narrative of a squadmate bleeding out back at camp also clashes with the pace you’re free to play the mission at. The trips back and forth to base camp can get tedious, and after a while the outposts start feeling very similar. And for players who come to Call of Duty for tightly scripted, cinematic moments, a slow-burn mission in the snow can seem like it belongs in a different game entirely. Call of Duty could do a lot more with this idea Still, I think Stranded points to something future Call of Duty games could build on. DMZ already has similar scavenging and crafting, but it comes with PvP and the constant pressure of other players hunting you. A co-op PvE mode built like Stranded, with open objectives and no other squads to worry about, would be perfect for players who just want to jump in with friends and take things at their own pace. Stranded has already laid the groundwork, and I’d love to see Infinity Ward take it further. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is available on Steam, Xbox, PlayStation, and Nintendo. item.title: SALES: Experience crisp, clean-tasting water with top Brita filter pitchers
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
Which Brita water filter pitchers are best? Since nearly all of your body’s major systems depend on water to function, drinking the proper amount of water is one of the most important things you can do to maintain your overall health. Unfortunately, many people do not like the flavor or trust that the water coming out of their tap is clean so they purchase bottled water. A much better alternative is to simply filter tap water through a trusted system. Brita has been filtering water for over 50 years. The best Brita pitcher will hold enough water for your needs and still fit in the refrigerator if you prefer your filtered water to be cold. The Brita 10-Cup Standard Everyday Pitcher, for example, is a large-capacity pitcher that is capable of holding 10 cups of filtered water. What to know before you buy a Brita water filter pitcher Why do I need to filter my water? According to the CDC, the “United States has one of the safest water supplies in the world.” However, that does not mean that water contamination can never occur. Tap water can be contaminated by sewage releases, naturally occurring chemicals, fertilizers and pesticides, malfunctions and more. Additionally, many people simply prefer the taste of filtered water. If you want an added layer of safety or you prefer the taste, you may benefit from filtering your water through a Brita pitcher. How does a Brita pitcher filter water? In most models, when you fill a Brita water pitcher, the water starts in an upper reservoir and trickles through a filter to fill the pouring reservoir. The Standard Brita filter uses a mesh screen and activated carbon to filter the water and reduce undesirable odors and tastes. The Standard filters also feature an Ion Exchange Resin that captures copper, zinc and cadmium. The company’s Longlast+ filters have additional pleated material that can help reduce contaminants such as lead, asbestos and cadmium. Alternatively, Brita has a stream filter that filters water as you pour it into your glass, which means you can fill the pitcher much more quickly, but filling your glass takes a little longer. What to look for in a quality Brita water filter pitcher If you drink a lot of water, you will probably want a pitcher with a larger capacity. If the model you are considering only holds five cups of water and you like your water cold, you may find yourself refilling the pitcher before the water even has a chance to get cold. While Brita does an excellent job of making pitchers that fit in a refrigerator so the water can stay cold and refreshing, not all refrigerators are the same size. Measure the shelf height inside your refrigerator and check the dimensions on the Brita pitcher you are considering to make sure it will fit inside your refrigerator. To help remind you when it is time to change the filter on your Brita pitcher, most models now come with a filter tracker. This handy little device is built into the lid of your Brita pitcher to keep track of how many times your pitcher is filled up. When it is time to replace the filter, the tracker will let you know. If your tracker runs out of power, your water will still be filtered; you just have to manually keep track of when it is time to change the filter. How much you can expect to spend on a Brita water filter pitcher The general price range of Brita pitchers is $15-$45. How much water should I drink each day? A. According to the Mayo Clinic, men need to drink roughly 99 ounces of water each day and women need to drink roughly 74 ounces of water each day. These numbers, however, are estimates and can vary depending on the amount of exercise you do, your environment and your health. One of the best ways to tell if you’re getting enough water is to simply pay attention to your urine color – if it is clear or light yellow, you are probably properly hydrated. Do I need to clean my Brita water filter pitcher? A. Yes, you need to clean your Brita pitcher. While Brita doesn’t specify how often you should clean your pitcher – the manual only recommends that you clean your pitcher “periodically” – every two months is a good frequency as this can be done whenever you change standard filters. To clean your Brita pitcher, disassemble the pieces and wash each one by hand using mild dish detergent and a nonabrasive sponge. When finished, rinse thoroughly and allow it to fully dry before reassembling. Can I leave my Brita out on the counter? A. Yes. If you prefer your water to be at room temperature, it is fine to leave the pitcher out on your counter. Just remember to completely empty the pitcher every few days and refill to ensure that you are drinking fresh water. What’s the best Brita water filter pitcher to buy? What you’ll love: This Brita pitcher is designed to fit on a refrigerator shelf so you can easily keep your water cool. It is compatible with both the Longlast+ and Standard water filters, has a locking lid to reduce spills and is easy to pour. What you should consider: Some users found this model tricky to disassemble for cleaning. item.title: REVIEW: Ugreen LinkStation eGPU Dock review: Desktop graphics for your mini PC over a single cable
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
My RTX 3080 now spends most of its life switched off, and that’s exactly how I want it. For years, I’ve wanted my mini PC to game like a desktop without bringing back a desktop’s heat, noise, and footprint, and USB4 finally makes that practical. Ugreen’s LinkStation eGPU Dock puts a full-size graphics card on the end of a single cable, and after a few weeks of plugging it in only when it’s time to play, it’s become my favorite PC gaming accessory. The Ugreen LinkStation eGPU Dock is designed to deliver desktop-class performance to any USB4- or OCuLink-enabled system. With an 850W power supply capable of driving the most power-hungry graphics cards on the market, the LinkStation includes four standard 8-pin PCIe power connectors as well as the newer 16-pin ATX 3.1 connector required by GPUs like the RTX 50-series. - Built-in 850W power supply with 12V-2x6 and 8-pin connectors - Hot-plugging gives you on-demand GPU power - Performance depends heavily on the host?s USB4 implementation The Ugreen LinkStation eGPU Dock is available to purchase for $500 direct from Ugreen and Amazon. The Ugreen LinkStation sets up in minutes And it supports almost every modern graphics card on the market There is little to assemble with the Ugreen LinkStation. It comes basically ready to go out of the box, and I was up and running in under 10 minutes. Mine came with a single set of PCIe power cables stuck out of the side already. My RTX 3080 has three 8-pin power connectors, so I unscrewed the side panel of the LinkStation to find that there was another pair of 8-pin connectors hiding in there. In addition to that, there is also a 12V-2x6 (16-pin) ATX 3.1 connector in the same compartment coming out of the power supply, making this eGPU compatible with essentially all graphics cards up to the RTX 5090. Speaking of the power supply, the Ugreen LinkStation has an 850W power supply pre-installed and ready to go. The entire chassis is made of metal and feels extremely premium, too. The power button is right on the front (though there is still a power switch on the PSU itself) and the status light is actually really handy. When the status light is orange, that means that the eGPU is either powering up or not connected. When it’s white, the connection has been made to your computer. The cables all come out of the bottom of the unit. That’s where the power supply is, as well as the USB4 port. I would have liked to have seen the USB4 port on the back, but that’s my only nitpick of this entire system. In my review, I’m going to focus on using the eGPU dock to add an external graphics card to my PCs, but that’s not all this dock can do. Really, this is just an external PCIe interface for your computer that connects over USB4 or OCuLink. That means you could use it for something like a capture card, networking card, or anything else that either won’t fit in your PC case or just can’t connect to your mini PC any other way. This eGPU gives a small PC a big graphics upgrade Desktop-class graphics are just a plug away Over the years, I’ve had all different sizes of gaming PCs. I started with a normal ATX system back in around 2014, moved to eATX in 2016, back to ATX after that, to mITX in 2020, and then back to eATX after that. So, it’s safe to say I have used all form factors possible for my computer. That is, until I got a mini PC. I absolutely love how small mini PCs are, but they aren’t all that great at gaming. Take the Yoga Mini 11 as an example. I love that little system and the built-in Intel Arc B390 is actually fairly beefy for the size of system it is, but it still doesn’t have the performance that I’d like. That market is exactly what the Ugreen LinkStation eGPU Dock is designed for. This eGPU has both OCuLink and USB4 on it to plug into a wide range of systems. I tested it with three different USB4 systems (sadly I don’t have anything with OCuLink on hand to test it with) to see how the performance stacked up across all of them. I’m actually surprised at how much extra juice the Ugreen LinkStation added to the mini PCs I plugged it into. It was able to turn a system that could game decently into a system that could game amazingly, all over a simple USB4 connection. My Strix Halo system already has a pretty solid graphics card in it with the Radeon 8060S, so the 3080 won't be a big upgrade there. However, the Lenovo Yoga Mini 11 saw some sizable gains by adding the 3080 over USB4. For example, the Yoga Mini was able to (surprisingly) hit 55 FPS on low settings at 4K in Forza Horizon 5, and 37 FPS in Forza Horizon 6 using the integrated Arc B390 graphics card. With the RTX 3080 over USB4, it hit 123 FPS on low in Forza Horizon 5 and 73 FPS in Forza Horizon 6. Bumping up to the extreme preset in both games, frame rates jumped from 29 to 71 FPS in Forza Horizon 5, and 20 to 40 FPS in Forza Horizon 6. I keep my 3080 switched off until it's time to play Plug it in, swap the display cable, and game Two reasons I wanted to switch away from a big desktop to a mini PC were the heat and noise it generates. My main gaming desktop for the past few years has been a Ryzen 9 7900X with an RTX 3080. It’s big, noisy, and puts out a ton of heat when gaming. But it also puts out a decent amount of heat at idle, too. A mini PC takes up a fraction of the footprint, uses barely any power at idle, and hardly produces any heat by comparison. My problem with mini PCs was always that they couldn’t game all that well. I wanted a way to have on-demand gaming power when I needed it, but tuck it away when I didn’t. The Ugreen LinkStation works in that exact way. Because it’s USB4, it actually supports hot plugging. This means that the LinkStation can be plugged into a Windows mini PC with the system on and everything just spins right up. Now, I do have to swap my HDMI or DisplayPort cable over to the GPU once I do that, but that’s not a big deal. I’m able to keep the LinkStation powered off when I don’t need it, and then I power it on when I do. Having on-demand gaming power is something that I never expected to have, but I am so glad that I do. There are some games or programs that might need a reboot to fully utilize the eGPU, but most of the stuff I tested it with worked just fine with simply plugging it in. I even tested the LinkStation with an NVIDIA GPU on my ACEMAGIC M1A PRO+ AMD Strix Halo mini PC with the Radeon 8060S GPU in it and it worked perfectly without having to use DDU. I just plug the eGPU with my RTX 3080 in when I need it, and unplug it when I don’t. Whenever I do plug the LinkStation in, though, my 3080 springs to life—heat and all. Since the LinkStation is completely open on basically all sides, there's fantastic airflow and the 3080 is able to keep itself cool without much hassle. But, there's also nothing to block the noise. So, it'll be as loud as your GPU is. The power supply is quite quiet though, which is really great. I heard no whine from the PSU and the chassis never heated up. On a good USB4 link, you keep most of a desktop 3080 I'm surprised just how close the comparison is with PCIe Something I was immediately curious about was the performance comparison between using the GPU in a PCIe slot compared to using it in the LinkStation. Native PCIe has about 6.4 times more bandwidth (at PCIe 4.0 x16) than USB4 does. In my testing of the actual bandwidth, it was about 3.3GB/s over USB4 compared to 26.9GB/s over PCIe, so about eight times more bandwidth. This means there will be a huge performance loss, right? Wrong. Let’s compare the Ryzen 9 7900X desktop with my RTX 3080 hooked up over PCIe to my Ryzen AI Max+ 395 Strix Halo system with the RTX 3080 in the LinkStation hooked up over USB4 with gaming performance. Also, for all images or benchmarks mentioned elsewhere in the review, I ran every game at 4K using in-game presets with no upscaling or frame generation of any kind. In Forza Horizon 5, a fairly solid benchmark game for me, the Strix Halo system over USB4 saw 132 FPS on low, 114 FPS on high, and 77 FPS on extreme. The Ryzen 9 7900X system with PCIe saw 196 FPS on low, 160 FPS on high, and 106 FPS on extreme. Forza Horizon 6 is a much newer and more demanding game, and the spread was somewhat similar. The Strix Halo system via USB4 saw 76 FPS on low, 63 FPS on high, and 41 FPS on extreme, while the Ryzen 9 7900X desktop over PCIe saw 118 FPS on low, 84 FPS on high, and 63 FPS on extreme. These numbers are much closer than I expected them to be. I know that the RTX 3080 is an older GPU, but it still goes to show just how little difference there is in the performance for some titles. Your USB4 port matters more than your graphics card My desktop's USB4 ports didn’t actually give me the full experience As I said, I tested the Ugreen LinkStation with three different systems: a Ryzen Strix Halo mini PC, my Ryzen 9 7900X desktop, and the Lenovo mini PC. All of the systems were able to make a USB4 connection with the LinkStation. However, my desktop (with the ASRock X670E Taichi motherboard) made a link at half speed. This meant that the performance was quite degraded compared to the other systems. Running 3DMark’s Time Spy hid this difference because it also reports CPU performance mixed with GPU performance. However, in real-world games, the difference is quite staggering. I tested all systems using 3DMark’s PCI Express Feature Test to test the bandwidth that the eGPU was able to deliver over USB4, and I saw on average 3.2 to 3.3GB/s of bandwidth between the Strix Halo and Lenovo mini PCs. However, because my X670E Taichi motherboard only linked up at half speed, it saw just 1.5GB/s transfer speed. All three systems are labeled USB4 with 40Gb/s connection capabilities, but not all systems performed the same. This isn’t the fault of the Ugreen LinkStation, either, as I used the exact same cable for each test. I believe it has to do with the hardware and drivers on the system, and the Intel Thunderbolt controller that is used on the X670E Taichi motherboard specifically. How does that limit translate to performance? Quite sizable, actually. The Ryzen 9 7900X system (the X670E Taichi) only hit 53 FPS in Forza Horizon 5 on the low preset. That’s a fraction of the 132 FPS that the Strix Halo system hit, and the 123 FPS that the Lenovo hit. I wish there was a hard and fast rule I could tell you to follow to make sure that you can connect with a full 40Gb/s connection on the LinkStation, but I’ve not been able to solidify it sadly. Should you buy the Ugreen LinkStation eGPU Dock? The Ugreen LinkStation eGPU Dock is not cheap by any means. At $500, it’s a sizable investment to say the least. However, it does a great job at connecting a graphics card to any USB4-enabled system. I particularly love how it supports hot-plugging so I can just have on-demand gaming performance sitting on my desk that produces zero heat when I don’t need it, and is ready at a moment’s notice when I do. If you’re looking to boost the performance of your mini PC and make it into a better gaming system without buying a whole new computer, I think the Ugreen LinkStation is absolutely perfect for you. It does the job well, and there’s even an OCuLink port for a faster (64Gb/s) connection if you have a system that supports it. If you have a desktop that has a PCIe slot, I would skip it for gaming. It just doesn’t provide an experience that’s materially the same as or better than PCIe, so I would stick with that. Just put your GPU in the PCIe slot. However, for other PCIe-enabled devices (like capture cards), the eGPU would be fantastic.

item.title: REVIEW: Lenovo Googlebook 15 review: I’m glad that’s over
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
- The bundled AI Mouse is weirdly designed, but still neat - Decent performance among other Chromebooks and Googlebooks - Does it work with your phone? Who knows? Right now, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 and the Googlebook platform delivers only slightly more than what the Chromebook Plus or Windows PCs do. It doesn’t justify the additional price. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined My first experience with a Googlebook is complete, and I’m happy it is. I’ve tested the Lenovo Googlebook 15 as thoroughly as I need to, and I’d simply prefer moving back to a more familiar, better-designed device. In some ways, this is the Chromebook 2.0, intended to be an evolution of the platform. Still, I found that both the software and hardware frustrated me in their own separate ways. The Googlebook 15’s keyboard was simply unpleasant and unproductive, and I felt like I’d seen better displays. My other complaints were with the Googlebook platform itself, from its inexplicable inability to connect to Samsung and older Android phones, to the incoherency of its interface. I’m left with the impression that the existing Google Chromebook lineup does everything more effectively for less money. It feels like it was rushed to meet a deadline, when the whole experience could have simmered for a few more months while everything came together. - Storage: 256GB-512GB PCIe Gen 4 SSD (512GB as tested) - Display: 15.3-inch (2880×1800) OLED touchscreen, 120Hz - Camera: 5MP IR camera with facial recognition and manual privacy shutter - Ports: Thunderbolt 4 40Gbps (2), HDMI 2.0, 10Gbps USB-A, 3.5mm headphone/mic jack - Price: $1,099.99 to $1,149.99 ($1,149.99 as tested); Lenovo includes its “AI Mouse” in the box Lenovo Googlebook 15: Design and build quality Lenovo’s opening message is that this Googlebook is different. It makes that clear through the “gray” (white, really) colorway, which also appears on some IdeaPad consumer laptops. Two design cues stand out. The underside of the keyboard features a ripple effect that differs from the usual flat surface. On top, Lenovo and Google have included the Glowbar, the evolution of the “lightbar” found on Google’s earlier Chromebook Pixel from a decade ago. On that device, a hidden feature allowed the lightbar to function as a battery gauge. On the Googlebook, that functionality is now a full-fledged feature, with a green bar indicating a battery level above 60 percent. I vaguely recalled that the Chromebook Pixel had included a lightbar, so I went hunting to confirm. What I found were just reminders of how sturdy the Chromebook Pixels and Pixelbooks were, prompting comparisons to the MacBook. Lenovo’s GoogleBook 15 reminds me very much of the ceraluminum-based Asus Zenbook, whose plasticky construction detracted from an otherwise excellent design. Nothing really feels particularly special here, although there’s nothing particularly bad, either. Setup was a relatively quick process. This Googlebook seems to recline slightly further than most Windows laptops (about 35 degrees off of the horizontal). The middle of the keyboard tray noticeably sags if you press down in the middle of the keyboard, though that doesn’t affect typing. The lip from the webcam enables this Googlebook to be easily opened with a single finger. Lenovo has added one USB-C (USB4) on either side of the Googlebook, which allows you to place the power cable or USB-C/Thunderbolt expansion dock on either side of the laptop. That’s ideal for righties and left-handers, who can put their mouse on whichever side they choose. The two Thunderbolt connections allow you to connect a Thunderbolt 4 dock for additional ports. Lenovo Googlebook 15: The Google experience Google’s Googlebooks launched and immediately alienated a sizeable chunk of their audience, including me, for their inability to connect to Samsung Galaxy phones. That’s still the case, sort of — even though some recent Samsung phones are still supported, you’ll need Android 17 to connect them. My colleague Alex Wawro received a Google Pixel 10 Pro XL from Google as a surefire solution to show off the Googlebook’s ability to connect the two devices and, by golly, it worked! What a pain for such little payoff, though. After setting up the Pixel, I had to upgrade it to Android 17. Then I had to ensure that the two devices were close to one another, with Bluetooth enabled and both connected to the same Wi-Fi network. I then dug through this support document to make sure I was doing everything correctly. I connected the Googlebook to a “connected group” of devices (including the Pixel) and made sure to turn on the appropriate services. The two key services enabled by “connected devices” (or “Better Together”) are Cast My Apps and Continue On. The first lets you access your phone’s apps directly from your Googlebook, and Continue On lets you, well, continue tasks like web browsing from your phone on the Googlebook. Some of these features have been in the Windows Your Phone app for years, which connects to an Android phone running Android 10 or higher. Neither Cast My Apps nor Continue On really justify the purchase of a Googlebook. Cast My Apps allows you to see apps on your phone, such as a game. But both Cast My Apps and Continue On open in the same landscape window. Games don’t really render correctly. Even worse, the game felt laggier on the Googlebook (probably because of the connection) than the phone. If you Continue On with a web page from your phone, it will open in that window. There’s nothing really wrong with that, but it does feel like the Googlebook and the phone are separate experiences rather than the single cohesive whole I expected. My other feelings about the Googlebook Aluminium OS and what it’s like to work in it are summed up in my newsletter, which was written using the Lenovo Googlebook 15. I do like some of the features, including the ability to create your own widgets. Remember that a traditional Chromebook offers a “phone hub,” basically an earlier, more rudimentary version of what the Googlebook provides. Maybe it’s just familiarity with the Chromebook environment, but the Chromebook still feels more focused. Googlebooks have some good ideas, but they also feel like they’re struggling to find a reason to be. OLED displays intrinsically look “better” than their IPS counterparts (at least to me) because their high contrast ratios enable deep, rich blacks. I wasn’t able to test the display as thoroughly as I’d have liked because our display analysis software isn’t coded for the Aluminium OS. My light meter confirmed that the display brightness was 466 nits or about the 500 nits the display is rated for. I like Lenovo’s Googlebook 15 OLED display a lot more when the screen is in motion, especially when I was watching a video. The display’s bright colors really pop against a black background, and the audio (discussed below) really shines. Lenovo’s Googlebook is at its best when the workday is over and you can kick back with a video on YouTube or Netflix. During the workday, I noticed the speckling on the display. I’ve noticed this on some other OLED screens, too. Squint and you can make the individual pixels out. I never really noticed anything while working on a document (shaded in either black or white, depending on my system preferences), but my eyes picked it up on a gray background such as the Google settings menu. The Googlebook’s speakers compare fairly well to the competition, with no audible distortion up and down the audio spectrum. The volume delivers the oomph you need and then some, delivered from two user-facing speakers on either side of the keyboard. I couldn’t see any audio enhancement technology, however. While the sound was clear at high volume, there was no real separation so certain tracks were just mashed together. For watching movies or YouTube, however, I don’t think you’ll have any complaints. I really hate using this Googlebook’s keyboard. My guess is that my fingers simply reject the way the keys seem to “begin” at about the height of the keyboard tray before depressing. The closest approximation that I can come up with is that some stairs are mounted too closely together, and your feet (and my fingers) tend to stumble over them rather than actually stride naturally. I always try to write a review on the laptop I’m reviewing, but I gave up. I had to. I went back to what at the moment is my preferred keyboard of choice — another Lenovo. That’s the point: Lenovo typically has superior keyboards. This Googlebook simply doesn’t. I don’t dislike what Lenovo has done with the row of function keys, which are far more populous than other Chromebooks I’ve used. This Googlebook places Android-style “back” and “menu” keys to the upper left, along with the more traditional keys for screen capture, adjusting the brightness and sound, and so on. Does this Googlebook use a haptic trackpad? The specs say it is. Otherwise, it feels like a normal scissor trackpad but clickable across its full surface. Functional yet sort of limp. I was a little surprised by the overabundance of biometrics. You can log in using either your face or a fingerprint reader mounted in the upper right-hand corner of the screen. That fingerprint reader has no other purpose, however. I’m used to fingerprint readers doubling as power buttons and this one doesn’t. It just sits there, somewhat redundant, taking up space. That plays into another question I have about this Googlebook. The device just seemed to forget about face login midway through the experience. I set up facial login using the webcam, which requires a PIN for backup just like Windows Hello — no surprises there. Tapping the Google key plus L locks the device. Early on, the device would try to recognize me using the webcam. After a while, it asked for my PIN or a fingerprint instead. Deleting my stored face allowed me to “re-enter” it again, where it worked as expected. I found the webcam to perform well when reproducing my facial tone and hair, and the 1080p webcam captured detail quite well. I just found that some of the color accuracy was off, such as rendering my blue shirt as sort of a blah gray. Finally, Lenovo includes a “Lenovo AI Mouse” as part of the bundle, at least when purchased from Lenovo. The AI Mouse is a squat, wireless mouse with a small, round “Gemini AI” button below the scroll wheel. Pressing it launches the Gemini application. I liked the AI Mouse more than I would have thought, even though it’s designed for right-handers. A light bar runs along the periphery, adding a nice little accent. Lenovo made an odd choice, though. Clicking the Gemini button launches Gemini, but you’d think a long press would open the Magic Pointer application. Nope! That’s handled by the front side button, which serves as a “page ahead” control, while the other small button takes you back a page. It’s a strange choice. You can also control the mouse with the keyboard, thanks to a “mouse keys” shortcut in the Google settings menu. The numbers below will tell you one thing. My experience says another. Using the Lenovo Googlebook’s Chrome browser sometimes felt laggy and slow, even with ad-blocking extensions turned on. Dragging an open tab to its own window caused the browser to pause for a second before it reloaded the page. I also recall times when simply moving the windows around the screen felt slow. (That wasn’t always the case.) Chrome even asked to restart on occasion. On the other hand, I would try opening a web page and it would open immediately. The consistency was all over the place. Since these are Googlebooks, we don’t have the option to run PCWorld’s normal suite of executable benchmarks. Instead, we make do with browser-based benchmarks as well as a version of the PCMark productivity benchmark coded for Android. We use the same benchmark to establish an estimate of battery life, looping it over and over. For now, we have five Googlebooks, from Acer, Dell, HP, Asus, and Lenovo. We have already reviewed the $899 Acer Googlebook 14, plus the $1,199 HP Googlebook 14, and to that we add the slightly larger $1,149 Lenovo Googlebook 15. Note that the processor on the other Googlebooks differs in architecture, including the HP Googlebook, which uses a first-generation Snapdragon X Elite. For additional context, I’ve tested the Asus Chromebook Plus CX35 from 2025, which costs about half of the Googlebooks at $479. We measured performance via Basemark’s Web benchmark, which gauges graphics performance. To that we added Motionmark, a similar test that measures complex scenes at a fixed frame rate. WebXPRT uses a variety of HTML5, JavaScript, and WebAssembly tasks to produce a final score. Most of these scores are fairly close, evidence of the similarity of the processor used. The older Chromebook, however, uses a much older though still viable 13th-gen Intel Core chip. While the Snapdragon X Elite was a competent chip strictly from a CPU standpoint, anything that brings the GPU into play favors the Intel X86 architecture. Qualcomm’s graphics performance improved significantly in its second-gen X2 Elite CPU, but that wasn’t included here. Otherwise, the Acer and Lenovo Googlebooks are within a few percentage points of each other. The Chromebook Plus is 12 percent slower than the HP Googlebook in this test. Motionmark, which shows how well a browser can animate scenes at a fixed frame rate, is where the difference between the older Chromebook and the newer Googlebooks is most pronounced. In real life, you’d see smoother performance with whiteboarding apps, sites with animated layouts, and probably some 2D games. From the standpoint of processing most Web frameworks, however, all three Googlebooks are essentially the same. Here, there’s basically no difference between all four machines. That’s fairly significant, as WebXPRT is specifically designed to measure browser-based tasks. Anecdotally, this somewhat tracks. The CX34 just feels snappier and more responsive to use. Although my colleague Ashley was able to measure the battery life of the other Googlebooks, I just wasn’t satisfied that I had a reliable number. Googlebooks lack the sophisticated tools Windows laptops have to estimate or record battery life. However, the PCMark Android application includes a battery rundown test. It’s not directly comparable to the PCMark test we use on Windows laptops, as it appears to be more intensive. Still, it’s a consistent number… though the number certainly wasn’t impressive. Five hours and 26 minutes isn’t a lot of time. (Note that I was able to set the screen brightness to the same level that we use for our normal PC laptop testing, which provides a more relevant result.) Should you buy the Lenovo Googlebook 15? For me, it’s a pass. I just can’t get past how unfamiliar and unproductive the keyboard feels under my fingers, which is where my dislike for the Googlebook 15 begins. That surprised me, since I assumed going in that the Googlebook hardware would be something that I would just accept without much thought. I reviewed Lenovo’s $899 IdeaPad Slim 3i, which uses a similar, though slightly more powerful chip from Intel’s “Wildcat Lake” family. My takeaway was that it was marginally better, though it had its quirks as well. However, I just liked how the older $479 Asus Chromebook Plus CX35 felt under my fingers, and how snappy it was. I think there’s room for the new Googlebook features, but remember that the Gemini app is also available on older Chromebooks. There’s some overlap between the two platforms. Personally, I’d opt for an existing Chromebook Plus before buying a new Googlebook.
