item.title: SALES: Dell Pro Laptops for Small Business in 2026: Pro 3 or Pro 5?
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Quick Answer: For a small business, the Dell Pro laptop lineup offers two practical starting points: Dell Pro 3 for everyday office productivity on a budget and Dell Pro 5 for power-users on a growing team. Both laptops share Dell's fleet of business-security tools, up to 70Wh batteries for all-day productivity, and offer Copilot+ configurations with NPUs rated up to 50 TOPS. A 2025 report from the SBA Office of Advocacy, an independent office within the U.S. Small Business Administration, found that the U.S. is now home to 36.2 million small businesses—up from 34.8 million the year before—and they make up nearly 46% of private-sector employment. As those teams grow, so does the need for reliable, secure, and power-efficient work laptops. But equipping every employee with the right machine, from the front desk to the finance lead, can be a challenge. Dell’s answer is the Dell Pro line, with two natural starting points for small businesses: the budget-friendly Dell Pro 3 for everyday office work and the stepped-up Dell Pro 5 for power-users who need room to scale. Here’s how to figure out which one fits your team. Which Dell Laptops Are Designed for Business? Dell’s laptops for business are the Dell Pro line, which replaced the Latitude name in a company-wide rebrand in 2025. For small businesses, the Dell Pro 3 and Dell Pro 5 are the two main options, with upgrades aimed at everyday work such as spreadsheets, video meetings, AI research, and managing sensitive data. - AI-capable Copilot+ PCs: Select models feature built-in neural processing units (NPUs) capable of up to 50 TOPS (trillion operations per second), above Microsoft’s 40-TOPS threshold for Copilot+ PCs. The NPU handles on-device AI tasks such as background blur and noise suppression on video calls, which frees up the CPU and keeps that processing on the laptop. - High-density battery technology: Models leverage a new high-density battery technology, allowing capacities up to 70Wh and battery life up to 22.8 hours**, enough for a full day of meetings and client visits. - Built-in security and tech support: A shared security stack includes supply chain assurance, BIOS-level tamper detections, secure credential storage, and tiered tech support to keep your team up and running. Dell Pro 3 and Pro 5 Laptops at a Glance How Do the Dell Pro 3 and Pro 5 Differ for a Small Team? Both laptops are portable, reliable options for growing businesses in 2026. The Dell Pro 3 is designed for budget-conscious teams whose day centers on email, web applications, Microsoft 365, and accounting software. For frontline staff, client services, and administrative leads, it delivers efficient everyday performance and essential business features without paying for hardware they won’t use. The Pro 5 makes more sense for heavier multitasking, larger datasets, and creative work. It offers higher-end processors and graphics configurations than the Pro 3, making it an excellent choice for power-users and data specialists who need room to scale. Premium display options paired with crisp Intel Arc graphics or AMD Radeon graphics also make it a good fit for people who spend most of the day in video meetings or pumping out marketing presentations. The Dell Pro 3 and Pro 5 are both excellent choices for small businesses that utilize on-device AI. Current Core Ultra and Ryzen AI chip configurations include NPUs rated well above Microsoft’s 40-TOPS threshold for Copilot+ certification, enabling background blurring during video calls and meeting summarization tools, plus other local AI tools. While both the Pro 3 and Pro 5 offer up to 64GB DDR5 memory, the Pro 5 is also available with 64GB of super-fast LPCAMM2 memory, letting your team blaze through intense projects without lag. Can a Dell Pro Laptop Last a Full Workday on One Charge? Yes, the Dell Pro 3 and Pro 5 fleets offer battery capacities up to 70Wh, empowering your team to work off-plug for long hours, and on long flights, minus battery-drain anxiety. The Pro 3 can deliver over 20 hours* of runtime, 31% above the previous generation. While the Pro 5 can run up to 22.8 hours** off-plug, 56% longer than previous generations. When the battery is low, ExpressCharge lets your team recharge and get back to work quickly. What Security and Management Tools Come With Dell Pro Laptops? Dell Pro laptops come with built-in security tools such as Dell SafeBIOS and Dell Trusted Device, physical camera shutters, and chassis intrusion detection. Additionally, Dell SafeID with ControlVault stores credentials and biometric data in a dedicated, hardware-protected chip that is certified to FIPS 140–3 Level 3 security standards. What Support Does Dell Offer Small Businesses? Dell’s ProSupport is Dell’s technical-support service for business PCs, with remote diagnostics, AI-driven monitoring and self-healing automation, and 24/7 access to experts, so a small team without dedicated IT can keep its laptops running. Technical troubleshooting can be a huge time suck for small businesses so Dell offers two main tiers. ProSupport includes access to experts, next-business-day onsite repairs, and proactive monitoring. ProSupport Plus adds AI-driven self-healing and remediation, plus a Technical Customer Success Manager. The Dell Pro 3 and more scalable Pro 5 are excellent picks for your growing small business team. Find out more here. Disclosures: * Dell Pro 3 14 tested with Series 3 Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 70Whr battery, WUXGA 500 nits SLP display, 1x16GB memory and 512GB SSD. Based on testing using the Mobile Mark 30 battery life benchmark test in May 2026. ** Based on testing using the Mobile Mark 30 battery life benchmark comparing Dell Pro 5 14 and Dell Pro 14 Plus, April 2026. Dell Pro 5 14 was tested with Intel 336H vPro CPU, UMA graphics, 32GB LPCAMM2 memory, WUXGA Non-Touch OLED display (dark mode) and 70 Whr battery. Dell Pro 14 Plus was tested with Intel U5 236V vPro CPU, UMA graphics, 16GB LPDDR5x memory, WUXGA Non-touch Super Low Power display, and 55Whr battery. For more information about this benchmark test, visit www.bapco.com. Actual battery life may be significantly less than the test results and varies depending on product configuration and use, software, usage, operating conditions, power management settings and other factors. Maximum battery life will decrease with time. The stated Watt Hour (Whr) is not an indication of battery life. What are Dell's laptops for business? Dell's business laptops are the Dell Pro line, which replaced Latitude in 2025. For small businesses, the Dell Pro 3 excels at value-driven everyday office productivity, and the Dell Pro 5 makes sense for power-users on a scaling team. What's the difference between the Dell Pro 3 and Dell Pro 5? Both share Dell's business security and management tools. The Dell Pro 3 is designed for everyday office work on a budget and is rated at over 20 hours* of battery life. The more scalable Dell Pro 5 offers more silicon choices and power-packed configurations, plus up to 22.8 hours** of off-plug use. How long does the Dell Pro 5 battery last? Dell rates the Dell Pro 5 14 at up to 22.8 hours** of battery life when utilizing the 70Wh battery configuration, enabling your team to stay focused and productive enough to get staff through a full workday and back-to-back client meetings without a charger. Do Dell Pro laptops have an NPU, and do you need one? An NPU (neural processing unit) is a dedicated processor that can efficiently handle on-device AI tasks such as background blur and noise suppression on video calls, plus generative AI tools, mitigating the security risks of the cloud. Everyday office apps can run without an NPU, it’s most valuable for teams who regularly use Copilot+ AI features. Microsoft requires an NPU rated at 40 TOPS or more for Copilot+ PC certification. Dell Pro 3 and Pro 5 models with qualifying processors offer up to 50 TOPS. What security features are built into Dell Pro laptops? Dell Pro laptops include Dell SafeBIOS, Dell Trusted Device, a camera privacy shutter, chassis-intrusion detection, Dell SafeID with ControlVault 3+ that’s certified to FIPS 140-3 Level 3, plus select models offer presence detection, which locks the screen when the user walks away. How do small businesses manage a fleet of Dell Pro laptops? The Dell Pro 3 and Pro 5 use a single BIOS package per silicon vendor, meaning you can run a wide range of processor configurations while keeping device fleet management straightforward. Additionally, Dell Client Device Manager (DCDM) streamlines device management by integrating software updates, security, and compliance rules into a single tool.

item.title: SALES: 8 new Echo and Alexa smart home gadgets that Amazon just announced
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Amazon often likes to unveil a plethora of products at the same time, and it's done so again: we've got eight different product announcements to talk about today, and they cover smart displays, smart speakers, and the wider Amazon ecosystem. Most of these products are available now, though some can only be preordered at the moment. Read on for all the details and pricing — at the time of writing international pricing is slowly rolling out, so we'll add that here as it gets announced. The brand new Echo Dot — the speaker for "everywhere you can imagine" as Amazon puts it, from the kitchen to the living room — gets a host of upgrades. There's a new full-range driver here for improved audio and 50% more bass, the addition of a fourth microphone so it can hear you better, and room temperature detection. There's some custom Amazon silicon inside in the form of the AZ3 chip, which should make Alexa+ faster and more responsive, and the smart speaker is now both a smart home hub as well as an Eero Wi-Fi extender. It's available now in Graphite, Glacier White, Agave Green, and Coral Pink for $99.99 / £94.99 / AU$199. If your kids are after their own Echo Dot, Amazon has you covered here too. There's everything you get in the regular Dot, with a choice of either Octopus and Penguin designs, and a year of Amazon Kids+ (featuring podcasts and audiobooks, usually $7.99 / £6.99 a month if you've got Prime). The Amazon Kids Echo Dot is yours for $109.99 / £104.99. The Echo Studio is the Echo speaker you go for if you want the best audio possible, and the newly unveiled model adds a feature called Advanced Room Adaptation that "tunes the sound to your space". There's also now Adaptive Volume, so audio adjusts as you move about the room to maintain a steady level. Also — surprise! — there's now a camera embedded in the speaker. Amazon says you could use it to check in on pets or make sure you've switched the lights off. The camera can also be used with Alexa+, to get info on whatever you're holding, and with Fire TV devices if you want to put video calls on your television. As always, you can turn off the camera whenever you like. The new Echo Studio with Home Camera is now available in Graphite for $249.99 / £239.99 / AU$479, and the existing Echo Studio (without the camera or extra audio features) remains on sale for $219.99. The Echo Time is a brand new smart speaker series from Amazon, and looks to be a more premium version of the existing Echo Spot. Yes, it's basically an Echo Dot with a clock on the front, but there's also smart alarm functionality here to wake you up at the best point during your sleep cycle, and routine settings for winding down at the end of the day too. With a 3.2-inch touchscreen, you've got a bit of extra control when interacting with Alexa+ and other features, and Amazon says it's been specifically designed for the bedroom (there's no camera, you'll be pleased to know). The speaker is available now for $199.99 / £184.99 / AU$379, in Graphite, Glacier White, and Coral Pink. There's a kid-friendly version of the Echo Time available as well for $209.99 / £194.99, in either Galactic Grape or Cosmic Lime. As with the Echo Dot, the version for youngsters bundles in a year of Amazon Kids+ (usually $7.99 / £6.99 a month if you also subscribe to Prime), so there's lots of audio content to explore, plus wind-down content curated especially for kids. Amazon is going big with the Echo Show 16, which boasts a screen measuring 16 inches from corner to corner (as you may have guessed from the name). Amazon says its the "most advanced, versatile smart display" it's put out yet: there's a refined design, Fire TV functionality built in, and a choice of three new Screen Styles. These Screen Styles are basically different widget layout options, focusing on smart home controls, displaying photos, or acting as a family organizer (with calendars front and center). The device is faster than previous Echo Shows, Amazon says, and the 13MP camera lets you use it as a security camera and video calling device too. Amazon is opening up preorders for the Echo Show 16 now, and it'll be available "later this year". The standard smart display costs $499.99, while one with a special anti-glare Nanomatte layer (as used in the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro) is yours for $569.99. Alexa Home Map is exactly what it sounds like: a map of your home, rendered in 3D. The idea is you can see at a glance how your smart lights, speakers, displays, and cameras are set up, and control them with a tap on the map. You can start setting up the map through the Alexa+ app on your phone, though it's not rolling out until later this year. The Alexa Photo Frame tasks the Alexa AI with picking out the best shots from your Amazon Photos library, and displaying them on the 10-inch touchscreen — though you can also manually specify albums and people you want to see. New photos can show up automatically if you want, as they're added to your library. Alexa is always on hand if you want to request a particular image, and you can even add voice notes to pictures and send them to friends and family with their own Alexa Photo Frames. The digital frame is available now for $199.99 in Black, and $229.00 with a real Birch or Walnut wood frame.

item.title: SALES: I ranked 11 high-protein yogurts. My favorite had as much protein as a can of tuna.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
Protein has entered every corner of the pantry as consumers aim to build or avoid losing muscle. There's protein popcorn, protein cereal, and even protein water. If a food product did not already contain protein, it does now, thanks to gym bros, social media, and Ozempic. Yogurt is naturally high in protein, but some brands are taking extra steps to ensure their yogurts — or dairy snacks, as some are labeled — have as much protein as possible. To see if they actually taste good, I compared 11 different high-protein yogurts from my local store's dairy selection and ranked them from least favorite to top pick. I ranked the yogurts based on taste and protein content. I considered any yogurt with over 12 grams of protein per serving — the equivalent of two eggs — to be "high-protein." Other brands, like Fage, also offer vanilla-flavored high-protein yogurts, but I only ranked ones I could find at my local store in New York City. Do we really need to be this obsessed with protein? Probably not. But if you're looking for easy ways to help meet your nutrient goals — or you just want a delicious-tasting snack — here's how some of the top brands of high-protein yogurts compare. Too Good Blended is marketed as a low-fat, low-sugar yogurt; it contains 2 grams of each. A container costs $1.99, an average for single-portion yogurts. It has 12 grams of protein, equivalent to two eggs. To me, Too Good Blended tasted chalky. Upon opening the cup, it smelled tart, and I could see vanilla bean powder in the yogurt, suggesting the flavoring was on the more natural side. However, I thought the taste seemed artificial. The texture was a bit runny, even though the yogurt had some separated whey that needed to be mixed in. Even though it was a bit liquid, this yogurt felt dry and had a grainy texture. To me, it tasted like chalk. Also from the Too Good brand, Too Good Zero Sugar offers a similar yogurt, minus the 2 grams of sugar in the Too Good Blended. With 5.4 calories per gram of protein, this yogurt is the best of the 11 I tried for people looking to increase their protein intake while staying low on calories. I thought Too Good Zero Sugar wasn't much better than Too Good Blended. Despite its favorable nutrient values, Too Good Blended was nowhere near my favorite in this ranking. Compared to some of the other yogurts, it was tartier, runnier, and more artificial-tasting. Although I didn't love the taste, it was still better than Too Good Blended's. My go-to before this experiment was Chobani Greek Yogurt, a staple nonfat Greek yogurt. While I enjoy this regularly, after comparing it to so many options, I was surprised to see it rank so low in my ranking. The yogurt has one of the highest sugar contents in the experiment, at 9 grams per container, tied with Icelandic Provisions and Siggi's. It is also the least protein-efficient for those looking to stay low on calories while increasing protein intake. It has over 9 calories per gram of protein, which is higher than any other protein in this ranking. Yoplait's Protein yogurt offering was the most surprising to me, nutrients-wise. Being the cheapest of all 11 I tried, the yogurt packs a solid 15 grams of protein while having 3 grams of sugar. It's also a larger size, at 5.6 ounces per container, so in terms of volume, you get the most bang for your buck. Yoplait Protein surprised me. I was skeptical about how Yoplait's Protein yogurt would stack up — I typically consider it a traditional yogurt brand rather than a protein-focused snack. But I was pleasantly surprised. When I opened the cup, I was instantly hit by a strong vanilla scent that reminded me of ice cream. While the texture was both thick and airy, it was also a bit grainy, and I thought the yogurt tasted a little artificial and bland compared to some of the other brands. So while I probably wouldn't seek it out over others on this list, it's still a good snack option. Oikos' Triple Zero name tells you everything you need to know: The snack has zero sugar, zero artificial sweeteners, and zero fat. It's the only one on this list with both zero sugar and zero fat. It is also one of the more protein-efficient options at 6 calories per gram of protein. Despite its nutrient values, Oikos Triple Zero didn't wow me. Oikos Triple Zero had one of the most unique flavors of the yogurts on this list. When I opened it, I was immediately hit by a slightly funkier smell than some of the other yogurts. After mixing the yogurt, which had separated a bit, the Oikos Triple Zero had a very rich and full texture. Its vanilla flavoring tasted different than some of the others on this list — it almost seemed smokier. While I rated it the same as the Yoplait Protein, its nutrient values gave it a boost for me, hence why it's ranked higher. Another of my usual go-tos, Siggi's nonfat Skyr — a type of strained yogurt — had some of the highest sugar content on the list, tied with Chobani Greek Yogurt and Icelandic Provisions. The yogurt is also on the more expensive side at $2.39 for a regular 5.3-ounce container. Siggi's Skyr was very different from some of the less-yogurt-y options. Flavored with a visible vanilla bean, Siggi's Skyr had the best vanilla flavor of all the yogurts I tested. While it was very tart and not sweet at all — which surprised me since it had 9 grams of sugar — the vanilla flavor still shone through. In terms of texture, Siggi's reminded me a lot of ice cream, both in appearance and in feel. I'll buy this again, but out of the 11, it didn't make my top five. Dannon's Light + Fit yogurt was my favorite discovery from this experiment. Having never heard of it before, I was impressed by this nonfat yogurt, which packs 12 grams of protein in 80 calories. While it does have 7 grams of sugar, I found that the flavor in this yogurt justified it. Oikos' higher-protein yogurt offering, Oikos Pro, is a much more protein-dense offering, having 20 grams of protein in a 5.3-ounce container, or a little more than three eggs. The yogurt also has 0% fat and 3 grams of sugar. It is also, however, one of the most expensive, at $2.79 for a regular 5.3-ounce cup. It's tied with Ratio for the most expensive in this ranking, being a full dollar more than some of the other options. Oikos Pro is a perfect post-workout snack. When you open a cup of Oikos Pro, you smell mild vanilla, which translates into a very tasty yogurt with a flavor that stays on your tongue longer than others. The texture was also very rich and moist, while not being runny. This texture also made it the most filling of the yogurts I tested, and it would make for the perfect post-workout snack. While not labeled as a high-protein yogurt, Icelandic Provisions' Skyr has 15 grams of protein, placing it in the medium-high tier among yogurts. It's tied with Chobani and Siggi's for the highest sugar content, with all three at 9 grams. Icelandic Provisions was one of my favorites. Icelandic Provisions is a skyr yogurt like Siggi's. It is similar in taste and texture, but I found it a bit sweeter and less tart, with a nuttier flavor, which I really enjoyed. This rich, full-flavored yogurt was one of my favorites out of the 11. With a whopping 25 grams of protein — nearly as much as half a chicken breast — Ratio Protein had by far the most protein content of all the products I tested. It was also the most expensive, tied with Oikos Pro at $2.79 a cup. The product, labeled as a "yogurt-cultured dairy snack" rather than yogurt due to the added vegetable-based fats in its recipe, is also the most calorie-dense, with 170 calories per cup. While the Ratio recipe does not meet the FDA's definition of yogurt, its fermented nature, dairy components, and use of yogurt cultures earned it a spot on my list. I will be looking to Ratio next time I need a quick protein-dense snack. Ratio Protein differs from the others in this list. Its taste is much milder, and it lacks the signature tartness of Greek yogurt. The texture was also quite unique — I could best describe it as gooey. It's runnier and smoother than the rest, and its taste stays on your tongue for much longer. To me, this just felt like dessert, and I easily forgot that I was having a meal's worth of protein. While I gave this and the Icelandic Provisions a 9/10, the protein content and unique flavor and texture made me rank Ratio higher. Coming in at No. 1 is Chobani Protein, which has 20 grams of protein in a larger 6.7-ounce cup. While it's larger, its calorie content is in line with other yogurts in this ranking, like Oikos Pro, which has the same amount of protein. Like Oikos, Chobani Protein has about the same protein content as a 3-ounce can of tuna. While the individual cup is pricier per unit, the larger size makes it cheaper per ounce, comparable to Dannon's Light + Fit. Chobani Protein is one of three zero-sugar yogurts in this ranking, the others being Oikos Triple Zero and Too Good 0 Sugar. Chobani Protein was by far my favorite. I was a fan of Chobani Protein before coming into this test — the high protein content and name recognition frequently earned it a spot in my fridge — but I entered this experiment ready to find a new favorite. I didn't. Although some of the other yogurts I tasted were surprising and very enjoyable, I still found Chobani Protein to be the best. It is rich, thicker, and very filling. It has a hint of the signature Chobani Greek yogurt taste while skipping much of the tartness. I enjoyed the taste it left in my mouth the most out of all of the yogurts. The only downside to this favorite is its slightly artificial taste from the zero-sugar sweeteners used to keep its sugar content low, but if you can move past that, you'll have an amazing post-workout bite or on-the-go snack at your disposal.

item.title: SALES: 19 books like Rebecca Yarros' 'Fourth Wing' to read while you wait for the next 'Empyrean' novel
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
Patience is the name of the game for "Fourth Wing" fans these days. "Fourth Wing" introduced readers to Violet Sorrengail, a student at Basgiath War College training to be a dragon rider as war looms outside the school. The 2023 novel was an instant bestseller for author Rebecca Yarros, who has since written two additional installments in the "Empyrean" series, as well as a novella (more on that in a minute). After it was published in January 2025, "Onyx Storm," the third book in the series, became the fastest-selling adult novel published in the past 20 years, with over 2.7 million copies sold in one week. The "Empyrean" series is set to have five books in total, and the fourth will hopefully resolve the cliffhangers Yarros left in "Onyx Storm." However, while Yarros has confirmed she started writing book four, she has yet to announce a publication date for the novel. It will be a while before the next "Fourth Wing" book hits bookshelves, but luckily, fans can read similar novels, like those with fantasy settings or enemies-to-lovers romances. Ahead of the release of the next "Fourth Wing" novel, Yarros published "Threshing Day" in September, a collection of stories set in the "Empyrean" universe. Each chapter in the collection tells the story of a different character's experience on Threshing Day, when riders are selected by a dragon during their training at Basgiath in a process that is often dangerous for participants. Violet doesn't have a chapter in the book, as her Threshing Day is covered in "Fourth Wing," but the 13 chapters are all told by her fellow riders, including her partner, Xaden Riorson, and her siblings, Brennan and Mira. The collections span multiple years, and the book is chock-full of lore about dragons and their riders, answering some questions readers had about the "Fourth Wing" universe. It's the perfect appetizer to hold readers over while they wait for the fourth "Empyrean" novel. "A Court of Mist and Fury" by Sarah J. Maas If you've read "Fourth Wing," you're probably already familiar with Sarah J. Maas' "A Court of Thorns and Roses" series about faeries. The second book in Maas' series feels most similar in tone to the "Empyrean" series. In "A Court of Mist and Fury," Feyre Archeron is adjusting to her newfound life as a faerie after she almost died under the mountain — as well as coming to terms with the deal she made with Rhysand, the High Lord of the Night Court, to spend a week with him every month. Despite it all, she got what she wanted: an immortal life with Tamlin, the High Lord of the Spring Court. However, Feyre's life in the Spring Court starts feeling more claustrophobic by the second, especially when Tamlin forbids her from leaving the house. To her shock, she finds refuge with Rhysand, where she uncovers truths about the Night Court, Rhys, and herself that will change everything she thought she knew. "A Kingdom of Flesh and Fire" by Jennifer L. Armentrout "A Kingdom of Flesh and Fire" is the second book in Jennifer L. Armentrout's "Blood and Ash" series, and protagonist Poppy is reckoning with the realization that nothing in her world is what she thought it would be in the sequel to "From Blood and Ash." Poppy was raised as the Maiden, believing it was her divine duty to sacrifice herself to the Ascended, the immortal beings that rule over her world. After falling in love with her new guard, Hawke, and running away with him, she realizes she's been betrayed by the Ascended — and Hawke. Poppy doesn't know who to trust, but Hawke is determined to protect her — especially as Poppy develops powers that could change their world. If you're a fan of the magical school setting in Yarros' series, you will love "The Magicians" by Lev Grossman (which was also turned into a Syfy series of the same name). At the top of the trilogy, Quentin Coldwater feels apathetic about the future, though his aptitude for math could get him into any college he wants. Instead, he still longs for the simplicity of his favorite fantasy series, taking comfort in the magical world of Fillory whenever he can. When he gets accepted into a secret magical college, Quentin feels like his dreams are coming true. Then, he accidentally taps into a darker side of his power and starts a chain of events that puts him and his classmates in danger — and opens the doors to Fillory. "Divine Rivals" has the enemies-to-lovers fun and secrecy of Yarros' series, though Rebecca Ross sets her fantasy story against the backdrop of a newsroom instead of a war college. Iris Winnow is desperate to get promoted to columnist at the Oath Gazette. Her mother has fallen into alcoholism since her brother left to fight in a war of the gods, and Iris feels like she is one missed paycheck away from falling into ruin. She's competing for the promotion against Roman Kitt, her infuriatingly handsome coworker who makes her feel small every time she sees him. As Roman continues to succeed, her chances of success grow slimmer with each passing day. Iris' only comfort is writing letters to her brother on her grandmother's old typewriter. She doesn't know where he is, so she slips the letters under her wardrobe, where they disappear. Iris is hopeful her letters are somehow reaching her brother — until a stranger writes back. Ross' story evolves into a fantasy full of romance and longing, which continues in its sequel, "Ruthless Vows." "The Serpent and the Wings of Night" by Carissa Broadbent You'll love the first book in Carissa Broadbent's "Crowns of Nyaxia" series, "The Serpent and the Wings of Night," if Violet's perseverance drew you to the "Empyrean" series as much as her romance with Xaden did. Oraya has spent every moment of her life fighting to stay alive since her father, the Nightborn vampire king, adopted her after his forces killed her entire human family when she was a child. Oraya is sick of being mortal in a world of vampires ready to kill her, so she decides to enter the Kejari, a tournament where the winner gets a wish granted to them by the goddess it's named for. She plans to avoid the vampires competing against her at all costs, but when she is forced into an alliance with Rhain, a handsome vampire she knows nothing about, Oraya will have to trust someone besides her father for the first time in years. The competition is deadly, especially as war looms beyond the arena, but Oraya's attraction to Rhain may be an even bigger danger. If you somehow missed the "Divergent" craze when Veronica Roth's books or the films based on them were released, it's the perfect series to binge while you wait for the fourth "Empyrean" book. In the first installment of the series, readers are introduced to 16-year-old Beatrice Prior, a girl on the precipice of changing her life forever. Beatrice lives in a society divided into factions based on people's aptitudes, and it's her turn to take a test that will tell her which faction she belongs to. Beatrice's results put her entire society's system at risk, and the only way she can survive is to keep her results a secret. She abandons her home faction of Abnegation to join Dauntless, hoping she can hide in the group that values bravery and strength above all else. But she's not the only one with secrets. Those drawn to the romantic tension of the "Empyrean" series might want to put "One Dark Window" by Rachel Gillig at the top of their to-be-read list. The only thing keeping Elspeth Spindle safe in her home of Blunder, a land cursed with darkness, is the monster she calls Nightmare, a spirit trapped in her mind. Elspeth's long-kept secret falls apart when she has a run-in with a highwayman, who turns out to be the king's nephew and captain of the guard working in secret to overthrow his uncle. Elspeth agrees to help the captain and his family in their quest to end the dark magic that rules their kingdom once and for all, even if it puts her own life at risk and forces her to face the Nightmare's power over her. Elspeth and the captain are on a time crunch to accomplish their mission, particularly as the Nightmare threatens to take her mind over for good. Still, they can't ignore the attraction between them, no matter the dangers coming their way. If the dragons in Yarros' fictional world were the most exciting part of "Fourth Wing" and "Iron Flame" for you, you may want to give Naomi Novik's "His Majesty's Dragon" a try. The novel is set in the 1800s during the Napoleonic Wars. Will Laurence is a normal captain in the British forces until he captures a dragon egg. When it hatches, he bonds with Temeraire and becomes a rider, fighting in the skies. Laurence will have to learn how to fly and fight in the middle of the war — or risk his and Temeraire's lives. "The Inheritance Cycle" series by Christopher Paolini may fall into the young-adult category, but the high-fantasy writing and the emotional coming-of-age journey the hero goes on throughout the series will make it just as exciting for adults as for younger readers. In the series opener, Eragon is just a teenager living a simple life on a farm with his family until he stumbles upon a blue stone, which turns out to be the first dragon hatchling born in his country in a century. Eragon immediately becomes a Dragon Rider when his dragon, Seraphina, hatches. The only living rider is supposed to be king, setting Eragon on a path of magic and danger. Like Yarros' series, "The Inheritance Cycle" is an epic journey of dragons and their riders, full of magic, romance, and adventure. Amanda Bouchet's "The Kingmaker Chronicles" is a three-part series full of magic, gods, and romance that will appeal to Yarros fans drawn to Violet's powerful signet and Xaden's dedication to her. In the first installment, "A Promise of Fire," Cat Fisa has been on the run for years. She was born with the ability to tell when people are lying, a once-in-a-generation power that makes her the "Kingmaker." Cat wants nothing to do with her power — or her family in the North that would use her for it — so she stays hidden, pretending to be a soothsayer in a traveling circus in the South. When Griffin, the general of a newly established human kingdom, sees her, he knows what Cat is immediately and takes her in the hopes of protecting his family's throne. Cat won't go down without a fight, though, and Griffin's hostage becomes even harder to control when powerful family members come looking for her. As they make their way toward his family's castle, Griffin will have to convince Cat his family is worth working with — a task that becomes even more difficult when he realizes he doesn't want Cat to just work with him; he wants her to be his wife. "House of Earth and Blood" by Sarah J. Maas If you liked the modern flair in the "Empyrean" series, you'll love Sarah J. Maas' steamy "Crescent City" series. In "House of Earth and Blood," half-fae Bryce Quinlan thrives after graduating from Crescent City University, living with her best friend, the werewolf and alpha of the Pack of Devils, Danika Fendyr. Bryce has everything she wants — until she comes home to find Danika and the Pack of Devils murdered by a demon. She thinks the culprit was arrested, but a year later, similar murders start up again in the city. Because she's the only one who saw the demon that killed her friends, Bryce teams up with Hunt Athalar, a Fallen angel enslaved to work for the Archangels who run Crescent City, to solve the mystery. As the investigation progresses and Bryce and Hunt's attraction to each other grows, the unlikely pair will discover secrets about Crescent City that could upend their world as they know it. To date, Maas has published three books in the series, including "House of Flame and Shadow" in January 2024. As Violet was raised to hate Xaden Riorson, Persephone Dimitriou's fear of Hades was instilled in her from childhood in "Neon Gods" by Katee Robert. Trusting Hades feels like Persephone's only option after her mother promises her hand in marriage to Zeus, the leader of the 13 houses in Olympus, whose wives mysteriously end up dead. Persephone decides to run away from the city rather than marry Zeus, seeking refuge with Hades, a man she wasn't even certain existed until she found herself on his doorstep. Luckily, Hades wants revenge on Zeus, too, and they agree that making him jealous is the best way to do it. Hades and Persephone decide to put on a show, but neither expects the real, palpable attraction that develops between them. A.K. Caggiano's "Villains & Virtues" trilogy has all the magic and enemies-to-lovers fun of the world of "Fourth Wing" with a heap of slow-burn tension and a lighter tone than Yarros' work. In "Throne in the Dark," Damien Maleficus Bloodthorne is determined to free his demon father from his magical imprisonment and take over the world by his side. There's just one problem: a beautiful, sickeningly sweet human named Amma, who accidentally becomes one with the magical weapon he needs to bring down the mortal powers that be. Damien has no choice but to travel the realm with Amma to find a way to separate her from the weapon. He could kill her, but Amma proves to be surprisingly helpful — and to his horror, she isn't the worst travel companion he could imagine. Amma has secrets of her own, though, and she and Damien must work together to get through their respective missions unscathed. And worst of all, as he spends more time with Amma, Damien starts to wonder if what he truly wants is the human by his side. Ali Hazelwood is best known for her New York Times bestselling, STEM-centered romance books. Still, her first paranormal novel, "Bride," can help "Empyrean" fans with their book hangover after they finish "Onyx Storm." In "Bride," vampire Misery Lark is about to marry Lowe Moreland, the Alpha of the Weres, as part of a historic peace deal. Most vampires would be afraid of agreeing to bind themselves to their natural enemies, but after spending most of her childhood as an emissary among the humans, Misery is ready to take on the risk — especially since she needs the Weres' resources to try to track down Serena, her human foster sister who went missing without a trace. Misery plans to avoid Lowe as much as possible, but from the moment they meet at their wedding, Misery seems to perplex and infuriate Lowe for reasons she can't understand (aside from their species' century-long feud). Soon, he's keeping a closer eye on her than she would like, but she might not mind his presence as much as she thought. "A Fate Inked in Blood" by Danielle L. Jensen The first installment in the "Saga of the Unfated" duology, "A Fate Inked in Blood," offers an enemies-to-lovers romance set against the backdrop of Norse mythology. Freya spent her childhood dreaming of becoming a warrior, but at 20, she is married to a man she hates, trapped in her fishing village, and guarding her most closely kept secret: She is a shield maiden, possessing magic that can protect her and others from attacks. Freya's years of secret-keeping come to an end when her husband betrays her to the local jarl. After she uses her magic to survive a fight against his son Bjorn, the jarl sees Freya as what her father always feared she could become: a weapon. The jarl magically binds Freya to him, enlisting Bjorn to keep her safe. Freya must prove herself as a magic-wielder and warrior to stay alive, but her pull toward Bjorn may put her at greater risk than her magic ever could. "Heartless Hunter" by Kristen Ciccarelli By day, Rune Winters is a vapid socialite. By night, she's the Crimson Moth, a witch trying to single-handedly save those like her that her government is determined to wipe out. When her vigilante efforts put her at risk, Rune needs a cover story, and none could be better than Gideon Sharpe, a witch hunter known for his dedication to the cause. If he falls for her, Gideon could offer the perfect protection, but Rune has no idea Gideon is onto her, happy to get close to Rune to find the witch he believes she is associating with. Rune and Gideon are lying to each other at every turn, but the feelings they develop along the way might be the one truth they can't deny. Book one in Kristen Ciccarelli's "The Crimson Moth" series, "Heartless Hunter," is packed with dizzying magic, political rebellion, and decadent enemies-to-lovers tension. If you loved the adventurous elements of the "Empyrean" series as much as the romance, Callie Hart's "Quicksilver" will be right up your alley. Saeris Fane is trying to keep her brother alive in their desert world, where water is nearly impossible to come by. She'll starve herself, steal from the Undying Queen, and use her illegal alchemical powers to do it, even if it puts her own life at risk. When she's finally caught for her thievery, Saeris is saved when she accidentally opens a portal, and a beautiful and intimidating fae named Kingfisher takes her to his homeland, where ice and magic abound. However, she'll find the fae are just as dangerous as the Queen, and after she makes a binding agreement to Kingfisher, she'll have to live among them until she can use her alchemy to fulfill her half of the deal. Saeris wants to get their bargain over with, desperate to get home to check on her brother. Yet it might be the magnetic pull she feels toward Kingfisher that derails her.

item.title: SALES: Best grocery store loyalty programs in the U.S.
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Joining your grocery store’s loyalty program is one of the easiest ways to save on groceries. Most programs are free to join and can offer benefits such as member prices, digital coupons and grocery rewards. You can usually stack savings from grocery store loyalty programs with the rewards you earn by paying with a credit card that offers bonus points or cash back at grocery stores. But grocery loyalty programs vary significantly: Some provide a predictable return on qualifying spending, while others focus on fuel savings or personalized deals. Here’s what you need to know about some of the best U.S. grocery store loyalty programs. Comparison of the best grocery store loyalty programs Before we dive into each program, here's a quick comparison of the best grocery store loyalty programs: In this guide, I’m covering a selection of the most useful free loyalty programs offered by national and major regional grocery chains. I'm excluding popular grocery brands with no loyalty program, such as Trader Joe's and Aldi. And I'm not discussing warehouse clubs such as Sam's Club or Costco or major retail brands that also sell groceries, such as Amazon, Target and Walmart. The Albertsons for U loyalty program is for Albertsons Companies brands, including Albertsons, Safeway and Vons. You can earn 1 point per dollar spent on eligible, qualifying grocery and pharmacy purchases, and 2 points per dollar spent to purchase eligible gift cards. You can redeem points for grocery items or discounts on gas at participating fuel stations. Specifically, you can redeem for free grocery items or tiered basket discounts, such as 300 points for $4 off, 1,000 points for $15 off or 1,200 points for $20 off. Or, you can redeem 100 points for 10 cents off per gallon on up to 25 gallons at participating fuel stations. The maximum discount varies by station and market; members can save up to $1 per gallon at participating company-owned stations, while partner stations may impose a lower maximum. Eligible Albertsons for U members can also enjoy a birthday treat offer (up to $10 value) during their birthday month and redeem an offer for a free item (up to $10 value) once per month. Unfortunately, points expire at the end of the month after the one in which they're earned. So, if you earn 100 points in January, those 100 points will expire at the end of February. You can avoid points expiration and get other perks with the Albertsons for U+ paid subscription. Club Publix doesn't offer any points or other redeemable rewards. However, if Publix is your preferred grocery chain, you may want to join Club Publix to enjoy digital coupons, deals picked for you based on your purchase history, an annual birthday treat and more. To earn rewards with Food Lion MVP, log in to your digital MVP account at the start of each month and activate personalized Shop & Earn offers. Then, as you shop at Food Lion and make purchases toward your offers, you'll earn rewards. These rewards expire at the end of the month after you earn them. Food Lion will automatically redeem your rewards on your next shopping trip unless you opt to donate your rewards to charity. You can earn with Giant Eagle myPerks as follows: - 1 Perk per dollar spent on grocery and gift card purchases, plus out-of-pocket prescription costs You can choose to redeem rewards at grocery or gas station checkout. You can redeem 50 Perks for $1 off your grocery or gas total, 100 Perks for 10 cents off per gallon of gas on a fill-up of up to 30 gallons at GetGo (and at Circle K locations in Ohio) or 150 Perks for 2% off your grocery total. Members generally have up to 12 months to use earned Perks; the exact expiration date appears in your account. It's possible to earn Giant Eagle myPerks Pro status if you earn 2,500 perks through purchases or make 25 qualifying trips within a January to June or July to December earning period. Once you earn Pro status, you'll keep it through the end of the next earning period. Pro members earn Perks at higher rates than standard members. The Hy-Vee Perks program offers member-only prices, digital coupons, personalized deals and fuel rewards. Members can earn fuel discounts when buying eligible products and utilizing limited-time promotions at participating Hy-Vee, Hy-Vee Drugstore, Hy-Vee Fast & Fresh and Dollar Fresh Market locations. Once you earn a fuel discount, it expires 30 days after your purchase. You can only reduce your per-gallon fuel cost to a specific amount (which varies by location), and each discount is valid for one fuel purchase of up to 20 gallons. You can redeem fuel discounts at Hy-Vee Fast & Fresh, Hy-Vee Fast & Fresh Express, Hy-Vee Gas and Casey’s locations, as well as participating Shell, Sinclair and Pump & Pantry stations. Hy-Vee currently offers free delivery on qualifying orders of at least $75 to regular Perks members. You can also pay for a Hy-Vee Perks Plus membership, which offers free delivery and faster pickup on qualifying orders at a lower minimum, plus spend-based fuel rewards and other offers. You can earn Kroger points as follows: - 1 point per dollar spent on groceries and general merchandise - 2 points per dollar spent on gift cards - 25 points per qualifying non-federally funded prescription, 75 points per qualifying 90-day prescription and 1 point per dollar in qualifying out-of-pocket costs on federally funded prescriptions You can redeem Kroger points for grocery discounts or fuel discounts. Specifically, you can redeem 100 points for a $1 off your grocery bill, generally up to 1,000 points or $10 off per day for standard members. Alternatively, you can redeem 100 points for 10 cents off per gallon of gas, up to 1,000 points and 35 gallons per fill-up. Kroger Rewards points usually expire at the end of the month after you earn them. You can also buy a Kroger Boost membership, which offers 2 points per dollar on qualifying purchases and free same-day or next-day delivery on qualifying orders. The Lidl Plus program offers straightforward earning of 1 point per dollar spent on qualifying items. You can earn points on up to five purchases per day. You can redeem Lidl Plus points via the Rewards Marketplace in the Lidl Plus app. In the Rewards Marketplace, you'll see options for redeeming points, which usually include products and coupons. Once you redeem points for a product or coupon, you can then apply it by scanning your Lidl Plus card at checkout. Points generally become available two days after a qualifying purchase. Once you exchange points for a reward coupon, activate it before scanning your Lidl Plus card at checkout. Unused points expire 24 months after becoming available. The Meijer mPerks program lets you earn 10 points per dollar spent on qualifying purchases, plus bonus points on qualifying prescriptions. You can redeem points through the rewards section of the Meijer mPerks app or website for options such as grocery discounts, free items, delivery discounts or fuel discounts. Meijer mPerks points expire 90 days after they’re earned, and you have 45 days to use a reward after selecting it. My Hannaford Rewards is a straightforward program that offers 2% back on eligible store-brand items. You'll collect these cash-back rewards each quarter and then can activate your rewards from the previous quarter each January 1, April 1, July 1 and October 1. Once you activate your rewards, they'll automatically be applied next time you scan your barcode or enter your phone number at checkout. Your rewards will expire if you don't activate and use them within 90 days of their availability. Save Mart Rewards lets you earn 1 point per dollar spent on qualifying items. You can redeem points on the Save Mart Rewards website or in the app for grocery rewards, up to $20 off per transaction. You can also redeem points for gas discounts at participating Shell stations at a rate of 100 points for 10 cents off per gallon (up to 20 gallons per fill-up). Save Mart Rewards points expire on the last day of the third calendar month following the month in which you earned them. However, once you select a grocery reward, you have 30 days to use it. The Schnucks Rewards program lets you earn 10 points per dollar spent. Once you've accumulated 500 points, you can get $1 in store rewards to use on a shopping trip. Your points won't expire as long as you earn or redeem points or rewards at least once every 12 months. You can use the Schnucks Rewards app to redeem points, activate Boosts, check for personal Double Points Day coupons and see your personalized savings opportunities. Schnucks Rewards members can also pay $24.99 per year for a Schnucks Wine Club membership (not available in Indiana), which provides 15% off wine bottles at Schnucks stores. The ShopRite Price Plus Club doesn't have a traditional rewards system. Instead, it offers members instant in-store discounts on weekly sale items and targeted promotional rewards. For example, ShopRite periodically runs targeted promotions that award a grocery or gas gift card after a member meets specified spending requirements. Interestingly, ShopRite will return your keys to you if you lose them with your Price Plus Club card attached and someone drops them in the mail. The Sprouts Rewards program gives members 5 points per dollar spent on eligible items, and members can earn additional points during member-only events. Once you accumulate 1,000 points, you can convert them into a $2 reward for a future shopping trip. Converted rewards expire after 60 days, and points expire on the first day of the seventh month after the month in which they were earned. The Wegmans Shoppers Club doesn't let you earn cash-back or points. Instead, it offers personalized digital coupons based on your shopping habits, gives you access to sale prices and lets you order pharmacy refills and check your prescription status via the app or website. Winn-Dixie Rewards gives you 1 point per $2 spent. You can redeem 100 points for $1 in grocery savings. Plus, percent-back offers let members earn more points on select items once they are activated. Winn-Dixie Rewards members also get access to member-only weekly offers, buy-one-get-one sales and personalized offers. Points expire on the last day of the month that is six months after the month in which they were earned. There isn’t one grocery loyalty program that is best for everyone. Instead, the most useful program for you will often be the one offered by the chain where you shop most. Even programs without points, such as Club Publix and Wegmans Shoppers Club, can provide personalized coupons and useful member benefits, while other programs offer grocery rewards or meaningful savings at the gas pump. Just don’t assume every reward will apply automatically. Some programs require you to activate offers or convert points before checkout, and many have relatively short expiration windows. So, be sure to check your account before you shop and use your rewards before they expire.

item.title: SALES: 22 Best Hotels in Nashville for Music City Hospitality
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Music City is rooted in the art of spinning a good yarn. There’s no country music, no Taylor Swift, no late nights chatting at the bar or mornings at breakfast recapping last night without storytelling. And while hotels may once have been merely places to rest your head, today’s best hotels in Nashville are as connected to storytelling as the city where they’re based. There are inns connected to the land and the story of Middle Tennessee; its outdoor adventures and rich soil. There are hotels that explore the city’s history from its role in the suffrage movement to its location on a railway hub to more intimate history about people and places that shaped Nashville. And of course, there’s the hotel that tells the story of Dolly Parton, from the Smoky Mountains to her philanthropic Imagination Library. The beauty of these hotels is that no two are the same, although their stories are interconnected. Each time you come to Nashville and stay at a different hotel, you get a different chapter of the city's full story. These are the best hotels in Nashville for a truly intimate take on the Tennessean capital. Read our full Nashville travel guide here, which includes: How we choose the best hotels in Nashville Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. - Read Full ReviewLots of Nashville hotels use guitar picks and instruments as décor as a nod to the city’s musical roots. But at The Countrypolitan, music is part of the hotel’s essence, not just its aesthetics. Thanks to a vibrant lobby bar/restaurant with live music daily and staff trained to help guests find and appreciate the best of the city, The Countrypolitan, a Hotel Indigo property, is a good home base for a Nashville adventure. Don’t miss the small lobby boutique curated by Nikki Lane. You’ll find vintage goods and cheeky souvenirs not available elsewhere. - Read Full ReviewIt’s an offbeat name, The Untitled, but it is fitting for a hotel that strives to be a little different. The idea is to title your own trip to Nashville at a hotel that prizes creativity. The hotel boasts three art galleries and a staff curator who offers tours, so you can learn about the local and regional artists on exhibit, all in an environment that is laid back and unstuffy. The location near The Arcade, Printers Alley, and Lower Broad makes for easy exploration of Nashville’s myriad creative charms. - Read Full ReviewNashville has a reputation as a place that tourists visit in groups, be they bachelorette parties, girls' getaways, or family vacations. If you want to spend lots of time with your travel companions and also want a little elbow room, book BODE Nashville. It’s an apartment-style hotel with on-site staff, a bar scene that attracts locals to hang, guest rooms with up to four bedrooms all in a location within easy walking distance to some of the city’s favorite attractions. Rooms are modern, sleek, and roomy, with the biggest suites the size of small homes. - Read Full ReviewOpened in 2026, this updated motel and swim club provides a budget-friendly, but still stylish, option for Nashville tourists. Designed as a spot for groups who want to hang by the pool and have a cocktail before heading out on the town, Salt Ranch delivers. Guest rooms are small, sleek and updated, and priced so everyone in a group can have their own room and then spend time together in the bar, restaurant or at the pool. Salt Ranch sits on more than two acres, with plenty of free parking and its own fenced-in dog park. - Read Full ReviewThe Chloe Nashville staff believe in the golden rule: While the boutique's neighborhood is small, buzzy, and infused with luxury touches, it's also friendly and welcoming—and that ethos applies to the locals as well as hotel guests. Situated in Hillsboro Village, in the former home of Asylum Records, The Chloe is a true local hangout. Neighbors have pool memberships, bring their families to the seasonal pumpkin patch, and the bar is a go-to for a nightcap. Each of the hotel’s 19 rooms have different décor, so it feels like this is a place to be lived in, not just visited. The signature praline ice cream sandwich (served at the bar, in the restaurant, and by the pool) mirrors the hotel itself: approachable and indulgent. - Read Full ReviewDyed-in-the-wool Dolly Parton fans probably already have reservations for the country icon’s new hotel, complete with an attached Dolly museum. But SongTeller isn’t only for Dolly acolytes: Just like Dolly’s appeal transcends gender, music genre, age and more, so, too, does her hotel. Her touches are everywhere, from the musical notes in the carpet to her songs being played once an hour in the lobby to her photos in every guest room. But the hotel is more than her, allowing guests to experience music the way she loved it. Singer-songwriters play in the lobby Listening Room, and jazz musicians play in the clubby upstairs Jolene’s bar. Access to the hotel is limited to guests with room or restaurant reservations, so it’s a safe, warm oasis from the hubbub of nearby Broadway, kind of like Dolly herself. - Read Full ReviewThe Hutton Hotel is thoroughly modern and recently renovated. It’s designed not just for people who want to listen to music, but people who want to—and do—make music. Music industry executives appreciate the hotel’s proximity to Music Row, where many record labels are located, and its on-site writing rooms. For all its new amenities, there’s an old-school vibe when it comes to service. This is the kind of place where the staff knows your name (and your dog’s name, if you are traveling with a pet), and they’ll offer you a drink and a chance to sit and catch your breath in the lobby before heading out on adventures. The on-site spa and music venue, Analog, make a compelling case for sticking around instead of heading out. - Read Full ReviewThis former train station-turned-hotel dynamically captures Nashville’s past and present. For more than 125 years, this building has stood as a lovely landmark on Broadway. Its head-turning lobby is worth seeing as a restored icon of a past era. Its location in the newly developed Nashville Yards neighborhood keeps Union Station young. Right out its doors are a new music venue, The Pinnacle, shops, bars and restaurants, plus easy access to Lower Broad a few blocks to the east. Nab an interior room with windows that open out into the atrium. - Read Full ReviewA stay at 1 Hotel Nashville is a sensory experience, from touch—with textured, reclaimed wood, and live plants on many surfaces—to smell—which is closer to a field of wildflowers in the countryside than a busy city block in the heart of honky-tonk action. The Nashville branch of the 1 Hotel chain, which opened in 2022, is representative of the brand’s commitment to sustainability, in a way that is engaging but not spartan or schoolmarmish. Devote time to exploring some of these choices, such as the hourglass in the shower to create awareness about the length of time you leave the water running, and the hangers in the closet made from recycled wrapping paper. Like all proper Nashville hotels, 1 Hotel has a rooftop bar with a view; this one is surrounded by the hotel’s signature greenery, contributing to the feeling that country and city co-exist. And they do it on a plush bed with organic cotton sheets. - Read Full ReviewThe W Nashville pulls off a trick that’s hard to execute. Somehow the W both cultivates a fun and see-and-be-seen vibe that befits its Gulch location and also is refined enough to avoid a party-at-all-costs attitude. That means its large lobby welcomes business travelers and enthusiastic travelers and offers quality people-watching perch in the Gulch neighborhood. The hotel welcomes people in (not just hotel guests), for live music, yoga, and swimming at the large L-shaped pool (reservations required). Locals also flock here to eat at celebrity chef José Andrés’s restaurants. The central location is a prime home base for shopping, eating, and drinking, close to the Station Inn, the Frist Art Museum, and 15 minutes from Lower Broadway and the Ryman Auditorium. - Read Full ReviewThe Russell is all about the wow factor. Formerly a 115-year-old church, the hotel retains many of the building's original elements, including a series of jaw-dropping stained glass windows. Bright, restored panes of glass play off modern decor and stylish new architectural elements. Each room is a different shape and size—such is the reality of retrofitting an old church into a new hotel. All of the rooms have good light, smartly designed charging stations in the pews-turned-headboards, and beautiful color schemes. - Read Full ReviewTravel should be fun, and the Graduate knows that. They incorporated cheeky, quirky art elements and attractions throughout the moderately priced hotel near the Vanderbilt University campus. You can belt out your favorite karaoke tunes while being accompanied by an animatronic band at Cross-Eyed Critters or go to the rooftop and take a photo with a giant, pink chicken-wire bust of Dolly Parton. (While many people refer to this as “Dolly Parton’s hotel,” the singer isn’t involved in it. She’s just someone the Graduate team loves.) Some of the details may seem offbeat at first glance, but the hotel takes making sure you get a good night’s rest seriously. Rooms are ample in size and comfortable, with well-appointed bedding and plush carpet to cushion your walk after a night on the town. For all the good-time vacationers who stay here, rooms are adequately soundproof. They can party, and you can sleep. Or vice versa. - Read Full ReviewIt’s easy to imagine a movie being filmed in the large, high-ceiled, light-filled lobby of the Conrad. With its sweeping staircase and nattily-dressed clientele, it feels like it is out of central casting for “luxury hotel.” This vibe of everything being just right permeates the experience of staying at the Conrad. From wise assistance courtesy of the concierge, to dinner at Blue Aster, capping off the day with an artfully prepared meal, to a long soak in a giant bathtub, to getting shut-eye by closing the blinds with a press of a button, a stay at the Conrad is designed to make your life easier. The Midtown location is close enough to the Ryman Auditorium, Lower Broadway, and other attractions to get there quickly, but also offers a respite from downtown congestion. - Read Full ReviewFor more than a century, the Hermitage has been the gold standard of Nashville accommodations. The gilded entrance transports visitors to a more glamorous era of travel, while offering more bang for your buck than other downtown stays—rooms are spacious, beds are plush, and service is beyond compare. In 2020, the hotel celebrated the 100th anniversary of the ratification of the 19th Amendment (the one granting women suffrage), which had much of its final push take place in the halls of the Hermitage before Tennessee became the state to put it over the top. That year, the hotel also kicked off a complete renovation of guest rooms, the lobby, bar, and restaurant, resulting in a look that is crisp and modern but still connects to the hotel’s considerable history. The overhaul of the Drusie & Darr restaurant was overseen by Celebrity Chef Jean-George Vongerichten, who opened his first restaurant in the South at the Hermitage in 2021. —K.L. item.title: SALES: 6 once-in-a-lifetime Alaska shore excursions worth the splurge
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Alaska is a bucket-list destination for many cruisers looking to experience the history, culture and wildlife of The Last Frontier. To really experience its fullness, however, requires taking some shore excursions — more than a few of which carry some hefty price tags. How hefty? For most of these excursions, expect to shell out at least $300 or more. Shore excursions in Alaska, as a rule of thumb, aren’t cheap. But as pricey as they may be, these once-in-a-lifetime excursions are exactly that: Unique journeys that showcase Alaska’s natural beauty like nothing else, creating lifelong memories along the way. Here are six picks for the ultimate Alaska shore excursions worth the splurge. Dog sledding and glacier adventure by helicopter — Juneau Coming in at a cool $750 per person, this is one of those unique experiences where the memories will far outweigh the hit to your credit card. Starting in Juneau, passengers fly via helicopter to a dog-mushing camp situated atop Norris Glacier, part of the vast Juneau Icefield that also includes Taku Glacier. Accessible only by air, the flight alone is worth the price of admission – until you land on the glacier and set foot on the pristine snow and ice. Then, it’s all up to the dogs. Along with a veteran dog sled musher, you'll be pulled across the ice by your team of dogs who know how to run. Alone in the wilderness of ice and snow, you may as well be at the edge of the Arctic Circle. It’s exhilarating, fun and absolutely bucket-list in every way. Grab the cameras and make those at home jealous with your Instagram posts: this is one for the books. Tracy Arm Fjord and Glacier Explorer — Tracy Arm You might notice Tracy Arm Fjord listed as a scenic cruising destination on your cruise itinerary. Home to the North and South Sawyer glaciers, the awe-inspiring fjord is filled with narrow channels, towering cliffs and pristine waters. What the cruise line doesn’t tell you is that your ship is unlikely to make it to the Sawyer glaciers, particularly at the start of the season when ice still chokes much of the fjord’s narrowest passage. But most cruise lines offer the Tracy Arm Ford & Glacier Explorer tour, and it’s well worth the splurge. Running about $300 per person, you disembark your ship right in the fjord and hop aboard one of Allen Marine’s small expedition ships for a cruise right up to the North Sawyer Glacier. You’ll be treated to wildlife, waterfalls and incredible sights of the calving glaciers before rejoining your ship in the Fjord. We’ve done this tour numerous times, and it’s never disappointed. The expedition ship also happens to sell some of the best seafood chowder we've tasted (but let’s keep that secret between us, shall we?). Denali peak flightseeing — Denali National Park This excursion is only available for those taking part in pre- or postcruise overland tours that visit Denali National Park, but it represents one of the most spectacular flightseeing experiences we’ve ever had in Alaska. You'll have to cough up more than $400 per person, but the experience is priceless. Setting out from Denali, passengers are bundled into a small airplane and taken for an amazing flightseeing adventure over Denali National Park, which somehow manages to look even more majestic from the sky. Here’s the real win: If conditions allow, your pilot will set the plane down on the mountain, on the snow, and give you time to walk around outside. Then, your plane – equipped with special skis or floats – races back along the snow and takes off over the majesty of Denali National Park. It’s a stunning journey unlike anything else available in Alaska. Luxury White Pass and Yukon Route Railway experience — Skagway A journey up the formidable White Pass and Yukon Route Railway is one of Alaska's signature experiences. Departing from the gold rush frontier town of Skagway, the railway whisks you up stunning heights into the mountains beyond Skagway, following the original Trail of ’98 up into the Canadian Yukon Territory to Carcross. Recently, the railway has offered an upgraded experience: a luxury rail car coupled to the end of the train for a select few passengers. Complete with plush leather seating, complimentary beverages and canapes, it's all elevated to match the scenery alongside the train. No kids are allowed, and the car comes with a private guide who will share the scenic viewpoints and gold rush history with you as you wine and dine your way up the White Pass to the summit. The nearly three-hour tour costs about $450 per person, but with the luxury service, you'll feel like a million bucks — and definitely not like a rugged prospector. If you love crab, you’ll love this gloriously indulgent excursion available in Ketchikan. The experience costs around $130 per person, and offers outsize value. Guides will show how crab pots are pulled from the water, and will even pass around a crab and explain their entomology and relevance to the region. Then, it’s off to the George Inlet Lodge where you can eat as much crab as you please – literally. Served up with butter and crisp Alaskan beer (non-alcoholic alternatives are available), the crab legs will mount as you enjoy your fresh Alaskan feast. How much is too much crab? That’s hard to say! Test your limits with this informative, scenic and scrumptious tour. Just be warned: you won’t be hungry afterwards for quite some time. From Juneau to Icy Strait Point to Wrangell and beyond, whale watching excursions are a must. They’re expensive, though reasonably priced when compared to some of the flightseeing excursions on this list. But if you want to be guaranteed a whale sighting, it’s best to book passage on one of these smaller boats. Tours run between $200 and $400 a person, depending on the excursion you choose. These small ships include both indoor and outdoor seating areas. But, even if it’s raining, brave the upper decks and the elements. The thrill of seeing a whale breech close by is like nothing else when viewed from the upper deck. While you may see whales from your cruise ship, they will likely be far off and in the distance. Officers on ships are trained to avoid whales like the plague and will typically steer away from any pods they see. Small ships, on the other hand, can get far closer than a big ship ever could. We’ve done whale watching tours in nearly every port of call in Alaska, and while we’ve had good sightings in various ports, two stand out: Icy Strait Point has offered some of the most consistently excellent whale watching experiences, while excursions from Juneau’s nearby Auke Bay have been well worth the price of admission, too. Either way, if you’re set on seeing whales, a whale watching excursion is a no-brainer. Bring a poncho (leave the umbrellas on the ship), some waterproof clothing and your camera, and get ready: you never know what Mother Nature is ready to surprise you with! Planning an Alaska cruise? Long before I had children I fell in love with South Africa – Cape Town first, to be specific. It’s one of the most vibrant cities I know, full of life, colour, history, flavour and some of the most wonderful shopping, eating and drinking known to mankind. The latter, especially, in the Cape Winelands. And not to mention exquisite hotels. After each trip I’d return with not only home goods, jewellery and bubble-wrapped wine but also adorable purchases for my friends’ babies and kids. I even started buying for my own future brood – handwoven lambswool blankets, leather moccasins, sweet jumpers, stuffed animals in vivid African prints – until finally it came time to visit with my 10 month old for her first safari and wine country excursions. Like in some parts of Asia where tiny humans are embraced wholeheartedly by locals, the people we’ve met in South Africa have always been ecstatic to meet and interact with my daughters. And the things we’ve seen across the country have expanded their growing minds tremendously. It’s not only the elephants, lions, cheetah, zebra and rhinos viewed up so close without barriers or boundaries that have enticed them to speak new words and ask curious questions. Those mindbogglingly vast landscapes – the Kalahari in particular is completely astonishing – plus languages, accents, foods, flora, stories and sounds are incredibly novel and enriching for the whole family. Traveling in this country with little ones is not exactly a time to completely relax and throw caution to the wind (unless perhaps you’re all frolicking at a Franschhoek wine estate with a glass of vino and a picnic), but I’ve never felt unsafe even if my husband felt quite tense when facing his first male lion as I nursed our baby in the Land Cruiser. There are countless reasons to visit Japan, but warm hospitality, unmatched design, and rich culture are just a few topping the list. And where better to draw all these elements together than at one of Japan's best ryokans? Roughly translating to “inn”, ryokans lie at the heart of Japanese culture, known for their home-cooked meals on cushioned floors and snug sleeps on tatami mats. Often built atop natural hot springs called onsen, communal bathing is also common to these cosy establishments, while sliding paper walls, called shoji doors, are also fundamental to these intimate spaces, cleverly filtering through natural light while maintaining absolute privacy. Ryokans are rooted in tradition and while there are plenty of historic places to choose from, a flurry of new developments have reimagined their iconic Japanese customs for modern audiences. Mineral-rich waters in private bathrooms, low rather than floor beds and entire ryokan rentals are just some adaptations which have entered the scene, but all share the same goal of immersing guests in the ultimate authentic experience. item.title: SALES: The Kitchen Gear That's Topped Our 'Best Of' Lists for a Decade
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
A deluge of feature-laden, Wi-Fi connected, “revolutionary” new cooking products come out every year, yet there are some kitchen necessities that just can’t be improved upon. Believe us: At BA, we’ve been testing products head-to-head to find the best cookware, tools, and appliances since 2015, and during that decade, our editors have returned to a small handful of favorites time and again. With boxes full of kitchen gear arriving at the office practically every single day for our team of kitchen obsessives to put through the wringer, the odds are stacked against any particular item finding a stable spot as a favorite. Yet, here we are, with a list of 15 timeless pieces that reached the top of our rankings and just…stayed there. As part of our Gear of the Year Awards, we’re continuing to recognize this core group of products—selected by our Test Kitchen editors and reviews team—as our Forever Award winners. Invest in these, and you can feel confident that they won’t soon be bested. People are always asking food director Chris Morocco what knife they should get. “It’s sort of like asking someone what car you should get,” he says. “It really depends on what you are trying to do with it, how fast you want to go, and how much time you plan to spend at the mechanic.” But the foundation of any set of kitchen tools begins with a chef’s knife you can count on every day. And since we first started reviewing how different models slice and dice, nothing has come close to the Mac MTH-80’s combination of versatility, sharpness, and comfort in your hand. It has a best of both worlds design, balancing the precision of a Japanese gyuto with the power of a German-style knife. As Morocco puts it: “The Mac will never let you down and is the one relatively affordable knife that you will never feel compelled to upgrade.” Nimble on a cutting board, precise enough to skin a fish, strong enough to break down a chicken, the mighty Mac is in “take it with you to a desert island” territory. Despite its reputation as a safety hazard when not in the hands of a professional chef, a mandoline makes prep work faster, easier, and more precise than a set of knives alone. And no mandoline does those things better than a Benriner. Light, sharp, and endlessly adjustable, the Super Slicer can produce identical slices of potato for a Hasselback preparation and a round of radish so transparently thin you can read a magazine through it. If you have ever encountered a recipe that directs you to thinly slice anything, this is the tool you want. If you’ve only ever cooked rice on the stove, you don’t know how much better the process can be using a dedicated rice cooker. With this induction-heated Zojirushi cooker, you consistently get fluffy, evenly cooked rice—with no attention or effort needed from you. Deputy food editor Hana Asbrink feels passionately about hers. “If pressed to pick just one appliance, this would be what I grab before fleeing a burning building (sorry, coffee maker!)," she says. “There's a reason I’m still using my 15-plus year-old Zojirushi rice cooker: its quality. It hasn’t faltered over that time, and the pleasing singsong alert remains a comforting joy to hear.” Zojirushi has come out with many fancier and more expensive models since the NP-HCC10 was first released, but none of them make better rice. In fact, we’ve done blind rice tastings multiple times a year and this one has come out on top every time. When the Technivorm Moccamaster received recognition from the Specialty Coffee Association in 2023, it reset expectations of what we ought to get from an automatic drip coffee maker. Specifically, it ushered in the idea that an automatic brewer could produce coffee that can compete with the taste of pour-over. In the spring of 2024, Fellow raised the bar again when it released the Aiden coffee maker. This machine didn’t try to compete with pour-over—it was pour-over for people who don’t have the time or inclination to engage in the ritual. Its endlessly tweakable options for time and temperature give you even more control over a pot of coffee than you have with a Chemex. And the user-friendly interface makes better coffee accessible to more people than it ever has been before. Breville’s diminutive starter espresso machine is not the fanciest one on the market, but it is as close to a perfect beginner coffee maker as we have ever used. It’s small and low commitment on the counter, affordable, and, as all Breville machines do, makes very good espresso. Breville has also perfected automatic milk steaming in a way that the uncertainty someone new to home espresso might feel is totally removed. We’ve tested almost every machine in this tier, and nothing comes close to the Bambino Plus as an espresso entry point. Cheap and plastic aren’t words you’d expect to describe an item we perpetually put at the top of our rankings, but the Escali Primo knows it has a single job to do, and it doesn’t need to get dressed up to do it. Former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic is a long time Escali Primo devotee. “If I could grow a strand of hair for every time someone tells me ‘I can cook but I can’t bake,’ I’d be hairier than Sasquatch.
