In return, I always ask, with great (and feigned) patience, ‘Do you use a digital scale?’” she says. “The Escali Primo is the one I have at home and at work, and the one I always recommend. My oldest one is 11 years old and still works perfectly fine. He’s been through two restaurant kitchens and a pandemic-era micro-bakery, so he’s really seen it all!” This scale weighs in grams and ounces, can handle a lot of weight, and has an easy-to-read display—even when a mixing bowl is sitting on top. Add on to that its incredibly low price and you have one of the best buys anyone can make for their kitchen. Once upon a time, cast-iron pans were smoother and thinner than the pans most people are familiar with today. Why did things change? Manufacturing costs, mostly. But the recent renaissance of high-end cast-iron cookware has brought back these vintage-style pans, and the Lancaster is our favorite of the bunch. The Lancaster pan is lighter and thinner than the popular Lodge, meaning its easy to maneuver and takes less time to heat on the stovetop. Its smooth cooking surface is more nonstick out of the box and continues to improve and develop over time. While the pans do come with a higher price tag, staff writer Wilder Davies insists that it’s money well spent. In his review of the pan, Davies writes, “If you want a pan that not only offers an exceptionally pleasant cooking experience but can also serve as an heirloom for generations to come, the Lancaster is worth it in every way.” Ask a professionally trained chef what the best cookware brand is, and they’ll likely say All-Clad. Ask us and we’ll say the same thing. After all his years using it in the Test Kitchen, Chris Morocco calls it “unkillable,” and in all our years of testing it, we’ve never had a piece of stainless-steel cookware challenge its supremacy in a serious way. Culinary schools use these pans, professional kitchens use these pans, and any home cook who wants long-lasting, high-performing cookware uses these pans too. Now, for a while, we resisted recommending cookware sets assembled and sold by brands because we thought taking the time to put one together yourself would let you choose the pieces you need. But All-Clad’s small seven-piece set (three of those pieces are just lids) represents universally necessary pieces—a sauté pan, saucepan, frying pan, and stockpot—and we can’t imagine recommending any cookware set besides this one. Thanks to a motor strong enough to move a small boat, Vitamix blenders have become, as Hana Asbrink observes, de rigueur in most professional kitchens. The 5200 is the Vitamix in its purest form. There are no touchscreens and special settings for hummus and smoothies, just the unvarnished power you need to liquify whatever you put in the jar. And, as Asbrink notes, you can put just about anything in the jar. “It’s the less-expected tasks for which I give my Vitamix my undying love,” she says. “Things like preparing a kalbi marinade in seconds; getting a pancake or crepe batter together in a flash; making consistent Oreo milkshakes every weekend; and even—brace yourselves—pulsing together a quick pie crust, relieving me from the need to pull the heavy food processor down from the dark closet.” The bells and whistles that other blenders come with, including other models of the Vitamix, are nice; but they aren’t necessary. While the new VX1 from Vitamix represents a slightly less expensive version of the brand’s excellent blenders, the 5200 is a classic that is hard to imagine improving upon. Sheet pans just aren’t “buy it for life” cookware; they inevitably take a beating. But it’d be your folly to think their disposable nature means all sheet pans are interchangeable. “After writing a cookbook that required me to bake hundreds of galettes, I feel confident saying Nordic Ware is the only brand of sheet pan I will recommend by name,” says Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser. Nothing else we’ve tried has ever had such an impressive combination of quick and even heating and durability. You’ll use this pan multiple times a week—for cookies, veggies, sheet-pan dinners—and the Nordic Ware sheet will never let you down. And it’s a bargain to boot. The Le Creuset Dutch stands at the ready in our Test Kitchen for any stewing and braising needs, and Firkser also swears by hers at home. “It’s my kitchen’s most-used pot—it comes out for tasks as varied as tossing together pasta, searing chicken thighs, deep-frying doughnuts, and baking sourdough bread,” she says. “It’s lighter than models from other brands, heats up quickly, and retains evenly conducted heat.” Heavy, versatile, and beautiful, it’s also a true statement piece in any kitchen. Expertly crafted from cast iron, one of these pots will outlast us all. Staub’s Dutch oven is a never-needs-replacing piece of cookware that can do just about anything you ask of it. Senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk says his is the most-used product of any kind in his home kitchen. “Staub’s chic design first drew me in, but its quality is what kept me around. I bake bread in it, braise meats in it, and have even cooked pancakes in it,” he says. And you don’t need to treat its finish with kid gloves in order to retain its seasoning: “I scrub it with reckless abandon using soap, and it remains pristine,” Szewczyk adds. Over the years, this inexpensive waffle maker has won over a string of staff members with its ingenious design and ability to make superbly crisp and fluffy waffles. Forget the tedious collection of settings, sensors, and automatic programs that premium waffle makers offer, the Presto proves that simpler can be better. It comes with a timer, but unlike most other machines, it won’t automatically shut off once the timer ends. This allows you to cook it until it’s just right—whatever that means for you. Its slim, vertical design also stands out among a field of countertop clunkers. Since waffles aren’t an everyday food for most people (power to you if they are), its important to be able to stash the machine away when you’re done with it. “The fact that it stores upright for maximum space savings just makes it all the more worth having a cooking tool that does just one thing, but does it well,” Morocco says. We’ve tried hard to find something newer and fancier to supplant the iconic style of Weber’s simple kettle grill and just aren’t sure it can be done. It has a compact footprint but a large cooking area, allows you to transition easily between searing and slow smoking, and is easy to clean (so important in a grill). The grill market tends to over-index at the poles of the price and quality spectrums (you tend to find either low-quality, inexpensive models or high-end specialty pieces), but the Weber Kettle strikes a pitch-perfect balance between performance and value. We’ve stood firm on our endorsement of this food processor. This has sometimes put us on the outs with steadfast loyalists of the ever-popular Cuisinart, the original food processor. Here’s the thing: The Cuisinart is great, but the Breville Sous is better. The two go toe-to-toe in power and precision, but the Breville’s intuitive assembly is a massive improvement on the Cuisinart’s notoriously fidgety and fussy locking mechanisms. “I feel a reassuring thrum whenever I turn the Breville Sous Chef on,” Morocco says. “The parts don’t rattle, and everything fits together precisely and tightly, delivering phenomenal cutting power to whatever I throw into it.” The way we see it, the easier an appliance is to use, the more likely you are to use it. For something like a food processor, which takes up a lot of space, comes with a lot of accessories, and is ultimately a bit of a commitment to own, the last thing it should be is frustrating to operate.

item.title: SALES: 11 best Turkish restaurants in London, according to Toyo Odetunde
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Turkish and Turkish-inspired cooking has become one of London’s most beloved and dynamic culinary offerings. 2026 has seen the capital continue to welcome new openings informed by Turkey’s culinary legacy, from a famed 19th-century Turkish institution making its overseas debut, to a modish Soho spot. The enduring appeal of Turkish cuisine is unsurprising, given the diversity of masterfully aromatic, colourful dishes that are as much a feast for the eyes as for the stomach. The seductive charcoal-y scent of skewered meats rotated above springing flames, the satisfying, creamy cool of silky or batter-thick dips dyed in rich vegetable hues, the buttery flakiness of a crackling borek bursting with pungent cheese, the tangy pinch and snappy bite of pickled vegetables… Turkish cuisine is lauded for its careful balance of boldness and creativity, with simplicity and freshness. The story of modern Turkish food in London began in earnest in the 1970s and 1980s, as waves of Turkish and Kurdish migrants settled in the UK, bringing with them culinary traditions that would quickly find a foothold across the capital. Harringay’s Green Lanes emerged as the nucleus of this movement – a lively stretch of North London now synonymous with ocakbasi grills, lahmacun ovens, and windows displaying towering pyramids of glittering sweets, crammed with nuts and lacquered with honey and perfumed syrups. But in recent years, the scene has expanded beyond these traditional hubs, incorporating gastronomic concepts from Turkey and its immediate surroundings. Today, Turkish dining in London spans from humble family-run eateries to chic, genre-defining restaurants that reinterpret Turkish flavours with contemporary twists or the personal mark of individual chefs. From Dalston to Canary Wharf and Knightsbridge, the city is dotted with standout restaurants celebrating not only the regional diversity of Turkish food, but its culinary relationship to interconnected parts of the Middle East, West Asia and the Mediterranean. Here are some of the best Turkish and Turkish-inspired restaurants in London. Walking into İskender, you immediately feel that you are entering not only a restaurant, but a space celebrating centuries of familial legacy and pride. Founded in Bursa in 1867, İskender is the storied institution credited with pioneering the döner kebab, a method of cooking meat on a vertical rotating spit now synonymous with Turkish cuisine. Occupying a renovated five-storey townhouse in Knightsbridge, their London opening at the end of last month is the group’s first outside of Turkey. Family photographs line the walls, including a picture of the original shopfront’s Ottoman-script sign. The London outpost of the fourth-generation business is led by brothers Oğuzhan and Kayhan İskenderoğlu, alongside their father, Yavuz. Upstairs, you’ll find a living room-like space furnished with intricately patterned rugs, a vintage Turkish radio and a standing clock trimmed with gold orb finials. The room is anchored by an ornate antique brass indoor mangal (a traditional charcoal brazier). Elsewhere, white walls, mosaic tiling, fluted lampshades and classical Turkish carpentry create an aesthetic of understated grandeur. Staff are dressed in starched uniforms, while Yavuz himself can be seen wearing the traditional white tasselled peştemal, a mark of culinary mastery rooted in Ahilik, a centuries-old guild-like tradition dating back to the 13th century. There’s no decision paralysis when it comes to ordering. The restaurant specialises in one dish: its signature Bursa İskender Kebabı. A hefty portion arrives with a base of finely cut pide, a soft, flat Turkish bread, layered with slices of juicy, perfectly seasoned lamb döner. A fizzing pan of melted butter follows, poured all over the meat whilst still piping hot. The bread soaks this up along with the meat juices. Together with the yoghurt dip and mix of fresh and charred tomato and long green peppers, it’s a thoroughly satisfying meal. To wash it all down, their fermented şıra drink is a must. Made from dried black Öküzgözü grapes, it’s bursting with currant flavour, its natural sweetness tempered with a little tanginess. A light dessert of kestane şekeri is a pleasant pick-me-up if you have room – dense, fudgy, syrup-soaked chestnuts that are loved across Bursa and pair well with their Turkish tea. Address: 30 Beauchamp Place, London SW3 1NJ Website: iskender.com (walk-ins only) Mangal 2 is very much emblematic of the ‘London restaurant’. An institution on Stoke Newington Road, it was opened in the 1990s by Ali Dirik, who founded nearby Mangal Ocakbaşı (or Mangal I). Today, his sons Ferhat and Sertaç Dirik have taken the family business in a more experimental direction, with a menu that draws meaningfully from Turkish food culture, but without feeling beholden to expectations of what Turkish and Turkish-inspired cooking should be. There’s an intentionality to the creative way ingredients are used – sometimes based on classical Turkish dishes, sometimes taking them somewhere new or fusing wider influences from the melting pot that is London’s restaurant scene. Tarkan’s Şımarık is among the fun, nostalgic pop playing overhead on my most recent visit. Simple wooden tables, an eclectic mix of paintings and textile art give the room an easygoing, lived-in feel. For dips, the smoked hummus is whipped to a creamy perfection, with a deeper, nuttier flavour than other renditions, and a pleasant subtle bitterness adding more dimension. Crumbled pickled vegetables bring a welcome crunch and sharpness, cutting through the thickness. The muhammara is richly concentrated and tart, with roasted walnut and radicchio adding texture and complexity. There’s a similar knack for balancing flavours in the cull yaw köfte. It’s juicy with bite, warmly spiced and sweetened by an apple sauce. Between the breads, I’d recommend the sourdough pide with cull yaw fat. The pide rings with a gentle sourness, while the full-bodied, savoury warmth of the fat seeps into the bread. Mains like the cod cheek şişlik (bouncy hunks of cod blanketed in charred red onion with pickled mussels, celery tarhana and black-eyed peas) offer a fresher, lighter, more vegetal counterpoint to richer plates like the lamb ribs with sour cherry molasses. The drinks list sees fruit and spice added to familiar formulas, such as the sumac margarita and pomegranate whisky. For something soft, the beetroot and apple shrub, blended with white wine vinegar, makes for a nicely puckery sip. Finish with the apple and tahini tart (best to share!) with the aromatic mahlep cream. Address: 4 Stoke Newington Road, London, N16 8BH Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, Kısmet is a joyful tribute to the spirit of the meyhanes (traditional taverns) found across Istanbul and Northern Cyprus. It’s the latest venture from restaurateur Dom Hamdy, of Crispin and Bistro Freddie, and chef Keiran Mustafa, formerly of BiBi (who also helped other Borough favourites such as Rambutan and OMA). You’ll be off to a flying start with the atom, contrasting the velvetiness and zippiness of strained yoghurt with the gentle warming heat of a rousing chilli butter. The bulgur köftesi are invitingly plump, cracking open to reveal a succulent, meaty and carefully flavoured beef and onion filling. Seafood lovers should not miss the karides güveç. The prawns arrive in a clay pot with a vigorous sizzle, juicy and sweet against the buttery garlic sauce and spiced bell peppers. Patates kızartması, the Cypriot fried potatoes, are herby and moreish, while the Kısmet salatası brings a welcome tanginess to cut through the heavier plates such as a delectable, expertly cooked lamb chops special. The atmosphere is particularly energetic in the evenings, when the room really comes into its own. As night falls, the lighting softens, and the room feels all the more cosy. On Thursdays, live kanun music adds a rippling, almost hypnotic soundtrack, its bright plucked strings weaving through the background noise of merry chatter. Waiters deftly swinging around broad metal pans lined with precisely cubed sheets of baklava and hanging silver tea trays (known as askılı tepsi) add to the convivial bustle. The interiors, dressed with lace, old-school metal tissue dispensers, flickering candles and a miscellany of framed photographs, complement the exposed brick walls and create a compelling sense of place. Save a little space for the salted pistachio ice cream that accompanies the baklava for dessert – indulgent, creamy and nutty, with just a touch of salt to elevate its flavour. Address: Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London, SE1 9AL Following the success of his family’s celebrated Mangal II, KID sees Sertaç Dirik strike out on his own, partnering with restaurateur David Carter. The menu draws on the foodways of Central Anatolia, also with broader Turkish touchstones reworked through a contemporary lens. The interiors here lean into a palette of dark chocolate browns, giving the room a distinctly grown-up feel that’s still warm and intimate. Starters kick off the menu confidently, from the assertively seasoned, toasty tombik pide, to the sucuk, lifted with a thrilling burst of fruitiness and sweetness from a grilled peach sauce. Worth ordering also is the aubergine ezme with garlic yoghurt and crispy grains. The pillowy yoghurt is infused with smoky, savoury allium flavours, and contrasts nicely against the shards of crunchy, matchstick-thin grains. The grilled quail with ezme is equally well judged, the cool tang of yoghurt providing a welcome contrast to the smokiness of the charred meat. For something a little different, the grilled onion salata with lamb belly and sweetbreads dances between sweet, sour and charred flavours. For mains, dig into the lamb lokma, medallions of yielding meat served with gently stewed vegetables. For larger groups, there’s the option of ordering the slow-cooked goat head dish that gives the restaurant its name, and also makes KID a particularly appealing choice for a more celebratory meal. There’s also an extensive wine list, organised around historical regions and trading routes, spanning countries like Georgia, Armenia, Greece and Turkey. Dessert brings two Turkish-leaning classics with a few thoughtful twists. The mountain tea rice pudding has a swoony buttery texture, with a subtle scent of orange blossom and a blistered, brûléed veneer. The cardamom baklava, meanwhile, is nutty rather than oozing with syrup, while the sharpness of plum and its accompanying fruity sauce brings a little excitement to a familiar dessert. Address: 53–55 Frith Street, Soho, London, W1D 4SJ The Turkish heritage of brothers Özgür and Sidar Akyüz informs the wider Café Beam group, whose four London cafés have made a name for themselves with all-day menus also drawing on wider Middle Eastern and Mediterranean influences. Their Canary Wharf outpost, however, offers a different proposition, bringing dinner service, Turkish mezze and charcoal-grilled meats to the table alongside cocktails and a carefully curated wine list. There’s a modern polish to the interiors – the back wall is lined with vintage vinyls, while patterned upholstery and tables and chairs with playful angular and curvaceous lines give the space personality. Start with dishes like the mücver, crispy spinach, leek and feta fritters with a golden, crunchy exterior giving way to a softer, savoury filling offset by the cool, garlicky tang of cacık. The seafood cigar börek is another crowd-pleaser, with crisp filo and a delicate cod and prawn filling, with a cured lemon and dill labneh sauce adding a bright, creamy lift. For larger groups, the Beam mixed platter is the way to go, bringing together Adana, chicken şiş, lamb şiş, chicken wings and chicken beyti, alongside grilled Turkish pide, bulgur and salad. The charcoal brings a smoky edge to the meats, all thoroughly seasoned for a robust, spiced hit. The menu also covers Turkish classics such as içli köfte, a bulbous bulgur shell filled with spiced minced lamb and onions. For dessert, the Beam baklava puts a playful spin on the Turkish restaurant staple. A layer of fluffy pistachio mousse brings a light, creamy contrast to the crunch of crisp filo and nuts, making for a particularly pleasing interplay of textures. It’s also worth exploring the Turkish wines, still comparatively underrepresented on London wine lists. For example, the Sevilen Plato Öküzgözü offers intense dark fruit flavours with cherry and blackberry notes. Address: 7 West Lane, Canary Wharf, London E22 3AA Opened at the start of the 90s by Ali Dirik, who had moved to London from Istanbul in 1987, Mangal Ocakbaşı helped introduce London to the pleasures of traditional Turkish charcoal-grill cooking, long before Dalston became a destination for the capital’s food lovers. Still a firm favourite today, its bright red signage is a local landmark, just a few minutes’ stroll from its younger sibling, or perhaps cousin, Mangal 2. Inside, brickwork and arched details set the scene for a no-frills dining room that’s still homely and welcoming. The menu is comprehensive, spanning Turkish staples from lahmacun – thin, crisp flatbread topped with minced lamb, onion and peppers – to falafel, simmered vegetable stews and sarma stuffed with rice and pine kernels. But the main event is, of course, the kebabs and charcoal-grilled meats. A smoky aroma hits as you walk through the door, courtesy of the enormous mangal at the entrance. The lamb şiş, or çöp şiş, is a particular highlight, with succulent pieces of meat with a rich, savoury depth from the charcoal, while the chicken beyti – minced chicken wrapped in lavash – is tender and delicately garlicky. For a more substantial feast, order a mixed grill and let the kitchen show off its range, with the meat arriving alongside warm bread, fresh salad and sauces that bring sharpness and heat. The lahmacun is another good choice, its thin base turning crisp around the edges beneath its savoury, well-seasoned topping. Part of the appeal here is the sense that little has changed over the years. This is a lively, often cramped room, where tables fill quickly, and queues can form outside, particularly at weekends and in the evenings. Come hungry, ideally with friends, and order generously to share. Mangal Ocakbaşı isn’t trying to reinvent Turkish cooking; indeed, its enduring success lies in doing the classics well, with the charcoal grill at the heart of it all. Website: instagram.com (walk-ins only) Right in the heart of Soho on Beak Street, yet somewhat tucked away with its understated, almost anonymous lapis blue facade, Yeni presents a refined and contemporary take on Turkish dining. It’s an offshoot of the acclaimed Yeni Lokanta in Istanbul, founded by chef Civan Er, whose approach combines a retelling of Anatolian flavours with artistic and elegant presentation styles. As a result, you can expect to sink into dishes that feel reimagined yet remain rooted in place. These plates spill outside the parameters of the familiar staples of Turkish cuisine, and whilst they’ll be something for everyone on the à la carte menu, I’d recommend the tasting menu for a comprehensive immersion into the restaurant’s innovative, artisanal style. The signature yeni manti transforms the meat-stuffed dumpling favourite, serving crispy, bouncy dumplings in a brothy fermented yoghurt sauce. Decorated (and seasoned) with jewel-like dots of full-flavoured emerald green and amber oils, it looks like a pretty kaleidoscope. Other favourites include fried kelle (a briny Turkish aged sheep’s milk cheese), wrapped in crispy yufka (similar to filo) and lathered in honey that’s heady with thyme, a square of grilled aubergine salted with Colston Bassett cheese and smoked almonds that's sweetened with port and fig, or the fleshy orkney scallop on clay-coloured muhammara with salty fingers. The setting is minimalist yet warm, with exposed-brick walls, soft lighting, pastel green tiled tabletops and open shelves displaying jars of spices and preserves. One for dates, groups, or solo dining alike. The Counter on Soho’s Kingly Street is chef Kemal Demirasal’s second London venture, on the heels of his successful Notting Hill debut. What distinguishes this site is its sleek and cosy subterranean bar. Fitted with a quality sound system, it makes for a nice listening space, where you can sink into vinyl playbacks or DJ set evenings. You’ll find bar staff shaking up cocktails with inventive touches, such as the ‘Cardamom Whispers’, bringing together fig leaf soda, cardamom-infused gin and lemon and white pepper cordial. Strokes of ingenuity run through the food menu in the main restaurant too. For instance, the white chocolate baba ganoush retains its signature smokiness, blending this with complementary hints of sweetness. As well as showcasing Anatolian flavours, dishes draw on Greek, Levantine and Aegean coastal influences. Hence you’ll find plates like a sweet and salty mastelo cheese saganaki with thyme, truffle honey and pistachios and livened with mango, or herby, smoky prawns cooked in metaxa spirit, as well as Turkish sujuk with clotted cream and cherry. Other enjoyable dishes include the lamb chops with subtly saffron-scented potato puree and the moist lamb adana. Address: 15 Kingly St, Carnaby, London W1B 5PS Gökyüzü on Green Lanes has earned itself a reputation as a cornerstone of London’s Turkish dining scene. A much-loved institution in Harringay since its opening in 1999, it was founded by the Yavuz family and retains a sense of family-run charm. There’s a bustling atmosphere, ideal for larger groups, with fuss-free, flavour-packed traditional and comforting meals. As well as pide and lahmacun, the menu covers classic hot and cold mezzes, from hellim (grilled halloumi and fig jam) and sucuk (fried beef sausage) to gloriously pure and viscous hummus or fluorescent pink beetroot tarator to be mopped up impatiently with oven-fresh, springy flatbreads. You’ll also find specialties like kizmarta (seasoned fried vegetables) and sarma beyti (spiced ground meat wrapped in lavash bread) – and of course an array of grilled meats. Portions are notably generous. During my last visit, even as a group of hungry diners, it takes us some time to plough through our mixed grill platters. These are cornucopias piled high with juicy, thoroughly seasoned cuts of lamb and chicken, bolstered with rice, red-orange bulgar, charred tomatoes and long grass-green chillies. But with the deliciously savoury and smoky flavours permeating the heaps of food, we rise to the challenge eagerly. Expect queues, especially on weekend evenings. As well as being a local’s haunt, diners from further afield will cross many postcodes for this renowned hearty fare. It’s worth it though. You can also find branches in Finchley, Park Royal, Walthamstow and Kentish Town. The closure of Oklava was a huge loss to London’s restaurant scene. But thankfully chef Selin Kiazim has returned to the capital with Leydi, a plum dining room serving sophisticated and embellished renditions of Turkish favourites. Sitting within Hyde London City Hotel, the dainty decor combines pastel pink walls adorned with an eclectic collection of photography and modern art, plush sofa seating, dark wooden-framed archways, geometric tiled floors and stylish light fixtures. It’s a white tablecloth affair, with the warm and decorous service to match. So, we’ve established it’s a pretty place, but does the food live up? We were immediately impressed just by the atom alone, a dip of garlic-y yoghurt that’s as pearly bright and thick as white paint, dressed with fiery urfa chilli oil. So simple, yet so resoundingly delicious. Ruby red chilli butter is a welcome addition to the hummus, and the tarama sings with umami. The brick-sized borek comes rammed with leeks, adding sweetness to the cheesy pastry, and the mixed grill was full of succulent cuts. I’m especially relieved by the juiciness of the chicken shish especially (is there anything worse than dry chicken!). “It’s because we only use the chicken thigh,” our waitress responds when I ask for the secret. If you drink, the Sultaniye is a lovely fruity, cardamom-spiced tipple. You’ll find Firin a short walk away from King’s Cross’ swanky development, wedged into a strip of more neighbourhood-feel eateries on York Way. Named for the Turkish term for oven or bakery, the restaurant does feel like a community hearth, the intimate space being filled with convivial chatter and mainly a mix of groups and pairs. As well as accommodating solo diners, the small, curved counter is a front-row seat to the flame-filled action of the large central oven that defines the restaurant’s space, and menu. As you’d expect, there are bread-based dishes like lengthy pides with wider Mediterranean influences, such as a summer-themed pide dressed with fresh figs, rocket and cherry tomatoes drizzled with balsamic and black sesame seeds, or mini lachuman flatbreads plastered with a blend of minced lamb, diced peppers, onion, garlic and parsley. But the oven is also put to good use for bubbling claypot dishes such as a delectable lamb tandir, slow-cooked lamb that falls apart into an ultra-savoury broth of meat stock with tomatoes, chillies and piquant ezme (chilli paste), or a ridiculously tasty roast chicken, brimming with chicken stock-filled rice alongside crispy roast potatoes. The beautifully simple yet aromatic imam bayildi (stuffed aubergine) is well worth a try too, and you can wash everything down with traditional drinks like tart cherry juice, homemade ayran (salted yoghurt) or salgam (fermented turnip juice). But to leave without ordering an ample slab of the house baklava would be criminal. Both flaky and gooey, generously filled with strikingly green crumbled pistachio, and thoroughly soaked in just sweet enough syrup, as a baklava fiend, I can say it’s among the best I’ve had.

item.title: SALES: Best Espresso Machines for Coffee Nerds & Beginners (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Just a decade ago a homemade morning cup of joe in the US pretty exclusively meant drip coffee; The only people I knew with an at-home espresso machine were my friend’s very wealthy parents. Now it’s easier than ever to pull a double shot with a perfect layer of crema on top in the comfort of your own kitchen. Companies like Breville and De’Longhi offer whole slates of espresso makers, and high-end manufacturers like La Marzocco, famous for its commercial machines, have come out with home versions. At the same time, access to high-quality coffee beans is expanding. Put these two trends together and the stage is set for an at-home espresso-making boom. - Best espresso machine overall: Fellow Series 1 - Best budget espresso machine: Breville Bambino Plus - Best espresso machine with a built-in grinder: Breville Barista Pro - Best super-automatic espresso machine: De'Longhi Prima Donna Aromatic This means the barista-curious shopper is tasked with navigating a saturated, confusing market. There are tons of similar-looking machines that all have similar-sounding features (seriously, do an Amazon search for “espresso machine” and see what you get). Sorting that out is why we’re here, and hopefully why you’re here too. Keep scrolling down for more on all our top picks. New in this update: We've got two new top picks! Lelit's MaraX3, which is the least expensive machine to offer pressure profiling (for the real heads out there) made my short list as did De'Longhi's flagship super automatic the Prima Donna Aromatic, which replaces the Bosch 800 series. Best espresso machine overall: Fellow Espresso Series 1 - A professional-style machine that’s still easy enough for beginners Size: 10" x 17" x 12.25" Weight: 24.5 lb. Water reservoir size: 67.6 oz. Cup clearance: 4.5" What I love: Brewing coffee, and brewing espresso specifically, has become an increasingly nerdy endeavor. I say that without judgement as a coffee nerd myself, who pays attention to details like pressure, temperature, and proper bean storage. Since the brand began releasing coffee brewing equipment, Fellow’s calling card has always been the ability for its products to serve both the coffee-obsessive part of the community and more entry-level daily drinkers. So it is with the Series 1. The Series 1 comes with a wide range of clearly labeled presets for different roast levels or brewing styles that, once activated, just require a simple push of the brew button; as simple as an entry-level Breville machine. Those presets correspond to different brewing parameters, such as water temperature and pressure profiles. It has similar presets for milk drinks, with a thermistor (basically a milk thermostat) that automatically shuts off when milk has reached the appropriate temperature for a flat white, cappuccino, or latte. Cross-checked with my own thermometer, the thermistor’s readings were true. All those parameters are also entirely customizable. Users who prefer to tinker with their coffee or change its taste from day-to-day can input exactly what they want across every aspect of the brewing and steaming process. It’s got some smart design choices, too, like a small heater right at the group head that provides an additional source of temperature regulation for more consistent brewing. The heater and boiler system gets water to temperature quickly as well. It was ready in well under five minutes, compared to other high-end machines that can take over 20. The Series 1 also has that distinct, modern Fellow styling and comes in five different colors. Aesthetics may not be the most important part of a coffee maker, but espresso machines are big enough to call attention to themselves. So yours might as well look good. What I’d leave: It’s worth saying something about the price: While I think its performance justifies it, and it is on the low end of average for a prosumer machine, $1,500 is a lot of money. And, for as nice as it is, the Fellow has more of a mass-market feel than other espresso makers in the same price range. It’s made with more plastic than some other high-end machines. And for those hard-core hobbyists who love the levers and dials that usually control their brewing, the digital screen of the Series 1 might seem more like a video game than a coffee maker. In the long run: In the months I've used it I haven't seen any issues, and it continues to be a very easy and fun way to make coffee in the morning. The pressure profiling and feedback provided by the machine have helped me get a sense of how altering the different aspects of brewing can change and improve different beans. Best budget espresso machine: Breville Bambino Plus - Tiny footprint nice for small kitchens Size: 7.7" x 12.6" x 12.2" Weight: 11 lb. Water reservoir size: 64 oz. Cup clearance: 5" Colors: Stainless steel, damson blue, and black truffle Food director Chris Morocco is into coffee. Like, really into coffee. Packs-coffee-beans-in-his-luggage into coffee. But he’s quick to recognize that not everyone wants to do a deep dive into espresso. “I see [making espresso] as a cascading set of decisions,” Morocco says. He thinks most people don’t want to deal with too many variables when they’re making coffee in the morning (some people don’t want to deal with any variables, and for them, he suggests a Nespresso Vertuo Plus; even though it’s a pod coffee maker, it still makes what Morocco thinks is a good cup of coffee). But if you can get over the hump of sourcing and grinding your own coffee beans, he points to the Breville Bambino Plus. This machine asks very little of you—you only need to load the portafilter with beans and push a button. The Bambino Plus comes with double-walled filter baskets, so you’ll be guaranteed a beautiful layer of crema every time. What I love: You can find the above features on plenty of mid-priced espresso makers, but what sets the Bambino Plus apart is its ability to froth milk automatically. Simply place a jug of milk under the steam wand, set the level of foam you want, and push the steam button. The machine takes care of the rest. It also heats up in a flash—about five seconds—so you don’t have to wait for your morning coffee. You can make some adjustments to the Bambino Plus if you want a more hands-on experience. You can adjust the brew temperature to low, medium, or high; set your own brewing time; and switch the milk steaming to manual mode. But you don’t have to do any of that to get good coffee from this machine. What I’d leave: It’s missing a manometer—a pressure gauge—to let you know that you’re getting a shot pulled with the right specifications. We found this machine brewed consistently, but generally we prefer having that feedback available in a semiautomatic machine. Editor’s note: Older models of the Bambino Plus don’t have a hot water dispenser, and you may see that missing feature referenced online. But that’s not the case anymore! To use the steam wand as a hot water dispenser in newer Bambino Pluses, hold down the One Shot and Steam buttons. Just make sure you have something under the wand to catch the water. The best espresso machine with a built-in grinder: Breville Barista Pro - Quality Baratza burrs in built-in grinder - Relatively affordable for a nice built-in grinder machine - Grinder can jam; you need to stay vigilant! Size: 14" x 13.5" x 16" Weight: 21 lb. Capacity 8-oz. bean hopper, 67-oz. water reservoir Cup clearance: 4" This is a tough one. For years I resisted recommending anything with a built-in grinder. That’s because, in general, built-in grinders are not very good. Their burrs are lesser quality than even inexpensive conical burr grinders, and they came with comparatively few settings. The minor inconvenience of having to plug in two machines was outweighed by the consistently better coffee. However, a few years after Breville acquired grinder company Baratza, it began integrating some of the brand’s higher-quality parts in its espresso machines. Because I think the purpose of a built-in grinder is to enhance convenience and that the kind of person who chooses one is after value, I chose the Barista Pro here because it is the most affordable option that includes the upgraded grinder. What I love: The Barista Pro is, by a wide margin, the least expensive of Breville’s espresso machines to use nicer Baratza parts in its on-board grinder and has 30 settings, which, while not what you’d get from a good standalone grinder, is enough for most people to be satisfied with their shots. Beyond that it had the reliable, quality espresso of every Breville machine I’ve used. The interface is a little different than almost any other Breville espresso maker you can get right now, but it’s very straightforward to use, and, if I’m honest, I liked its low tech set up using dials and buttons rather than the touchscreens of the most expensive Breville offerings. The steam wand isn’t automatic but did produce velvety milk just the same. And the Pro has a couple other nice bits of convenience in its dedicated hot water dispenser and thermojet heating that has it ready to brew in just a matter of seconds of turning on. What I'd leave: First, know that you will have to make sure you keep the grinder clean. It can jam. That happened to me after grinding a lighter roast bean quite finely, which resulted in a clog. My experience with this particular machine is that you can use coarser settings than you might assume you'd need. Also, just remember, with the Barista Pro (and any machine with a built-in grinder) is that, if the grinder fails, you can't just send it off to get fixed. You have to send the whole machine to get repaired. When you consolidate all your coffee equipment into one piece, you risk needing to replace it all at once instead of just being able to fix the part that broke. Also, given what I said above about an all-in-one machine being for someone who prefers convenience to hardcore coffee nerdery, the fact that the Pro lacks the automatic milk steaming function of even the Breville Bambino Plus is notable. That either allows or demands (depending on your outlook) more effort and control from you, the home barista. - Most affordable pressure profiling on the market Size: 8.7" x 16.25" x 13.75" Weight: 44.1 lb. Water reservoir size: 84 oz. Lelit (purchased by Breville in 2022) took everything that was great about the MaraX that occupied this spot in my top picks previously, and added to it, both functionally and aesthetically. What we love: The X3 has the same incredibly effective heat exchanger design its predecessor did. For those not too deep in the engineering of espresso maker temperature maintenance, there are basically three options—single boilers, dual boilers, and heat exchangers. Each could get its own full post of explanation, but here's the TL;DR: A single boiler is the cheapest and slowest of the bunch. It uses one boiler to heat water both for brewing coffee and steaming milk. Dual boilers are the most expensive and fastest, with separate boilers for each of those tasks. Heat exchangers, that use copper tubes to help drop and stabilize the temperature of the brewing water, thread the needle on price and efficiency. As a result the Mara X3 brewed very consistent shots across more than a month of regular use. It has the same powerful steam wand of the original MaraX that quickly textures milk of the dairy and alt varieties, and while it doesn’t have a digital PID, it does have three temperature settings fro brewing: warm (197℉), hot (201℉), and very hot (205℉). The X3 is also “mug-friendly,” meaning it comes with plenty of clearance (4.5 inches) to fit your favorite cup under the nozzle. This was surprisingly rare in the prosumer machines we tried. The big change from the original Mara X to the X3 is the addition of “Pagaia,” a flow control system that lowers or raises the power going to the water pump by rotating a knob. Flow control lets you change the brewing pressure during a shot, and once you get the hang of it, lets you totally change the flavor of the coffee. I’ve found it particularly fun for lighter roast coffee. It’s a more advanced bit of engineering that, before now, was mostly available on much more expensive machines, which is why for a coffee nerd, it’s exciting to see it come to a more mid-level prosumer model. It has the same wonderful, tactile experience of the Mara X, operating with a substantial stainless steel lever and knobs for the steam wand and hot water dispenser, but the finishes have been upgraded with beautiful zebrawood. This is a machine that deserves to be on full display. What we’d leave: Like almost every other prosumer machine I’ve tried, it takes a while to heat up. Like its predecessor it takes almost 20 minutes from the time you turn it on until it’s ready to brew. The descaling process is also both long and laborious; it can take several hours. Compared machines with automated cleaning cycles like the Fellow, which take more like 20-30 minutes, it’s a bit of a to do. Luckily you only need to do it every six months or so. In the long run: Several months into using the X3 daily it’s proved as reliable as the original MaraX. I’ve also been pulling shots with and without using the pagaia pressure control knob, and for anyone who doesn’t want to mess with pressure profiling, it’s easy to leave it open, forget about it and operate the machine like you would any other semi-automatic espresso maker. The only unpleasant surprise was that the heavy stainless steel cap in the redesigned portafilter came loose after a couple months. It didn't fall out, but it could easily be pulled out by accident. The best super-automatic espresso maker: De'Longhi Prima Donna Aromatic Dimensions: 18.25" x 10.3" x 16" Water tank capacity: 60 oz. Cup clearance: 5.46" What we love: In general, super automatic espresso machines—the one-button wonders that grind, dose, tamp, brew, and steam on their own—are not for people looking to perfect their espresso shots, but instead for a high quality (and easy) cappuccino or latte every morning. With that in mind, the primary criteria I have for these is their capacity to make delicious milk drinks. And the De’longhi delivers, not only on the basics, but with more than 30 different drink options, both hot and cold. In my opinion, the thing that separates good automatic machines from great ones is how differentiated their milk drinks really are. For some, everything they produce drinks like a cappuccino of one size or another, which is disappointing. Why would I put up having to scroll between all those options and pay an upcharge to have them if they all do the same thing? But with the Prima Donna, the body and texture of the milk really do change based on drink selection in a way that justified the existence of all those extra settings. With respect to the coffee it brews, the Prima Donna has automatic adjustment software that will take your feedback on the taste and consistency of the espresso, and change the grind size and water temperature to produce a properly extracted shot. And while the straight shots don’t have the depth of flavor semi-automatic machines can produce when calibrated just right, the software worked and the espresso tasted good. The Prima Donna has a couple other nice design features, like a front-loading water reservoir that’s easier to remove and fill than the top-loading reservoirs lots of espresso machines have. What we’d leave: All the adjustments on the machine are digital, so you can’t actually see or feel the changes you make to the grinder. We didn’t have any issues with it during testing, but there is something that just feels a little off when you can’t verify the adjustments you’re trying to make. The cup clearance, about 5.5 inches, is also a little on the low side for something I think users may want to utilize travel mugs with. We made a lot of coffee. We brewed at least 10 shots on every machine and repeatedly steamed both dairy and oat milk as well. Machines that performed well after that initial round got continuous use over the course of a month; our top picks are still in regular use. But testing espresso makers is a little different than testing, say, nonstick pans or toasters. Even asking “what is the best espresso machine” is sort of like asking “who is the best painter.” There’s not a single answer to that question because people want very different things from their espresso machines. Some want the full, hands-on barista experience of a prosumer machine, some need an affordable and easy-to-use option, and some need something completely self-contained with one-button operation. So we picked options that accommodate a range of prices and experience levels. Does it make tasty coffee? Perhaps this goes without saying, but it’s table stakes for an espresso machine to make a shot of espresso that has nuanced flavors, full body, and a rich crema on top. Machines achieve that with the right mix of temperature (about 200℉) and pressure (about 9 bars). Don’t be fooled by listings that say an espresso maker has enough power to reach 20 bars of pressure. Typically that kind of claim is code for the fact that it doesn’t actually regulate its pressure very well. Does it steam milk well? Besides pulling shots, these machines’ other main job is steaming milk. A good steam wand should produce smooth, rich milk without large bubbles. It should also heat the milk evenly; you don’t want some milk scalded while some of it’s barely warm (we’ve had it, and it’s gross). Finally, we prefer wands that can handle alternative milks in addition to dairy. Making espresso drinks can be a finicky process—weighing your coffee beans, getting the grind right, tamping the beans with the right amount of pressure, and that’s before you even get to brewing. Anything a machine can offer to make the process easier and more reliable is welcome. That could be a quick heat up time, brewing on a timer so you don’t have to start and stop the process, or an easy-to-control steam wand for texturing milk. Here’s the bad news: With espresso makers, you get what you pay for. According to Isaiah Sheese, owner of the three Archetype Coffee shops and roasteries in Omaha, Nebraska (and a national Barista champion), “anything under $500 and you’re not going to get that great of a machine.” Generally, that’s because those machines lack things like PIDs. The Breville Bambino Plus sneaks in under the $500 mark, but it’s the exception rather than the rule. Does it look good? This sounds superficial, but whichever espresso maker you pick, it’s going to be sitting on your counter for everyone to see for years, so you should like the way it looks. We liked all these machines; in fact, several were winning picks in earlier versions of our testing. They span styles and price points, and we think they all represent good buys, even if they aren’t our top picks. Almost everything that’s great about the Lelit MaraX3 is present in the original MaraX: The great heat exchanger system, the powerful steam wand, the pleasant tactile experience of its lever operation, the beautiful styling. It’s been bested with the addition of the X3’s pressure profiling capabilities, but if that’s not something you think you’ll use, you can save yourself $300 and get this earlier model. The Victoria is a step down in Lelit’s lineup from the MaraX. It costs about 40% less, but we thought the trade-offs for those savings were too much. It’s a single-boiler machine without a heat exchanger, so we had to wait almost a full minute to steam milk after pulling a shot. And when we did steam milk, it lacked the texture we got from the higher-end model. It does have a PID controller and shot timer, which are nice features, but ultimately, we think you can get similar quality for less money with a mid-priced Breville machine. We added Lelit’s Anita into our testing mix as part of the process of reevaluating the idea of built-in grinders and found a lot to like. The grinder is stepless, meaning you can make teeny-weeny adjustments in order to properly dial in the grind for your particular beans. It’s also one of the least expensive machines we’ve tried with a digital PID controller. Most important, the espresso came out nuanced and flavorful. But there are challenging parts about using this machine. The Anita has a relatively small 250-ml boiler, which comes with its pluses and minuses. It can reach a stable temperature much more quickly than bigger, more expensive machines; we could start pulling shots in less than 10 minutes. It can also switch between pulling shots and steaming milk more quickly than most single-boiler machines. However, because the boiler is so small, the temperature drops quite quickly. That’s not great for pulling longer shots and makes steaming milk a real race against the clock. We also struggled to get enough body with dairy milk and couldn’t get oat milk to the consistency we wanted. The tamping setup isn’t great either. The machine doesn’t come with a tamper; instead, an attached plastic piece serves the purpose. You have to push the portafilter up rather than pressing down with a tamper, which is a messy process and makes an uneven puck until you get the hang of it. But, if you want the convenience of a built-in grinder, the Anita is still a good all-in-one solution, especially if you add your own tamper to your setup. We’re splitting hairs to some extent in placing any particular machine at the top of our rankings. The Bello+ here is just as worthy of consideration as the MaraX for someone looking for a prosumer machine. In fact, it has a few features the MaraX doesn’t, like an adjustable digital PID, a shot timer to help you hone your shots, and programmable pre-infusion. It also heated up faster than the MaraX, clocking in at around 11 minutes. But to us, those bells and whistles are nice to have, not essential. You can get a shot timer from an affordable espresso scale, and pre-infusion can be done manually on many machines, including the MaraX. Where the Bello+ fell short was its steam wand. It was the most powerful we tested, which made it too easy to overwork the milk. It’s also quite a bit more expensive than the MaraX, which is ultimately why it didn’t earn a top spot. That said, it’s still an excellent and consistent espresso machine. A step down from the Diletta Bello+, the Mio is another prosumer machine that pulls a nice shot and makes a nice cappuccino. The Diletta Mio uses a thermoblock heater for steam instead of the heat exchanger of the Lelit or the dual boiler of the Rancilio, which keeps both the cost and the weight a bit lower than they otherwise might be. This machine also heats up much more quickly than its competitors—under 10 minutes, which is super speedy for a higher-end espresso machine. However, we had an issue with longevity. After about six months of use, we started having trouble with the water temperature dropping. It took very regular flushing to keep things on the up and up. One other issue with this Diletta is very low cup clearance, which meant that for milk drinks, we needed to brew into a shot glass instead of the cup we intended to drink out of. This is a good first foray into a prosumer machine at a price that's lower than the Fellow Series 1. A favorite of Bon Appétit food director (and fellow traveler in coffee nerdom) Chris Morocco, the Rancilio Silvia Pro X is a lovely machine to use. It’s a dual boiler, so the water used to steam milk is always at the ready and at a different temperature than the brewing water. It has a useful pressure gauge, which a previous Rancilio model did not have, and an adjustable PID controller you can set to the degree. Ultimately, we thought both the coffee tasted better and the milk frothed a bit better using the Lelit, but we are willing to admit some subjectivity there. The Rancilio also has a more industrial look that may not fit quite as nicely in your home coffee bar. In terms of performance, though, we have no issues with the Rancilio Silvia Pro X and recommend it. A step up in features and price from the recommended Barista Pro, the Barista Touch Impress also uses Baratza M2 burrs in its grinder (the same ones used in the Baratza Encore ESP). It’s got a brilliant, color touchscreen that has presets for more than a dozen drinks. It also has Breville’s Impress tamping system designed to provide exactly the right pressure to compress the ground coffee. The tamping system also gives you feedback on how to adjust the grind of the coffee for better flavor. All that comes at a price though. The Touch Impress costs as much as many of the prosumer machines I’ve tested, though it is decidedly for beginners. We expected a lot from a $3,000 machine, and the Oracle Dual Boiler delivered. Breville’s Oracle line occupies a sort of strange space in the espresso maker world. They are, in almost every way, super-automatic machines: They grind, they tamp, they brew, and they steam milk. However, Oracle machines use 58-mm portafilters rather than the built-in spouts of a true super-auto, and you have to move them from the grinder section to the group head. The Oracle Dual Boiler is a step up from previous Oracle editions. It’s widely customizable with presets for the standard drinks we’re used to (flat whites, lattes, Americanos, cappuccinos), along with presets and instructions for newer options (espresso martinis, for example). The dual boiler means that one boiler controls brewing and one controls milk steaming, and you can do both simultaneously. That’s not so important in the home setting—it’s more of a priority in a café setting where baristas need to make lots of drinks at once. But it’s a nice feature, and by dedicating one boiler to pulling shots, it helps keep a more stable temperature at the group head. The big upgrade, though, is the Dual Boiler’s manual mode. Older Oracle machines only had single-press, automatic brewing options. If you select the manual mode, you can control things like bloom time or pre-infusion on the fly instead of preprogramming them. It still uses a touchscreen interface (which definitely takes some getting used to), but you can use the Oracle Dual Boiler more like other high-end espresso makers. After more than half a decade of espresso machine testing, one idea has become almost axiomatic: Cheap espresso machines are bad. But with this Cuisinart, that miraculously isn’t the case. At under $400 at the time of writing (and often on sale for even less), this petite machine pulled relatively rich espresso shots with a 15–20 second extraction time (on the fast side, I know) that outperformed everything else in the sub-$400 range. The EM-320 even comes with a bottomless portafilter, which is unheard of for a machine this cheap, likely because it makes it impossible to hide any cut corners or shortcomings. It’s a bold choice, and one that’s not undercut by the machine’s performance. Other nice features include a removable water tank that pulls out from the front and enough cup clearance to fit a 20-ounce travel mug. It also has a cold extraction option, which works about as well as any we tested. But if you're interested in any of these “cold” settings on espresso machines, know that across the board, they still can’t match the flavor quality of more time-consuming methods like immersion cold brew or flash chilling. The main reason the Cuisinart didn’t make our list of top picks is its steam wand, which didn’t perform nearly as well as its brewing operation. The milk texture came out uneven and typically quite thin. We still think that, for anyone who finds the $500 price for the Breville Bambino Plus high, this makes a good entry into the world of espresso machines, but making cappuccinos will take a bit more patience. The Solis Barista Perfetta Plus is a tremendous budget machine. It has an adaptive PID (though setting it requires pushing a combination of buttons à la a cheat code in an old Sega Genesis game), which is practically unheard of at this price point. The built-in pressure gauge provides useful feedback, and we have to give a hat tip to its powerful steam wand, which outperformed some machines that cost hundreds of dollars more. And finally, it has one of the smallest countertop footprints of any machine we’ve seen. Why don’t we have it recommended up at the top? We’ve seen it out of stock for long stretches, and don’t want to leave you in a lurch. Besides Breville, De’Longhi is the other big name you’ll see again and again in the $500–$1,000 home espresso machine category. The La Specialista Touch is De’Longhi’s latest answer to the Breville Barista Touch, and in our opinion, is the best offering from the brand yet. It brews nine different coffee drinks, both espresso-based and not. It helps you dial in the grind using its built-in burr grinder and measures extraction time to guide you. You can also save settings for different beans, making it easy to switch between blends and maintain consistency. The machine features automatic milk texturing, though you can switch the steam wand to manual if you prefer full control. If we had to choose, we’d say Breville’s auto-steaming works a bit better, but the Specialista Touch reliably produces five distinct milk drinks: cappuccino, flat white, latte, and latte macchiato. Like all De’Longhi machines with built-in grinders, it includes a screw-on funnel that fits over the portafilter, keeping the grinding and tamping process cleaner than what you get with many other brands. It also includes a cold extraction setting, which runs slower than most and produces a smoother-tasting coffee compared to its hot brew. It’s not a standout feature for us, but it could be useful for someone who wants to experiment with cold coffee at home. One note: During extended testing, the steam wand failed to work twice, though the issue resolved itself after turning off the machine and back on. The Infuser is a slightly older Breville model from a time before the brand included grinders on most of its machines. It’s essentially the Barista Express without a grinder, and we think that makes it a pretty strong option for its price range. It brews flavorful espresso, includes a pressure gauge, and has an adequate steam wand. The dial that toggles between steam and hot water doesn’t feel quite as nice as the push-button operation of newer Breville machines, and because it’s older, it can sometimes be a little harder to find in stores. Overall, we think the Bambino Plus presents a better package of features, but if you find one of these on sale, we say snap it up. Terra Kaffe’s super-auto machine is, hands down, the most handsome automatic espresso machine we’ve tried. The matte white model in particular gives a real modern, elegant look to whatever space it occupies. But this is not a beauty contest. Fortunately for the Terra Kaffe, it actually makes pretty good coffee (for a super-automatic machine, that is). Espresso didn’t taste flat, as it often can from super-automatics, and milk drinks frothed up nicely. This machine is also easy to fill, clean, and empty, as the water tank and grounds container both come out from the front of the machine instead of the side or the back. The TK-02 is incredibly user-friendly with a huge, intuitive touchscreen and an effective app. We will note that the standard cup of coffee, like the cups of coffee from every automatic machine we’ve tried, was underwhelming—hot and lacking in flavor. Ultimately, the reason we recommend the Bosch coffee maker instead of the Terra Kaffe is that it can brew everything the TK-02 can and then some. But if you’re in the market for a super-automatic machine, you’ll like what you get from the Terra Kaffe, particularly if you treat your kitchen as a bit of a show space for people to gather. What to make of the new release from the maker of the most aesthetic automatic machine we’ve tried? It’s light and slim thanks to the fact that it does away completely with the ability to make drinks. Having a cappuccino at the push of a button is kind of the point of these super-automatic machines, so we have to dock points right there. However, what it does (espresso shots, lungo shots,Americanos, and “drip” coffee) it does well. That short list of drinks makes the Demi more akin to a Nespresso machine than the other super-autos we tested. But it offers meaningful upgrades to the Nespresso experience (although it offers them for more than double the price). Instead of Nespresso capsules, you get to use fresh coffee beans, which, for as good as Nespresso pods taste, always makes better coffee. Within its short menu, the Demi is also much more customizable than a Nespresso machine. You can change the volume and the brewing temperature for each drink. We also think it looks more like a statement piece than any Nespresso models, though for $700, it should. The Bosch makes just as many differentiated drinks as the De’Longhi Primadonna Aromatic, the espresso is just as good, and the interface is as easy to navigate. The choice to recommend the De’Longhi over the Bosch came down to smaller design items: The water reservoir is harder to refill (something that, anecdotally, we’ve found needs to be done more frequently on automatic machines), and the milk container sticks out further, making a larger countertop footprint for a machine that’s already a bit of a space hog. If those sound trivial to you, I still recommend the Bosch wholeheartedly for anyone in the market for a super automatic machine. As we’ve continued to test super-automatic espresso makers over the years, we’ve found the new offerings from more established brands make better and better coffee. KitchenAid’s KF7 is a good example. The espresso shots came out rich and a little fruity, much like the shots we enjoyed from Bosch and Jura machines. The true test of a super-auto, as far as we’re concerned, is its performance with milk drinks, and the KitchenAid did well there too. The KF7 is the mid-tier machine from KitchenAid that comes with a milk container attached to the brew head with a hose. The flat white came out a little more like a mini-latte than we would have liked, but the cappuccino had a rich head of smooth foam. One KitchenAid feature that we’d tell every maker of a super-auto machine to consider adding is the removable bean hopper. It’s impossible to tell in super-automatic machines how much coffee is left in the hopper, and you can easily end up with half the beans you need as it runs to empty. Not only does the removable hopper solve for that, but it also makes it easy to clear away old, stale beans and replace them with fresh ones. The fancier of the two De’Longhi super-automatic machines we tested delivered once we got it dialed in. The burr grinder on the Eletta Explore has 13 settings and we found we had to set coarser for espresso than we would have thought, around 6. With the milk container attached it can make around 50 different drinks, though many of them are just iced versions of the hot drinks. The touchscreen is intuitive and provides step-by-step instructions when necessary. The water tank is big enough that a two-coffee-drinker household should only need to refill it once during a week. Both the straight espresso and the black coffee tasted a bit flatter than the drinks from the Bosch, and the foam was a little thinner. This machine can, however, make cold foam if you like iced cappuccinos. Using the Flair Pro 2 is an entirely different experience from every machine we’ve covered up to this point. It’s a manual lever machine, which means you have to heat the water and produce the necessary pressure for brewing with your arm strength. There were some messy moments as we figured out how to use it, but the Flair did produce some delicious espresso. The trick, which someone from Flair shared with us, is to allow a brief period of pre-infusion during which you don’t pull too hard on the lever. It lets the pressure build more slowly. Because of the brewing process, a lever machine like the Flair is a commitment to operate and the small 46-mm filter basket is a little tedious to fill. But if hands-on experimentation is your thing, this is a fun machine. It’s also great to travel with: It comes apart and fits into a case about the size of a large tablet. As with the Flair, it doesn’t make much sense to compare the 9Barista to say, a Breville or De’Longhi machine, because it’s a stovetop espresso maker. If you’ve ever used a Mokapot, it works sort of like that, except much better. Its boilers actually produce the correct pressure for an espresso shot, and those shots tasted better than everything except the very best prosumer models we tested. The little brewer is dense; it weighs in at almost four pounds (a mark of quality in our opinion), and if you’re up for a more manual experience, you won’t be disappointed. Some of the machines on this list performed well. Some even made delicious coffee. We also know that there are entries here that have passionate devotees. But for each one, we thought the negatives outweighed the positives enough that we’d encourage you to consider one of the espresso makers above instead. For example, the Rocket Appartamento is beloved by many, but the performance of several other prosumer machines was better and those machines cost less. The Profitec 500 took the longest to heat up of the high-end machines we tested at close to 24 minutes. It was also one of the most finicky. Dialing in a shot took the longest and the machine demanded a very precise grind and tamp that we needed to adjust sometimes on a day-to-day basis. If you’re willing to take on all that, the machine is a beautiful feat of German engineering. The look is a little steampunk for our liking, but that’s a personal thing. Like most of the prosumer machines we tried, the Rocket Appartamento uses a heat exchanger to keep water hot for brewing and steam. It’s a little slower than most, though, so there was a longer wait between brewing and steaming milk. The included tamper, which could be replaced, didn’t fit flush in the portafiler that came with the machine and left some loose coffee on the edges. It doesn’t have a PID controller (though a newer model that will get future testing does allow some adjustment) and it also has a bigger footprint than our top pick. The Express Impress was a big jump forward in technology for Breville. This was the company’s first machine to use a combination of smart grinding and tamping to let you know the grounds in your portafilter were all set for a good shot. After grinding, the machine measures whether it’s able to compress the coffee grounds with the right pressure. If it can’t compress them enough, it means the grind is too fine or there is too much coffee. If it compresses too much, the reverse is true. It worked wonderfully for a while in our testing, providing useful feedback. The espresso and milk steaming worked at the same level they do in all the mid-priced Breville machines we tested—both consistently good. The problem we ran into with this machine was that it began jamming up with lighter roast beans. We asked Breville why this is and didn’t get a definitive answer. But issues like this are why we typically stay away from espresso machines with built-in grinders. They tend not to have as many settings or as much power as standalone grinders. As noted above, Breville has been improving its built-in grinders with the same burrs used in Baratza grinders, but only on models at the Barista Touch level and above. The one caution we’d have about this machine is the same one we mentioned above about built-in burr grinders. But the Barista Express is an affordable espresso machine that makes the kind of consistent coffee Breville is known for. The grinder itself is a little annoying to adjust—you have to free-hand the grind time on a dial that is just labeled “less” and “more,” but we were able to get it in range after about 15 minutes of trial and error. The La Specialista Arte has a built-in burr grinder as well as a built-in hot water dispenser, which you can select with a dial near the group head. The steam wand wasn’t quite as powerful as those on Breville machines, but it still produced some texture to the milk. A small accessory that makes a difference is the included funnel. It attaches to the portafilter and keeps the grinding process cleaner than it would be otherwise. Aftermarket funnels are available for most machines, but it’s a nice accessory to have in the box. One thing to know about semiautomatic De’Longhi machines is that their portafilters are a slightly different size than many other machines. You could, for example, use the Solis portafilter in a Breville machine or vice versa. But the De’Longhi portafilers are deeper and narrower. We think the Specialista Touch is enough of a jump forward that we recommend it, but if you are sticking to this simpler interface we’d recommend a Breville. Casabrews is one of the brands that frequently shows up as an affordable espresso alternative to Breville on Amazon results pages, and if you’re intent on a true budget espresso machine, it will produce reasonable results. The Neutron Pro, one of Casabrews higher-end machines, has several features going for it. It uses a 58-mm portafilter, which nothing else in this price range does. It also has a digital pressure readout, automatic Americano setting, and an interface that allows easy adjustment of brewing and steaming temperature. The espresso was better than what we’ve come to expect from lower-priced machines, coming out sweet and smooth, if a little thin. The machine is quite light and the removable water tank felt thin enough we could crush it in our hands, but that’s the sort of trade off we’d expect for something that costs about 40% less than the Breville machine it resembles. The one real drawback of this machine was its milk steaming. It uses a thermometer built into the steam wand to let you know when the milk has hit the temperature you want, but when we measured milk temperature with our own thermometer we found that it heated unevenly. It also lacked the structure we want for a cappuccino, perhaps because of that uneven heating. The wand struggled even more with oat milk, producing almost no body at all. In our product testing, Ninja has distinguished its products by giving them two main features: They are less expensive versions of their best-known competitors (think this blender instead of a Vitamix) and they have some quirky extra capabilities (think this double stack air fryer). Ninja’s entry to the semiautomatic espresso world fits right in. It is clearly here to offer a less expensive option to the Brevilles and De’Longhis of the world and, in addition to espresso drinks, it also claims to do drip coffee and cold brew. The Luxe Café Premier does indeed deliver tasty espresso shots. It also effectively uses similar smart grinding to the Impress series from Breville that figures out the right grind for you. But there’s a little too much going on. The drip coffee tasted fine, though not as good as what we get from top drip coffee makers. The cold brew tasted a bit flat instead of rich and smooth. The real problem (and the one that kept us from considering it as a budget pick) is the Ninja’s milk frothing. In addition to steam, the milk jug uses a built-in whisk to stir the milk like standalone milk frothers do. The result was a lot of bubbles and not much body in either dairy or alt-milks. Let’s start with the good for the Philips Barista Brew: It has a heavy, 58-mm portafilter (the same size you’ll find on true high-end machines), it has a high quality steam wand that repeatedly produced thick, smooth tops for our milk drinks. It also has a built-in Americano button. This machine had one major issue though: The built-in grinder couldn’t grind fine enough to generate enough pressure to pull a satisfactory espresso shot. We’re quite sure the problem was the grinder because when we used a Fellow Opus and a Baratza Encore ESP to try this machine we were able to pull delicious shots with the right pressure. The Gaggia Classic Pro shows up as a top pick on a lot of other lists of best espresso machines, probably because it has the look and feel of a prosumer machine at an entry-level price. It’s the least expensive machine we tested that comes with a 58-mm portafilter, and it has a nice steam wand too. It’s a single boiler machine, though, so be ready to wait between brewing and steaming. One disappointment with the Gaggia we tested was that, despite many quality parts, it came with a cheap plastic tamper. We couldn’t get a good tamp and all the espresso we made using it came out under-extracted. Using the Gaggia is also a full analog experience. You start and stop the brewing and steaming process by flipping a switch. That’s not a knock on the machine—it’s how the Lelit, the Dilettas, and many nice espresso machines work. We mention it because someone buying a machine at this price point might be expecting the automatic stop that comes with something like a Breville machine, and you won’t get it here. Overall the Gaggia is fine, but we prefer Lelit’s machines—for an extra $150 you could get the Lelit Anna, which offers the same functionality and a digital PID controller. Like Casabrews reviewed above, Gevi is another perpetual top seller on Amazon. But unlike the Casabrews Neutron Pro, we didn’t find anything redeeming about Gevi’s coffee. It’s tiny portafilter only came with double-walled filter baskets, and even though using them produced readings in the “espresso” range on the pressure gauge, the shots themselves tasted over-extracted and bitter, with no body and a crema that dissipated almost instantaneously. The steam wand produced jugs full of disappointingly bubbly milk. Even with the bargain basement prices we think you should skip this one. As a rule we expect very little from espresso machines that cost less than $200 because they tend to lack the temperature and pressure control needed for good coffee. But the Cuisinart surprised us. We pulled shots with nice crema on top (the machine only came with double-walled filter baskets, though, so it was kind of cheating). The steam wand was a bit overpowered and tough to control (again, an issue when you don’t have good temperature and pressure regulation), but did produce a headier foam than most other machines around this price point. No crema, over-extracted espresso, and an irritating steam wand that was almost always in the way during brewing; it’s features like these that scare us off cheap espresso machines, and they’re all present on this De’Longhi. The milk foam was also so thick we could almost cut it with a knife. The Dedica looks like it should be a nice machine, but it felt cheap and was mostly plastic. That wouldn’t have to be a dealbreaker, but the espresso also lacked much flavor. We actually prefer capsule coffee from a Nespresso VertuoPlus, which costs around the same amount of money. If you’re looking for something less expensive we’d point you either to that, the Solis Barista Perfetta, or Cuisinart’s EM-320. Hamilton Beach makes some good inexpensive small appliances—toasters and kettles, for example—but this is not one of them. We hesitate to call what was on top of the espresso shots crema. It was closer to pudding. The steam wand couldn’t evenly heat the milk: Some of it badly scalded before everything in the pitcher was heated through. The Philips Lattego was easy to use, perhaps because it can only make five different drinks. The espresso wasn’t super flavorful, but it wasn’t bad. The issue with this machine wasn’t with its coffee, it was with its milk. The milk came out with very little texture, regardless of whether we made a latte or a cappuccino. What else do you need to make espresso? Unless you go the super-automatic route you will need to tamp your own coffee grounds. A spring-loaded tamper, like these from Normcore, will ensure you tamp with the right amount of pressure every time. Just double check that you have the right size tamper for your machine. For Breville or Solis machines like we have listed above, you’ll want a 53.3-mm tamper (sometimes listed as 53 mm or 54 mm). For prosumer machines like the MaraX or Rancilio Silvia, you’ll want a 58-mm tamper. Any coffee machine is only as good as the coffee grinder you use alongside it. That’s because it takes a fine, even grind and you need to be able to make very small adjustments to the grind size to get the texture just right. There are now some good entry-level espresso grinders that will get you what you need without breaking your budget. We’ve gotten great results from both the Fellow Opus and the Baratza Encore ESP. Because espresso takes such a fine grind, the coffee grounds can clump up, preventing water from running through them evenly. You use the needles on a distributor to break those clumps up before tamping. A few important espresso terms: Good espresso makers are precise, complicated instruments, so I want to lay out a few terms that usually come up in any discussion or comparison of different machines. Semi-automatic espresso machine: These are machines that require you to actually load a basket with finely ground coffee beans and lock it into place. Some semi-automatic machines operate on timers and will stop brewing themselves, others require you to push a brew button or move a lever to start and stop the process. All of them use pumps to generate the pressure needed for great espresso. Super-automatic espresso machine: Super-automatic machines do all the work for you.
