They have built-in grinders, tampers, and brewing processes. All you have to do is place your cup under the spout, push a button, and wait. Manual espresso machine: A machine that does not have a pump. All the pressure is generated by you during the brewing process. Prosumer: A portmanteau of professional and consumer used to refer to high-end espresso machines (it’s also used for other quasi-professional home appliances like Vitamix blenders). Prosumer models usually offer similar functionality to machines you find in specialty coffee shops, just in smaller packages. Filter basket: The little mesh basket that you put ground coffee into. A single-walled filter basket lets coffee flow through all the little holes in the mesh. A double-walled filter basket has an extra layer of metal over the mesh that forces all the coffee through in one spot and guarantees the correct pressure for espresso, making it easy to achieve a lovely layer of crema on top. Portafilter: The handled piece that locks the filter into your espresso machine. Snap your filter baskets into the chamber at the front, then twist the handle to lock the portafilter onto your machine. Group head: The part of the machine that dispenses water. It’s what you lock the portafilter into. PID controller: This stands for proportional-integral-derivative, which sounds like something out of a frightening college level math course…and it is. But, for our purposes, a PID controller is like a super accurate thermostat. It provides precise temperature control for your brewing water and keeps it consistent. Tamp: The act of compressing ground coffee into the portafilter with a tamper. Steam wand: A pipe on the side of an espresso maker that shoots out high-pressure steam for making milk drinks like cappuccinos and lattes.

item.title: SALES: The 38 Best Restaurants in Barcelona, According to a Local Food Guide
item.description:
Source: Eater
From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year. Despite Barcelona’s famed cuisine, it’s also easy to have a downright disappointing meal if you settle for any old paella-slinging bar along Les Rambles (known in Spanish as La Rambla) or La Barceloneta. (Tip: If a restaurant has to pay someone to stand outside and hassle pedestrians, the food isn’t worth it.) The 38 Best Restaurants in Barcelona, According to a Local Food Guide From local Catalan cuisine to a burgeoning global food scene, here are the best meals in Barcelona right now Start with some classic tapas and paella (both great but neither entirely Catalan) and be sure to seek out local gems like bittersweet vermouth, seasonal seafood, and homestyle Catalan cuisine. But after writing and revising this list for nearly a decade, I have to insist you don’t overlook the city’s burgeoning global cuisines; save room for Calabrese paninis, Northeast Asian sharing plates with natural wines, towering fried chicken sandwiches, South Indian fish stews, and nose-to-tail yakitori. We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Barcelona dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30. New to the map in October 2026: Lluritu, a Mediterranean marisquería with three locations across the city; a parallel universe of Catalan culinary history in a former water bottling plant at Franca; and the trendy modern Catalan cuisine of Manda Huevos. Sam Zucker is a freelance writer, photographer, filmmaker, travel Instagrammer, and gastronomic tour guide in Barcelona. He has contributed to Monocle, National Geographic’s “48 Hours” guides, Culture Trip, and Vice Travel, among others. Simplicity in concept but perfect execution is what pushes Bemba to the top of the smash burger heap. The menu is brief, with just three burger options: regular cheese, double bacon, and the house special Bemba Burger, which comes with chimichurri and a smashed patty of chorizo criollo sausage in addition to the standard beef patty. Bemba has cultivated a flock of loyal regulars with the conscious selection of quality ingredients, fast service, and careful caramelization of each smashed patty. There’s also a beet and quinoa smash burger, great fries, cold draught beer, and homemade pickles — what more is there to ask for? Know before you go: It’s small so get there early, or order your burgers for takeaway and eat them in the beautiful Plaça de la Virreina just a few blocks away. Open for: Lunch and dinner; closed Monday and Tuesday An offshoot of Mantequerías Pirenaicas, whose truita de patates (Spanish omelet) is famous throughout the city, La Fonda de Pirenaicas is founder Miguel Puchol’s homage to the slow-cooked and indulgent dishes his own grandmother used to prepare; a place to sit and enjoy the flavors of honest Catalan home cooking. With a prime location at the epicenter of the Gràcia neighborhood, “La Fonda” specializes in stews and braises, with a star dish in the macarrones de la iaia Alberta (Grandma Alberta’s macaroni): a gratin of penne pasta tossed in a rich meat ragu and topped with cheese that is melted and caramelized under the searing broiler. Trying at least one of the estofats (stews) is a must — the chickpeas with black sausage and egg, for example — but don’t miss the small plates and tapas, either Here you can find Catalan classics like grilled artichokes with cured egg yolk, bombas, esqueixada de bacalao (a refreshing salad of chilled salt cod pieces with olives, onion, and tomato), and of course, the legendary truita de Pirenaicas. Know before you go: If you enjoy La Fonda de Pirenaicas, try the affiliated Brasa de Pirenaicas literally next door, specializing in grilled meats. Barcelona is in the throes of a natural wine renaissance, and Masa Vins is opening some of the most interesting bottles in the city. The cuisine of co-owner chef Antonella Tignanelli is rooted in the Mediterranean but globally inspired. Delicate dishes like seabass crudo with mandarin oil and sumac share space on the menu with bar snacks like the kimchi grilled cheese “bikini.” Brimming with youthful energy, Masa Vins was created by Tignanelli and co-owner Dani Bajc to be a place to hang with friends, drink unique wines, listen to music, and eat excellent food. Of the 250 natural wines on the list, there’s an emphasis on Eastern European labels, and the food menu changes every three months with the seasons. Know before you go: The place is nearly always busy and there aren’t many tables, so get there early or expect to wait. Groups bigger than five people can book a table between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., exclusively through Instagram direct message. From restaurateurs Majid and Mani Alam along with Bilal Khan, Achaar Bar is part of the growing roster of restaurants under the Alam Brothers umbrella. Their latest is an Indian canteen and natural wine bar named for the ubiquitous South Asian pickled vegetable condiment (which they make in-house). The menu spans the breadth of India, as well as adding in some Pakistani favorites like the Lahori samosa, a nod to the Alam brothers’ Punjabi roots. The 150 natural wines on offer have been curated by sommelier Irene Cavalli to pair excellently with the bold seasoning, heat, and aromas of dishes like Kima Mutter Pav (spicy ground beef with peas and brioche bread), spicy coconut prawns, Madrasi vegetables, and Goan fish curry. This kitchen has breathed new life to a space that was once a warehouse, embracing the stripped-down post-industrial aesthetic in Poblenou, a district akin to the Brooklyn of Barcelona. Order as much as you can; the menu isn’t huge, so with a handful of friends you might be able to try it all, and you’ll be happy you did. Must-try dish: If you’re a meat eater, don’t miss the tandoor-roasted lamb chops, the unassuming star of the menu. Shoronpo is one of the most popular ramen spots in the city, and it’s equally famous for the eponymous soup dumplings, which are the Japanese version of xiaolongbao. Fillings range from classic minced pork to foie gras, and there is even a dessert shoronpo with chocolate, olive oil, and sea salt. The ramen comes in 10 varieties including three vegetarian options, but the star is the rich and creamy tantanmen with sesame-laced chicken broth, ground pork, and springy noodles that chef Keita Tanaka may have introduced to Barcelona. Booking can be done online and is a must, and keep an eye out for a new location outside the Estació Sants train station soon. Must-try dish: The karaage (fried chicken) and the yude ebi wantan (boiled shrimp dumplings in sichuan chili sauce) should not be missed. The team at pizzeria Sartoria Panatieri focuses on seasonality, artisan production, and ingredient provenance, taking the pies to a whole other level and making this one of the hottest spots in the city; in fact, they were awarded the title of 2nd Best Pizza in the World in 2024 as part of the the Best Chef Awards. This self-described “farm to pizza” restaurant meticulously selects every ingredient that graces their creative pizzas. Tender crust from local, organic flour is the base for toppings like sobrasada with Mahón cheese, wild fennel, honey, and mozzarella; adobo pork jowl with celeriac puree, smoked mozzarella, and Brazil nuts; or apple compote with bleu cheese, celery, freeze-dried apple, and caramelized almonds. Make sure you try their house-made salumi as well, especially the papada and the Gascón pork tartare. Know before you go: The location on Carrer de Provença is the flagship location with the most creative and seasonal pizzas, while the location in Gràcia on Carrer de l’Encarnació serves popular classic pies. Don’t be misled by the old-school appearance and simple menu at Ultramarinos Marín. Seats at chef Borja García’s open kitchen are among the most sought-after in the city, and for good reason. This humble-looking asador (grill-centric restaurant), only open for breakfast and lunch, is a temple of product-driven Catalan cooking, dedicated to holding classic recipes to the highest standard. Through his training at the iconic Etxebarri and Noma, García works magic with minimal ingredients, a hot plancha, and a smoldering wood-fire oven. The myriad preparations include grilled langoustines, braised pork shanks, mackerel in escabeche, stewed snails, massive steaks, smoked beef tongue, funky garum, and briny sea urchin toast. Don’t miss the fish charcuterie or the simple yet extraordinary grilled smashed potatoes with garlic alioli. Know before you go: In April 2025, García opened Ultrapaninos Marín next door, a casual sandwich shop and grocery selling some of the house products, from pickles and garums to T-shirts. Don’t miss out on the street-style hot dogs. Chef Rafa Panatieri, of the Panatieri-Sastre chef duo, loves to say that of all the carefully imagined and artfully presented dishes at Brabo, everyone remembers the bread. Grilled in a pan over glowing coals and served with smoked butter, this unforgettable starter is even better when enjoyed with the salumi that Panatieri and fellow co-owner Jorge Sastre have perfected at their award-winning Sartoria Panatieri pizzería. Most dishes — grilled quail with young garlic, chuletón steak of thickly-marbled Friesian, spring peas with white sobrasada sausage, whole-roasted fish of the day — pass over the grill in Brabo’s kitchen, which is open to the intimate and dimly-lit dining room. Must-try menu: Opt for the 90 euro tasting menu which includes snacks, appetizers, main dishes, and dessert (the quivering flan with quince caramel should not be missed). Open for: Dinner on weekdays, with lunch on Friday; closed weekends Berbena is a leading reference in the blossoming world of chef-driven, modern Catalan cuisine in Barcelona. Take a seat at one of the handful of tables, and begin your meal with hearty chunks of sourdough smeared with rich, smoked butter. Then dive into the assortment of seasonal small plates featuring whatever is fresh that day, from monkfish cheeks with cod tripe pil-pil and beef tongue with bustard, to guinea fowl with parsnips in a Catalan vi ranci sauce and artichokes with truffle; vibrant vegetables often play a starring role in the nightly specials. The cheese selection is impressive, as is their list of the over 600 wines, with more than 30 of them served by the glass. Linger over dessert as you enjoy excellent coffee from nearby SlowMov specialty roasters and espresso from the gleaming La Marzocco machine. Know before you go: The restaurant has a policy of no children under 12 years old allowed so keep this in mind if traveling or dining with children Parking Pita is a virtually unmarked restaurant in the corner of what was once a cavernous parking garage. The team uses a wood-fired oven to bake fresh pitas for their popular falafel and shawarma sandwiches. The menu is packed with Mediterranean and Levantine dishes, but also includes forays into North Africa and South Asia — sweet potato and parsnip latkes, Harissa-topped French fries with roasted garlic mayo, beet hummus dotted with pine nuts and feta, grilled leeks with hazelnut dukkah, and roasted cauliflower with curry and pistachios are all great starters. The pitas range from falafel with pickled cabbage and lamb kofta with sumac, to chicken tandoori and charcoal-roasted lamb shawarma. Diners sit at a long communal table and service is quick, making it a popular lunch spot for the neighborhood working crowd. Know before you go: Parking Pita is just a small part of the Parking Pizza concept —- the excellent and innovative pizzeria at the back of this same, former parking garage. Try their pizzas at several locations around the city, or seek out the massive, grilled ribeye at Parking Sotano, their chic underground steakhouse in Sarrià-Sant Gervasi. Rooq makes everything in-house, from the herb breading, tangy marinade, fermented pickles, and pillowy brioche buns for their fried chicken sandwiches, to their side dishes and brownies. The menu is minimal: chicken nuggets, salads, and sandwiches. All the chicken sandwiches (fried, spicy fried, grilled, or the new Sichuan-style hotpot flavor) are made with juicy, corn-fed Catalan chicken breasts, and . vegetarians can choose from jackfruit or tofu in either nuggets or sandwiches. Pick your main course and round out the meal with twice-cooked fries tossed in the house spice blend and a side of coleslaw (vinegar- or mayonnaise-based). There’s also a wide selection of craft beers and seven house-made dipping sauces. Know before you go: On Monday and Tuesday nights, the restaurant has fried chicken wings with special flavors that change weekly. Seyma Ozkaya Erpul is originally from Turkey but has called Barcelona home for over a decade. She left her previous career as an engineer and marketing professional to pursue her passion for great food and design, opening the first Funky Bakers in the heart of El Born. While that original location remains a popular takeaway coffee shop, the full Funky Bakers experience can be had at the Eatery and Deli location in Eixample. One side is a highly curated gourmet grocery, gift, and coffee shop, while the other is a bistrot serving colorful and creative dishes from around Northern Europe and the Mediterranean, all paired with natural wines. Know before you go: If you find yourself in the neighborhood of Poble Sec, check out the new Funky location inside the chic Hotel Brumell, with a beautiful interior courtyard tucked away from the busy city center. Founded in 1898, this family-run colmado has long been one of the most iconic gourmet shops in the city. With an impressive stock of over 200 cheeses and a huge selection of wines, conservas, and cured meats, the famed dry goods store was renovated in 2022 to accommodate an array of high bistro tables, as well as a more formal dining room tucked away behind storeroom doors. The kitchen, led by chef Jordi Vilà of Michelin-starred Alkimia, offers a take on Catalan cuisine that is both elegant and nostalgic, with dishes like wild sea bass tartare with sour cream and caviar, stewed mushrooms with poached egg and zucchini panna cotta, and lamb shoulder braised with Chartreuse. Know before you go: There are two dining areas, each with its own booking system: the less-formal Colmado Múrria shop space with high tables, and the backroom Rerebotiga with low tables and tablecloths. Mikan comes up again and again when locals in the know are asked about their favorite spots in the city. Serving what the team calls Northeast Asian cuisine, the project, created together with partners Woody Wang and Arthur Holland Michel, is an evolution of various businesses — private dinners, a lunchbox delivery service, homemade chili crisp — that chef Dan Jin (who goes by Tan) developed at the start of the pandemic. Chef Tan has a particular passion for the dishes of her native region of Northern China, but she also loves the flavors of Japan and Korea. Mikan is a bargain for lunch, when a fixed-price menu includes a variety of dishes, soup, and dessert (including vegan and vegetarian options). In the evenings, the exciting a la carte menu is perfect for sharing. Dishes like grilled koji-cured mackerel with green onion oil, daikon, and shiso, spicy beef salad with cilantro and chile, or Iberian pork loin katsu are paired expertly with an eclectic selection of natural wines, all from small European producers. Know before you go: One Saturday per month, the bar features rotating local DJs starting at 11 p.m., and there are often collaboration nights with unique, thematic wine pairings by visiting sommeliers, so keep an eye on their Instagram. The exposed stone walls and traditional Catalan vaulted ceilings of the former water bottling plant that now houses Franca set the scene for what its founders call “invented local cuisine.” The kitchen imagines a parallel universe of Catalan culinary history, delivering dishes inspired by regional classics updated with creative twists. The food is unpretentious yet elegant and modern, forgoing fine-dining clichés like spherifications, heaps of microgreens, and overwrought plating. Instead, the menu focuses on fine-tuned, deeply flavored sharing plates that look deceptively simple, from a custardy Passard egg served in its shell with concentrated garum and local ratafia liqueur, to a salad of ten heirloom Spanish bean varieties, grilled monkfish tail with roasted pepper sauce, and the cuttlefish bikini — a sandwich reminiscent of shrimp toast made with cuttlefish paste pan-fried between crisp bread and served with a smoked pork demi-glace. Must-order dish: If visiting with a group, order La Festa — a large roasted sharing platter featuring suckling lamb shoulder or pork collar depending on the season, served with seasonal side dishes like tomato and peach salad with charred onions, pork belly skewers, grilled green beans, or roasted potato terrine. Open for: Dinner, with lunch on Fridays and Saturdays The Palace hotel, which first opened as the original Ritz Barcelona in 1919, still dazzles with opulent, old-world decor, making it a perfect stage for chef Rafa Zafra’s homage to classic fine dining. Zafra, former head chef at El Bulli, has come to be known for his elegant and simple approach to seafood at his lauded restaurant Estimar, but at Amar the preparations and presentations are decidedly more ornate; there is even a section of dishes inspired by the original Ritz hotel restaurant. The menu also has a section of dishes that pay homage to chef Albert Adrià, as well as top-quality seafood, seven dishes highlighting caviar, a handful of modern Catalan mains, whole grilled fish and steaks, vegetable sides, and Mediterranean tapas. Must-try menu: There is currently a special menu celebrating the 175th birthday of César Ritz himself, in addition to the standard 12-course tasting menu. Born in Uruguay and trained in Basque, Spain — both centers for meat in their own right — chef Joaquín Ignacio Sánchez is at the helm of Carnal, a Barcelona boho take on the traditional Spanish steakhouse. At this buzzy spot, hefty cuts of dry-aged beef are charred over oak embers, served medium-rare, and finished at the table on a searing-hot stone slab, allowing diners to dial in their preferred doneness. The steaks on offer come from around the globe and are aged in-house between 45 and 150 days, with prices that range from accessible to wildly extravagant; the menu’s most luxurious item is the 120-day-aged, 2-pound ox chuletón (bone-in rib-eye) from the legendary Bodega El Capricho near León, Spain. Before the main event, warm up with some American black angus beef cheek croquettes, flame-grilled maitake mushrooms, or A5 wagyu tartare kissed with a blowtorch and served over a caveman-esque length of roasted bone marrow. For those who don’t partake in red meat, there is a decent selection of seafood, poultry, and vegetable dishes, providing some welcome balance. Must-try dish: Do not overlook the “Jamón de vaca Rubia Gallega,” marbled beef from Galicia cured in the style of Iberian ham, which yields intense flavor and fat that dissolves on the tongue. Chef Rafa Peña’s passion for food is as great as his disregard for formality and fine dining accolades. A favorite among the city’s chefs, Gresca is a must-visit for lovers of nose-to-tail cooking who want to experience the best of seasonal Catalan cuisine without the stuffy service and delicate portions of some Michelin-starred restaurants. The menu can change from day to day, but there are some mainstays that every first-timer at Gresca should experience, such as the roasted chicken with fines herbes, the calf’s brain with butter and lemon, the pan-roasted sweetbreads, and the grilled quail. Know before you go: The best seats in the house are at the open kitchen pass, where diners get a front row view of the action. It’s worth calling the restaurant to reserve your spot, since they don’t provide this option when booking online. In an antique bar space with over 100 years of history, on a coveted corner in one of the trendiest parts of the Eixample, Soma opened in 2021 to instant accolades from the gourmands of Barcelona. Cozy decor and a Parisian-style terrace set the stage for a menu of Catalan tapas with a strong Italian character and hints of France. Look for veal liver with onion and red pepper jam, socarrat de risotto (a risotto cooked until compact and crispy like the bottom of a classic paella) with kale and honey, octopus with bacon and paprika potato purée, and ragu-stuffed rigatoni. Best for: Soma is known as a vibey spot for lunch or dinner, but weekday breakfasts on their tiny outdoor terrace with coffee, pastries, and sandwiches make a perfect, slow morning. Created by Priscilla Alfaro, a Mexican American woman who grew up in Los Angeles, with her partner Gaston Gabrielli and chef Nick Hosea, this is an excellent, modern American diner where the draw is simple: truly delicious food and bottomless filter coffee from specialty roaster Three Marks Coffee. The pancakes are fluffy, the bacon is crispy, the breakfast burrito is hearty, and the Nashville hot chicken sandwich is tongue-numbingly good. Too many brunch spots in Barcelona rely on Instagram-worthy visuals to compensate for mediocre flavors and cookery, but Gringa All Day is the real deal. Expect a line on the weekends, but the wait is worth it. No reservations. Know before you go: If you’re a fan of Gringa, check out their burger and fried chicken window at the rock ‘n’ roll/biker-themed cocktail bar Motor Oil BCN. It’s rare in Barcelona to see a classic trompo slowly, perfectly charring pork, but Xuba Tacos takes tacos al pastor very seriously. The restaurant lovingly layers spiced pork on the spit, shaves it into thin slices, and serves it on supple, handmade blue corn tortillas. Alongside classics like al pastor and carne asada, there are also modern creations, like black beer-batter sea bass tacos with crispy leeks and sauteed lobster tail tacos with cilantro emulsion. Keep an eye out for seasonal specials, like wild mushroom and roasted chestnut tacos, and don’t miss the micheladas. Best for: For a great deal, opt for their weekday fixed-price lunch menu that includes a starter of guacamole, three tacos of your choice, and a drink (water, soda, or beer). With no signage or any identifying information visible from the street, the small Suru Bar makes meals in its intimate space feel like serendipity. A row of counter seating gives diners a view into the open kitchen, where chefs prepare star dishes like grilled chicken skin skewers with chilled shrimp tartare, vibrant spring peas with smoked chorizo and cured egg yolks, and a brochette of crunchy pig ear with charred chicken gizzard and tender squid. The cuisine is seasonal, thanks to the prime location just across the street from the famous Ninot market, and the dishes range from yakitori on a traditional Japanese grill to explorations of all things offal, with an extensive wine list to round out the meal. Must-try dish: Don’t miss the grilled veal sweetbreads with a silky puree of toasted cauliflower and pickles. Crowds flock to Taktika Berri to down copious amounts of ice-cold beer and funky, sour cider while perusing the platters of pintxos that adorn the well-polished bar. Highly traditional without being kitsch, this popular Basque bar, founded in 1995, feels like it’s been transported straight from the industrial port city of Bilbao, complete with old photos and jai lai baskets. The bar area at the entrance can get packed with an after-work crowd, who graze classic pintxos like fried chistorra sausage, anchovies with piquillo peppers, and tortilla de bacalao (salt cod omelette). But don’t be deceived; the pintxos on display are just a small fraction of what the menu has to offer. Take a look at the carta and order from a selection of Basque mainstays like almejas con refrito (sauteed clams with garlic, cayenne, and cider vinegar), the two-person serving of cogote de merluza (a large center-cut piece of whole hake, roasted and served with garlic and parsley), fried monkfish loin, or a well-marbled txultetón steak. Know before you go: In addition to the cold or room-temperature pintxos on the bar, there is also a menu of hot pintxos that can be made-to-order (try the morcilla black sausage). To drink, choose a caña (small draught beer), Basque hard cider, or Txakoli (a famous, lightly-sparkling, kind of saline, low-alcohol wine from the Basque region). True to its name, eggs take center stage at this relaxed restaurant known for spins on the classic Spanish potato and egg omelet (truita de patates). In the quiet, upscale neighborhood of Les Corts, Manda Huevos combines the relaxed energy of a trendy vermutería with sharp, modern branding. Chef and co-founder Ot Salvans draws on his experience in some of Spain’s top fine-dining kitchens while bringing flavor influences from around the globe. Catalan mainstays like cap i pota veal stew, langoustine-stuffed roast chicken, and macarrons del nét (baked pasta with meat ragù topped with a broiled cheese gratin) share the menu with fusion creations like roasted bone marrow with scallop tartare, fermented lemon, and caviar, and the chili crab-stuffed eggs. The nine truita varieties on the menu range from guanciale carbonara and Menorcan sobrasada with Mahón cheese, to red shrimp tartar with shrimp jus and the signature “bomba” omelet filled with pork ragù, spicy brava sauce, and saffron alioli. Omelets come in three flexible sizes, with the exception of the open-faced garlic lobster omelet, which skips potatoes entirely and comes topped with sherry-confited piquillo peppers and lobster roe. Know before you go: Wednesday through Friday at lunch, take advantage of the fixed-price four-course meal. It includes an aperitivo, first course, second course, dessert or coffee, and a drink, showcasing many of the menu’s best-sellers. With Taberna Nardi, founder Martín Pimentel of the Grup Amicks restaurant group has traded the vibrant red color scheme and meat-heavy menu of his popular Bar Pimentel for a calming vibe of deep maritime blue just a few doors down. Nardi is a self-proclaimed “irreverent seafood tavern” with a shimmering wave-like mirrored ceiling, just a handful of tables, and an inviting bar with open kitchen where the day’s catch is displayed on ice. Try the cumin-spiked hake pincho moruno skewers off the smoky Japanese robata, the grilled zamburiña scallops with tomato confit and garlic, the delicate cured horse mackerel with ginger and jalapeño, or the surprisingly meaty braised tuna cheek with potato purée. Wash it all down with a saline-heavy white wine, a natural sparkling, or their famous oyster-infused dry martini. Must-try dish: While it may not be the immediate choice for most diners, the rich, buttery cube of toasted brioche topped with a dollop of tangy crème fraîche and a succulent cured anchovy is a single bite that should not be missed. And don’t forget the cheesecake for dessert. Since 1946, Gelida has been an important social hub for the neighborhood, be it old friends meeting for a weekend lunch or workers loading up on calories before sunrise. The menu is full of classic Catalan dishes, but the breakfast-forward spot is best known for esmorzars de forquilla, or “fork breakfasts.” In modern Barcelona, many people opt for a light breakfast (think croissant and coffee), but the tradition of beginning your day with a hearty plate of stewed veal, tripe, snails, pig trotter, chickpeas, or pork cheeks is still alive at institutions like Gelida. You’ll see heaps of fried potatoes topped with a runny fried egg and spicy chorizo on tables as life-long regulars drink cafe con leche and mini draught beers simultaneously. Must-try dish: Cap i pota, a gelatin-rich stew of veal head and hoof (though Gelida uses veal necks, which are meatier). The sauce is meant to be sopped up with pieces of crusty baguette and washed down with a house Gandesa, a golden, long-macerated white wine from the region of Terra Alta. With a wave of modern kebab shops hitting Barcelona over the last year, sometimes it feels good to go back to an all-time favorite. Carrer de Joaquin Costa is always buzzing with activity, as is its most famous kebab shop, Bismillah Kebabish, a halal mainstay in the Pakistani community of Barcelona since 2003. Crowds pack into the minimalist dining room, often sharing tables with strangers, just for a taste of the famous and affordable chicken shawarma — fresh naan that is pulled by hook from a tandoor oven and loaded with fragrant, bright-red shavings of spiced chicken thigh, carved from the spinning skewer that the team prepares daily (it’s much better than the beef version). Mixed with roasted peppers and onions and topped with your choice of fresh vegetables, chile sauce, and garlic sauce, this is the go-to meal from many regular customers. However, dishes such as the lamb curry, beef shish kebab, and the tandoori chicken skewers are also quite popular; you can even mix and match multiple dishes together on the combo plates with rice and salad. Know before you go: This is one of the last Barcelona institutions that is still cash-only, so come prepared. La Mudana is celebrating its 10th anniversary in 2025, and over the last decade it has become an anchor of the local culinary scene of Sants, a neighborhood known for its tight-knit community and support for local businesses. La Mudana is equally suited as a spot for friends to catch up over a few tapas and a beer as it is for a refined multicourse dinner. The food draws influence as much from Mediterranean and Catalan cuisine as it does from the flavors of France and Asia, with a little Latin American influence as well. Pick from dishes like the kimchi juice and comté cheese oyster, meaty cap i pota rice with teriyaki eel, ox tail-stuffed brioche with smoked sabayon, and the Iberian pork katsu sando with mole and ají amarillo, or opt for a fixed-price two-person tasting menu of six all-star dishes, plus dessert, that includes vermouth to start and cava to finish. Must-try dish: No table at La Mundana is complete without the picturesque patatas bravas — two perfectly-sculpted rectangles of potato, fried crisp and topped with classic spicy brava sauce as well as the funky black garlic alioli. This small corner bar just one block from the old port of Barcelona has been serving the same four dishes since 1945. Though the salted anchovies, fried sausage, and tomato salad are all delicious, pescaditos (fresh, floured, and fried whole anchovies) are the true star. Now run by the grandson of the original founder, Bar La Plata sells over 85 pounds of the little fishes per week. Know before you go:The place is nearly always busy and only has a few tables, so either show up right when they open, or do as the local crowd does and eat standing up at the bar or even in the street if no seats are available. Drinking alcohol outside isn’t allowed but you can get the pescaditos to-go in a paper cone. Plump pork meatballs braised in tomato sauce, creamy stracciatella cheese, grilled zucchini, and a dusting of grated ricotta salata come together in one of the newest sandwiches on the menu at Compà, a panini shop dedicated to the flavors of Calabria. In addition to the original location a few streets over from the Barceloneta beach, owner Vittorio Cicero has recently expanded with a new shop in the uptown neighborhood of Gràcia, with panini like mortadella with burrata and pistachio pesto or Calabrese lardo with spicy ‘nduja spread, smoked provolone, and roasted potatoes. Choose from nearly a dozen sandwiches including rotating specials, all served on 48-hour slow-fermented focaccia, pressed and piping hot. Know before you go: There are a few tables, but the sandwiches are meant as street food, so get yours to-go and head to the beach or the nearest plaza. Just don’t forget the napkins, and a tiramisu for dessert. One of the oldest restaurants in the beachside neighborhood of La Barceloneta, this is the birthplace of the famous “bomba de la Barceloneta,” a mouthwatering fried potato croquette stuffed with savory ground beef and topped with aioli and hot sauce, which now appears on menus all over the city. In addition to the bombas, try the calamars a la planxa (grilled squid), and in summer get the grilled sardines. If you have a taste for offal, add a plate of cap i pota, an old-school Catalan stew of tripe, veal trotters, and veal head in tomato. Know before you go: You’ll likely see a line of people waiting outside, but don’t get behind the last person. Go straight to the door instead of queuing up and ask to be put on the waiting list. They will call out names in order, no need to wait in an orderly line, just linger nearby. Suculent isn’t defined by one genre of cuisine, but packs its tasting and a la carte menus with as many delicious dishes as possible. It’s a favorite among chefs for nose-to-tail cooking and fine dining makeovers of grandma’s Catalan comfort food (with influences from Asia and Latin America). Dishes change with the seasons, but don’t miss mainstays such as the beets with beurre blanc and smoked eel, the royal custard of porcini mushrooms with sea urchin, and the braised hare canelon with foie gras and Codium seaweed. The creation of chef Victor Ródenas and brothers Ignasi and Marc García, this youthful take on a simple Catalan casa de menjars (house of food) combines the best parts of a traditional vermouth bar with the refined, seasonal Catalan cooking of a fine dining veteran. The lively yet casual atmosphere is the perfect place to enjoy the varied dishes: confit artichokes with spring peas, sunchoke puree, and romesco; escabeche oyster shooters with chicken jus; beef tendon stew with fried hake and pickled chile peppers; and mini paella with shrimp tartare and pig trotter carpaccio. This is a gathering place for neighborhood regulars first and foremost. Must-try dishes: There are always some special off-menu treats to be discovered, just ask your server. This beachside restaurant has had five different names since it opened in 1942, but has always stayed within the same family. In 2023, it was born once again as Casa Costa, a modern concept with playful branding, refined food, and natural wines that still gives timeless Mediterranean flavors and aesthetics — few places capture the true essence of Barcelona as well as Casa Costa. Start your meal with a spicy bomba croquette of potato and slow-cooked beef, clams in green sauce, or tomato salad with rosemary gelee, to be followed by star dishes like the whole roasted seabass for two with Mediterranean vinaigrette, and the pig trotter roulade with red prawns. There are always seasonal specials too, from tuna tartare with pickled summer cherries and confit spring artichokes with pancetta, to fire-charred calçots — the iconic Catalan winter onions. Know before you go: The outdoor terrace is always bustling, but the best sea views are to be had from the second-floor dining room with panoramic windows and cozy banquets. Now with three locations across the city, Lluritu’s stripped-down approach to a Mediterranean marisquería has made it a must-visit in the Barcelona food scene. Its ethos of shunning complex sauces, tablecloths, and deep fryers in favor of simple, wood-fired and planxa grilling means diners get the pure flavors of the region’s best seasonal seafood. With a fishmonger aesthetic of white tiles, marble counters, and stainless-steel serving trays paired with the energetic service of a festive neighborhood bar, Lluritu is one of the best spots in the city for grilled razor clams, zamburiñas, giant prawns, and whole roasted fish — all washed down with a cold beer or house vermouth. Don’t miss the famous polp sec (dried, flash-grilled octopus), the smoked eel and tomato salad, the crispy lluritu (a small, hyper-seasonal fish and the restaurant’s namesake), or any of the daily blackboard specials. Know before you go: While all three locations share core menu highlights, each has unique offerings, most notably the rice dishes like the squid ink-infused arròs negre and traditional suquet seafood stew, which are exclusive to Lluritu 3 on Passeig de Sant Joan. Some high-end seafood spots in the city are places to see and be seen; this intimate, traditional marisqueria is a place to eat. For nearly 30 years, the supreme quality and freshness of the fish has kept any desire to modernize or adulterate classic Catalan cuisine at bay. Just a block from Plaça d’Espanya, El Camarote d’en Tomàs displays the day’s catch on heaps of ice at the bar, an impressive sight that immediately greets visitors. Expect wild-caught fish roasted whole, grilled giant prawns, impossibly tender sauteed baby squid, clams, scallops, and plump sea urchin roe scooped from the shell and laid across a butter-smeared cracker with a dash of lemon on top. Whatever you pick, be sure to start with the superb and refreshing esqueixada de bacallà, a popular cold preparation of salt cod bathed in olive oil, tomato, and olives that is near and dear to the hearts of many Catalan people. Must-try dish: If you want to experience the legendary Spanish delicacy that is percebes (gooseneck barnacle), this is a perfect place to try them — just brace yourself for the lavish cost per kilo. Open for: Dinner, with lunch on the weekends Tiberi Bar was born from the Tiberi Club, a popular organizer for creative events and pop-ups that fuse eating and art. Tucked away on a quiet street in Poble Sec, the minimalist, airy interior, with high ceilings and plenty of windows, is the perfect scene for a rotating roster of colorful sharing plates inspired by Catalan traditions and the flavors of the Mediterranean, paired with natural wines from small local producers. Duck terrine with pistachios, crunchy polenta with sage, smoked sardine with sour cream and whole grain mustard, and a pork confit sandwich with red cabbage play upon well-worn local staples with surprising flavors. Know before you go: Tiberi Bar organizes a periodic Sunday morning special menu, dubbed Granja Tiberi, with novel takes on brunch such as croissant with ricotta, sobrassada, and honey, and fried eggs with peas, artichokes, mint, and ham. Check the Tiberi Bar Instagram for scheduling and booking info. Open for: Dinner, with lunch and brunch over the weekend At Margarit, on a narrow tree-lined street on the slope of Montjüic, Greek chef Stefanos Balis paints with broad Mediterranean brushstrokes while paying homage to his Hellenic homeland. There’s a standout list of both traditional and natural wines, with some especially interesting and potent Greek reds, which pair nicely with refined dishes dispatched from a sleek open kitchen. Favorites include the salty taramas fish roe spread with cured bonito tuna, the grilled eggplant with pistachios and honey harissa, the mini chicken souvlaki on fresh sourdough pita, and the braised lamb neck with yogurt sauce and tender root vegetables — dishes built on tradition and memory. Know before you go: Weekends are a bit different at Margarit, with a rotating daytime menu that captures the flavor and energy of a slow Sunday meal around the Mediterranean.

item.title: SALES: 11 best hotels in Colombo 2026, from Geoffrey Bawa dreamworlds to reimagined family homes
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
The best hotels in Colombo span a multitude of styles and budgets, including intimate architectural marvels, luxe global chains and old-world stalwarts overflowing with history. And while long-stay travellers to the city might prefer one of the many well-designed Airbnbs that have popped up in abundance in recent years, a vast array of Sri Lanka’s best hotels are hidden within the capital, ensuring flawless all-round bases from which to explore. Often overlooked in favour of the glossy green tea plantations, quaint south coast beach towns and the Kandy to Ella train journey that just reopened after a nearly year-long hiatus following landslides in 2025, Colombo has been quietly transforming without fuss and fanfare for decades. Today, with plenty of intriguing cultural spaces to visit, as well as top-notch restaurants like Biling and GINI, along with cool bars to hunt out (don’t miss Kampong), it’s deserving of at least a few days, if not longer. What's more, with British Airways’ newly launched direct flights connecting London Gatwick with Colombo International Airport, it’s never been easier than to hop over to Sri Lanka for a cool cultural trip. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Colombo - For an affordable stay: Galle Face Hotel How we choose the best hotels in Colombo Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We're always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. item.title: REVIEW: Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition 2026 review: Nice, but doesn't justify the price
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition 2026 review: Nice, but doesn't justify the price $320 is a lot to pay for a well-balanced device in an aluminum case with pogo pins. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. I'll be honest. I don't have much to say about the new Kindle Colorsoft. It doesn't feel like that long ago that Amazon introduced its first-ever color ereader, but that was in October 2024. At the time, the product was novel for the company, as it presented a technical challenge. How was Amazon going to offer a paper–like color reading experience while preserving the quality of a black-and-white ereader? The company used nitride LEDs and custom algorithms to finetune how lights were beamed through individual pixels to maintain contrast levels, and also made sure that pages turned faster than previous devices. The original Colorsoft only came in one color, which felt like a staid container for its relatively vibrant contents. Cut to October 2026 and Amazon has a new Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition for the world. It's a bit thinner than before, with edge-to-edge color and a new color option: Fig. With this variant, the Colorsoft's front bezels also match the rest of the case, so you won't see unsightly white or black bars like on previous models. This Kindle Colorsoft generation starts at $290, but if you pay $30 more, you can get the Signature Edition, which is what I'm reviewing here. What's new (or not so new) in the Kindle Colorsoft 2026? Everything else about the Kindle Colorsoft is basically the same as its predecessor. You're still getting a screen with 300 pixels per inch (ppi) for black-and-white reading, or 150 ppi for color. Nothing has changed about the color representation here – you still get the "vibrant" mode in addition to the standard rendering to get a bit more saturation out of your pages. I'm not a huge graphic novel reader, and most of the pops of color in my Kindle Colorsoft experience are in the book covers in my Library or when I highlight particular sentences or passages. They were pleasant little touches, but for me, the novelty of paperlike color E Ink displays has largely worn off. If I'm not reading something where the colors are actually integral to the storytelling, I don't need an ereader to deliver a broad spectrum of shades. All that is to say – the reading experience on the Kindle Colorsoft this year is largely the same as last year, minus the early troubles our reviewer (and some other people online) encountered with yellow bands on their devices. Since Amazon resolved to fix the issue, it should not impact current and new Colorsoft models, and I did not notice this during my testing. I didn't experience any obvious issues when reading on the Colorsoft either. Pricing is a bit confusing to compare, so bear with me. At launch in 2024, Amazon only made a "Signature Edition" of the Colorsoft available, and it started at $280. This year, the Colorsoft starts at $290 for the base configuration with 16GB of RAM and goes up to $320. That additional spend will get you the Signature Edition's aluminum case, pogo pins on the back, twice the storage and the choice of black or maroon. So you can say the Colorsoft costs between $10 and $40 more than before, and for that money you're mostly getting a slightly more refined flush-front design and thinner chassis. In real life, much as I appreciated the aesthetic tweak, it didn't have a huge impact on my reading experience. I never struggled to hold the previous Colorsoft (or many other recent Kindles) so the thinner body, while nice, wasn't a huge change. The new Fig finish was a nearly identical match for my Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro, though, so if you love matching your gadgets to each other, this might be worth considering. More importantly, I liked the sturdiness and premium vibe of the aluminum housing. My Kindles live in my cluttered purses, and their ability to withstand scratches is crucial. In my two weeks with the new Kindle Colorsoft, I've thrown it in my backpack with no regard for its safety, and it's still managed to remain pristine. I did decide to put a case on it midway through my testing so as not to tempt the review Gods, though, to ensure I could get a good photo of it before my recklessness marred it forever. I haven't had a chance to connect the Colorsoft to any new accessory that's compatible with its new pogo pins in the real world yet. But I can at least say that based on a short demo ahead of Amazon's launch, I enjoyed how easy it was to snap the Signature Edition Colorsoft onto a magnetic case and use page turning buttons on a cover that connected via the pogo pins. I'll need more time to judge the responsiveness, consistency and ease of use, but for now, color me intrigued. I do wish Amazon hadn't removed the ability to wirelessly charge the Colorsoft. It's so handy to just drop the tablet onto a charging stand, and those who have already bought those accessories might be miffed at the omission. That said, I never worried about charging the Kindle Colorsoft, because like most other Kindles, its battery lasts forever. I mean quite genuinely, because every time I pick up one of the many abandoned Kindles lying around in my house, they always still have juice left. I was slightly concerned when, after a day or two of focused reading, the Colorsoft's battery dipped by 10 percent to 90 percent. But then I remembered I had the same experience with the larger, more energy intensive Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. And that thing remains alive on my couch without me even thinking about plugging it in. I won't say that I've had enough time to properly evaluate the Kindle Colorsoft's battery performance, but suffice it to say that nothing in my two weeks with it has been a real cause for concern so far. Like I said, I don't read a lot of stuff that's better in color. But I can tell you that the Kindle Colorsoft is not your only option out there – Signature Edition or no Signature Edition. Our favorite ereader overall is the Kobo Clara Colour, which costs just $150. It has a slightly smaller 6-inch screen, so if that's too small and you have more money to spare, the Kobo Libra Colour is also a solid offering. It has a 7-inch screen that's a respectable color E Ink display, and costs $260 on Kobo's website. As a bonus, it has physical page-turn buttons onboard so you won't have to spend even more money on a case for that feature. However, it does only come in black or white options. At that price, the Kobo Libra Colour comes in at $30 under the Kindle Colorsoft's starting fee, and still manages to offer 32GB of storage and stylus support. The thing is, Kobo's interface and library simply can't hold a candle to Amazon's, which isn't just vast, but is easy to use across various platforms. You can browse for books through the Amazon store on your Kindle, and for anyone that's already amassed a library in one place or subscribed to Kindle Unlimited, then leaving presents a lot of friction. I also like how I can read on my phone, tablet or Kindle and my progress is synced anywhere I leave off and wherever I decide to pick back up. The Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition feels like an unnecessary splurge for me. But for anyone who regularly reads color ebooks, the Colorsoft might be a treat. Plus, if you are also a fan of the Fig color option, are locked into the Amazon ecosystem and might want to use your Kindle Colorsoft with the page-turn cover one day, the Signature Edition is a capable ereader that won't disappoint.

item.title: REVIEW: Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026) review: Updated in all the right places
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026) review: Updated in all the right places Are you willing to pay $50 more for the upgrades? We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. There's no denying the chokehold Amazon has on the ereader industry. Its library is massive and its entire lineup of Kindles are consistently reliable devices that meet readers with varying budgets and needs. As part of the company's 2026 lineup, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition ($250) sits squarely in the middle in terms of both capabilities and price. Amazon saw fit to refine an already compelling mix of design and performance, with key changes to how you use this Paperwhite as well. But as we noted with the 2024 Signature Edition, the best premium ereader may not offer any exclusive features that you can't live without. Amazon didn't try to reinvent the wheel with its updates to the more premium Paperwhite. There's now an aluminum back, but overall, it's still an IPX8 waterproof design with a high-contrast, 300 dpi display (more on the screen changes later) and 32GB of storage. The company did color match the front bezels on the Seaglass Green version so it matches the back panel. This is certainly a welcome change as it definitely looks better than previous models that had colorful cases but with gray fronts. The 2026 model is also one millimeter thinner than its predecessor — a variation you're unlikely to notice, but one Amazon will gladly tout. Amazon also moved the power button to the top right edge, a location that will be more familiar for anyone who uses a smartphone. I honestly prefer it there, because even though I've been using a regular Kindle Paperwhite since 2024, I never got used to the power button on the bottom edge. Now, the USB-C port is the only component that still resides there. Perhaps the biggest change on the 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition is the introduction of pogo pins on the back cover. Amazon ditched the 2024 model's standard wireless charging (via Qi-compatible and Amazon accessories) in favor of this arrangement. The four pins accommodate new accessories, most notably the Page Turn Cover ($80) with physical page-turn buttons, and there's also a $60 charging stand with an unknown shipping date. I should note that both of these accessories also work with the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, which has the requisite pogo pins onboard as well. In my opinion, the Paperwhite line offers the best reading experience on a Kindle. I don't need a color screen, but I do prefer the adjustable warm light and larger display over the standard Kindle. Of course, the IPX8 waterproofing is also nice to have, as I like to take the Paperwhite to the beach, and you can certainly feel safe using it during a bath or at the pool. To further enhance the overall experience, Amazon employs an oxide-thin film transistor backplane and offers a contrast ratio that it says is its highest yet. The company promises deeper blacks and crisper text on the 2026 Signature Edition compared to the previous version, although my eyes are unable to discern the difference in either of those. I couldn't distinguish between the sharpness on my 2024 Paperwhite and this new Signature model either, but I could tell them apart by the slightly warmer overall glow of the latest release, even when the Warmth slider on both Paperwhites was set to 0. Still, the Paperwhite display continues to offer the best ereader performance among the company's lineup for my money. The auto-adjusting front light feature returns, using an ambient sensor to increase the brightness in daylight or dim it at night without you having to do so yourself. Of course, you can disable this feature and swipe the slider as you see fit. There's also a new double tap gesture that allows you to turn pages by double tapping on the left and right sides. Two taps on the right edge to go to the next page, or two taps on the left to go back. I didn't use this very much, probably because I'm conditioned to just tap once on the sides of the display to turn pages (which still works here). I'll also mention there's an accelerometer in this 2026 version for automatic screen rotation, but I don't have much use for it, so I left rotation locked during the bulk of my testing. One area I wasn't able to test in the two weeks I've been using the new Paperwhite Signature Edition is battery life. Amazon says you can expect up to 12 weeks of battery life on a charge, and with past Kindle devices, I've left them unused for months and come back to enough juice for multiple reading sessions. Simply put, Kindles last for what seems like forever, and that's not going to change here. My 2024 Paperwhite has never been sluggish when it comes to downloading books or searching, but the 2026 Signature Edition seems to be slightly quicker with both of those tasks. They both wake up with equal quickness though, which is more important to me than how adept these devices are at navigating menus. If you don't like the Paperwhite, there's likely to be something else to suit your needs in Amazon's own lineup. Of course, the company's advantage over other ereaders is its massive library that's accessible right on its Kindle devices. There's also the Kindle Unlimited Kindle+ subscription that gives you access to millions of books, magazines and comics for $12 a month. That integration and convenience gives Amazon a leg up on its competition. If you prefer a non-Amazon ereader, the most recent one we've tested is the Boox Go 6 (Gen II). The Android-based device gives you access to more reading apps than a Kindle would, plus there's a microSD card slot and stylus support. This model has shorter battery life than some ereaders and there's no water resistance, so there are some trade-offs. I'll also note that we named the Kobo Clara Colour the best overall ereader in our buyer's guide. You do have to contend with a limited library here, and the screen isn't as sharp or bright as we'd like. There's still a lot to like though, from the snappy processor to the color display and access to local libraries. While the price of the 2024 version eventually went up (like everything else these days), the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is $50 more than that model was at launch. It's clear the changes Amazon made add more polish to an already winning formula, but as someone who typically uses a regular Paperwhite, there's nothing here I can't live without. The regular $200 version still packs the high-contrast display, which is the most essential element of what the Paperwhite has to offer. Unless you're someone who needs the extra storage, or just likes the idea of pogo-pin accessories and double tapping to turn pages, the Paperwhite Signature Edition is more of a splurge than an essential purchase.
